papers.abstract: DeepSearch LLM agents repeatedly search and carry retrieved sources into subsequent reasoning steps. This expanding context increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning. We propose Query-Relevant Attention Entropy (QRAE), an online context compression method that uses sparse evidence-assessment heads to decide which intact retrieved chunks should persist across reasoning steps. It scores bounded candidate batches through paired prefills: a query-free control suppresses shared attention responses, while normalized entropy measures the breadth of the positive response within each chunk. High-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist and are included in the reasoning context. Uncertain chunks remain outside the reasoning context but are retained in a candidate cache, where they can be retrieved for later reevaluation. QRAE requires neither an additional generative compression pass nor modification of the attention operator. Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively. These benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.
bullets: Targets context growth in iterative DeepSearch agents, where many retrieved sources are not useful for later reasoning.
Uses sparse evidence-assessment heads and paired prefills to score candidate chunks via normalized attention-response entropy.
Persists high-scoring chunks in an evidence whitelist; uncertain chunks remain in a cache for possible later reevaluation.
Across multiple benchmarks and reasoning models, it improves task success by 2.35 percentage points on average, while reducing latency by 30% and reported token usage by 45%.
The approach generalizes to a model with nearly 100B parameters and requires no extra generative compression pass or attention-operator changes.

papers.selection_reason: Online context compression for LLM agents via attention-entropy chunk selection, reducing token usage and latency.
papers.title: QRAE: Query-Relevant Attention Entropy for Context Compression in DeepSearch Agents
papers.tldr: QRAE compresses DeepSearch contexts online by retaining only query-relevant retrieved chunks, improving success while reducing latency and token usage.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is prohibitively expensive, making informative frame selection essential for accurate video understanding. The default uniform sampling often misses task-relevant keyframes, while recent training-free selectors instead pick frames by how well each one matches the question under an image-text alignment (ITA) score. However, we show that ITA signals correspond poorly with the MLLM's true needs: their rankings correlate weakly with downstream accuracy and are even negatively correlated on over 40% of questions, whereas the MLLM's internal yes/no judgment yields a much stronger signal. We present ProbFaS, a training- and label-free probabilistic pipeline that fuses both signals for key frame selection. ProbFaS treats dense ITA scores as cheap, biased measurements and sparse MLLM judgments as accurate, costly ones, unifying them via co-kriging, a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, to calibrate relevance across all frames. A temporal determinantal point process then selects frames capturing relevance peaks while preserving temporal coverage. Across Video-MME, MLVU and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS is the most accurate among fourteen state-of-the-art training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings (8-128 frames), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 3.1 percentage points. On MLVU and LongVideoBench, 32 ProbFaS frames match or surpass the top baseline at 128 frames and uniform sampling with up to 768 frames.
authors: Tianru Zhang, Mayank Nautiyal, Hugo Eidmann, Prashant Singh, Ekta Vats
bullets: Uniform sampling can miss keyframes, while image-text alignment rankings often poorly reflect the MLLM’s actual needs.
The training- and label-free method fuses dense ITA scores with sparse, more accurate MLLM yes/no judgments using co-kriging.
A temporal determinantal point process selects relevance peaks while maintaining temporal coverage.
Across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS leads training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings.
Using 32 frames, it matches or surpasses top-baseline performance obtained with 128 frames on MLVU and LongVideoBench.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free keyframe selection for MLLM video understanding; combines efficiency and video understanding.
papers.title: ProbFaS: Probabilistic Video Frame Selection for MLLMs via Multi-Fidelity Calibration
papers.tldr: ProbFaS improves long-video understanding by calibrating cheap frame–question scores with sparse MLLM judgments before selecting diverse, relevant frames.

papers.abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv
bullets: Addresses object loss in long videos when uniform token merging accidentally coarsens fast-moving targets.
Uses velocity-shifted and block-matched mask unions, camera-compensated surprise checks, uncertainty delegation, and an all-objects-lost fallback.
On LVOS V2, improves J&F over ALGM by 2.76 points at ViT-S and 3.89 points at ViT-B, with 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs at ViT-S.
Remains close to dense-encoder accuracy on DAVIS 2017 validation, within 0.19 J&F points at ViT-S.
Reduced counted encoder FLOPs did not translate into lower startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time; latency depends on implementation and regime.

Rings sized by each object’s speed and search regions around lost objects form the middle tier, merged by the compared merger’s own rules; the rest is merged aggressively. papers.selection_reason: Training-free focus-map token merging for efficient long-video object segmentation.
papers.title: Focus Only on What's Important: Training-Free Focus Maps for Frozen Vision Transformers in Long-Video Object Segmentation
papers.tldr: A training-free focus-map policy for frozen ViTs preserves high-resolution processing around likely objects, improving long-video segmentation accuracy while reducing counted encoder FLOPs, though not necessarily end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.
authors: Hong Liu, Rui Cen, Junhan Shi, Lin Niu, Runzhi Fan, Zhaojing Zhou, Haodi Lei, Jiebin Zhang, Saiyong Yang, Junqiang Zheng, Zhenghai Xue, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu
bullets: Targets the memory, prefill, cache-hit, and concurrency costs of maintaining a drafter-side context cache.
Shares each target layer’s cached KV states and selected context positions with its paired drafter layer.
Uses block-parallel drafting without independently scoring or caching context positions.
Across DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Hy4~flash, accepts more tokens per step than same-recipe DFlash and DSpark.
Reported gains are larger on long-context and agentic workloads; at high concurrency on two 64K DS-V4.1-Flash sets, throughput is 62% and 81% higher at matched per-user decode speed.

papers.selection_reason: Shares the target's sparse attention selection and cache to speed up speculative decoding, directly addressing token selection and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
papers.tldr: DFly2 accelerates speculative decoding for sparse long-context models by reusing the target model’s KV cache and query-specific sparse attention selections, avoiding a separate drafter cache and scoring pass.

papers.abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Daiqi Shi, Shuang Li, Liao Zhang, Yang Cai, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sampling frames for queries requiring either holistic video understanding or fine-grained local evidence.
Uses a Determinantal Point Process to select relevant, non-redundant backbone frames spanning key moments.
Infers query needs from the backbone’s temporal distribution and allocates remaining budget to local or global context.
Local enrichment captures short-range dynamics and causal relations, while global enrichment connects isolated evidence across the video.
Shows consistently superior performance when integrated with three leading MLLMs on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU.

papers.abstract: Classifying a whole-slide image requires encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles with a pathology foundation model, which accounts for most of the inference cost. Existing efficient methods reduce this cost by selecting fewer tiles, but typically train a new model around their selection strategy. A largely unexplored alternative is to keep an existing full-bag model frozen and run it on selected tiles at the same encoder cost. We introduce this comparison, alongside random tile sampling at matched cost. To select tiles, we fit a lightweight selector with 3.3K parameters to the attention of a frozen model, without additional slide labels. The selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail, encodes the top K regions at 5x magnification, and selects b for processing at 20x. We evaluate seven frozen MIL aggregators on six tasks and compare them with nine efficient methods trained on the same features and splits. At a budget of (K,b)=(1000,10), encoding costs about 6.6% of the full bag and is 10-14x faster, excluding tiling. The AUROC drop is no more than 0.005 in 33 of 36 aggregator-task pairs. At (500,10), the cost falls to about 4% and inference is 13-22x faster, but AUROC drops by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, where small metastases are easily missed. Selection improves over random sampling by about 0.10 AUROC on tasks with focal lesions, while random sampling performs well on diffuse tasks. In our comparisons, the frozen model at (500,10) is ahead of nine efficient methods in 55 of 60 paired comparisons. Giving an existing WSI model fewer tiles is thus a baseline that a new efficient model should be compared with at matched encoder cost.
bullets: Motivation: Whole-slide classification is dominated by encoding thousands of high-resolution tiles.
Method: A 3.3K-parameter selector ranks regions from a slide thumbnail using a frozen model’s attention, then encodes only the top regions at higher magnification.
Evaluation: Seven frozen MIL aggregators were tested on six tasks against random sampling and nine efficient methods at matched feature and split settings.
Results: Encoding 10 selected tiles from 1,000 candidates costs about 6.6% of a full bag and is 10–14× faster, with AUROC loss ≤0.005 in 33/36 aggregator-task pairs.
Scope: More aggressive selection can miss small focal lesions; at 500 candidates, AUROC dropped by up to 0.035 on CAMELYON17, while random sampling worked well for diffuse tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Tile selection to reduce whole-slide image encoding cost; directly relevant to token/tile selection efficiency.
papers.title: Rank Before You Encode: Reading a Few Percent of a Whole-Slide Image
papers.tldr: A lightweight thumbnail-based selector lets frozen whole-slide models process only a few percent of tiles while largely preserving accuracy and greatly reducing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Video large language models incur substantial inference costs from long visual token sequences. Existing video token compression methods mitigate these costs by exploiting spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy across frames. However, many approaches impose predefined processing orders or fixed allocation ratios for spatial and temporal compression, limiting their ability to adapt to the varying balance of spatiotemporal redundancy across videos. To address this limitation, we propose PURA, a training-free method that prunes visual tokens through unified spatiotemporal redundancy assessment. For each token, PURA constructs spatial and temporal reference candidates and selects the reference with the lowest representation error across the two dimensions. The representation error is combined with token importance to determine each token's removal cost. To avoid the time overhead of removing the lowest-cost token one by one, we introduce Coordinated Pruning, which iteratively groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches for simultaneous execution and updates the pruning state after each batch until the target budget is reached. Extensive experiments on three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks demonstrate that PURA achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Hongli Yuan, Shuang Li, Tao Deng, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of long visual token sequences in video large language models.
Builds spatial and temporal reference candidates for each token and selects the one with lower representation error.
Combines representation error with token importance to estimate each token’s removal cost.
Uses Coordinated Pruning to batch compatible low-cost removals instead of pruning tokens individually.
Experiments across three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks show a favorable performance–efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward approaches mark a paradigm shift in novel view synthesis by eliminating the reliance on per-scene optimization, directly inferring 3D representations from input views. However, their reliance on global scene-token context incurs substantial memory and latency overhead, constraining their ability to handle increasingly dense source-view contexts. Compressing source representations offers an intuitive way to limit this token budget. Prior general-purpose compression methods are not tailored for novel view synthesis, as their fixed, target-agnostic nature fails to adapt evidence allocation to individual target views. To overcome this, we introduce TACC, a target-aware compression module tailored for feed-forward latent NVS. Specifically, TACC organizes each source view into a progressive carrier hierarchy. Driven by source-target geometric relevance, it adaptively retrieves tokens to dynamically allocate exact computational quotas. This selective retrieval directly yields a compact, target-conditioned representation. Extensive experiments on the RE10K demonstrate that under dense input settings, TACC achieves $9.23\times$ and $64\times$ higher Effective FPS than Full Context on LagerNVS and LVSM, respectively. Effective FPS excludes one-time source encoding and Carrier construction.
authors: Yiming Fan, Yijia Guo, Zewen Guo, Liwen Hu, Yuheng Yuan, Yang Li, Zhiwei Li, Xitong Ling, Caihong Yuan, Shengbo Chen, Tiejun Huang, Lei Ma
bullets: Feed-forward NVS methods face memory and latency bottlenecks as source-view context grows.
TACC builds a progressive carrier hierarchy for each source view.
Source-target geometric relevance guides selective token retrieval and target-conditioned compression.
On RE10K, TACC improves Effective FPS by 9.23× on LagerNVS and 64× on LVSM under dense inputs.
Effective FPS excludes one-time source encoding and carrier construction.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) outperform single-agent systems, but inter-agent communication incurs substantial token overhead. While assigning a large LLM to every agent is common, it results in inefficient resource utilization, leaving the system far from the Pareto frontier. The cost of answering a query is set jointly by how many agents are recruited, the role and LLM assigned to each, and communication topology among them. Most existing routers treat cost only implicitly rather than as an explicit optimization constraint. A fixed accuracy-cost preference also cannot express how much a caller is willing to pay for a particular query. We introduce MeterRouter, a budget-aware dynamic router that incrementally synthesizes a collaboration graph by selecting each agent's role, LLM, incoming connections, and termination conditioned on the query and a per-query monetary budget. We initialize the router by imitating successful execution graphs, then jointly refine its decisions with a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) whose reward favors correct answers and penalizes spending and budget overruns. Across five benchmarks and a three-tier LLM pool, MeterRouter is (1) accurate, achieving performance comparable to the strongest MAS; (2) economical, reaching that accuracy at 82% lower cost than the strongest MAS router and extending the accuracy-cost frontier beyond the ceiling of single-agent systems; and (3) controllable, adapting its spending to the specified budget while rarely exceeding it.
authors: Yue Xu, Leikun Yin, Ruiming Min, Yufeng Lai, Justin Andrew Johnson, Sitao Luan, Xiaotong Shen
bullets: Targets inefficient LLM assignment and communication overhead in multi-agent systems.
Selects agent roles, LLMs, incoming connections, and termination decisions conditioned on the query and monetary budget.
Initializes from successful execution graphs and refines routing with a GRPO variant rewarding correctness while penalizing cost and budget overruns.
Evaluated on five benchmarks with a three-tier LLM pool, it matches the strongest MAS while using 82% lower cost.
Adapts spending to specified budgets, rarely exceeds them, and extends the accuracy–cost frontier beyond single-agent systems.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models excel at image and video generation, but iterative denoising incurs substantial inference latency. Recent token-adaptive acceleration methods select Taylor prediction orders for the full-model residual using shallow-layer proxy scores. However, candidate orders are evaluated on these proxy features but used to predict the full-model residual, creating a proxy--target mismatch: the proxy-preferred order may not minimize residual prediction error. To address this mismatch, we propose \textbf{TORE} (\textbf{T}aylor \textbf{O}rder selection via \textbf{R}esidual \textbf{E}rror estimation), which selects token-wise Taylor orders based on estimated prediction errors for the full-model residual. Yet direct error evaluation requires future ground-truth residuals, which are unavailable during order selection. TORE therefore estimates prediction error by analyzing how errors arise in Taylor extrapolation. Specifically, it decomposes prediction error into truncation error and finite-difference derivative error, then estimates both contributions from cached residuals to preselect token-wise orders for upcoming skip steps. Extensive experiments show that TORE achieves $4.31\times$ speedup on FLUX.1-dev and $4.18\times$ on Wan2.1 while maintaining high generation quality and fidelity.
authors: Lei Tang, Baoquan Zhang, Yakun Zhang, Yunming Ye
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between shallow proxy scores and full-model residual prediction accuracy in token-adaptive acceleration.
Decomposes Taylor prediction error into truncation and finite-difference derivative errors.
Uses cached residuals to estimate these errors without unavailable future ground-truth residuals.
Preselects token-wise Taylor orders for upcoming denoising skip steps.
Reports 4.31× speedup on FLUX.1-dev and 4.18× on Wan2.1 while maintaining high generation quality and fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TORE, a method for token-wise Taylor order selection in diffusion models to accelerate inference. This directly addresses computational efficiency in generative models.
papers.title: TORE: Token-Wise Taylor Order Selection via Decomposed Residual Error Estimation for Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: TORE accelerates diffusion generation by selecting Taylor extrapolation orders per token using estimated full-model residual prediction errors.

papers.abstract: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.
authors: Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Liyuan Cui, Yuan Li, Jiaxin Huang, Lutao Jiang, Runze Zhang, Yingda Yin, Xiaoyang Huang, Kai Yan, Keyang Luo, Xin Wang, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation in long-horizon camera-controlled video generation.
Uses geometric correspondences to guide attention and retrieve relevant historical scene content.
Restricts observed regions to matching historical tokens plus local context, while retaining dense attention for novel regions.
Adds correspondence-aware attention biases and order-invariant historical positioning for stable retrieval across long temporal gaps.
Reports improved camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity while substantially reducing attention computation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. System Overview. For each target chunk, SPARC establishes token-level correspondences with historical observations through local geometric projection, and then prunes the backbone’s native self-attention to focus on geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context for previously observed regions, while newly revealed regions retain dense attention for flexible content synthesis. Historical RoPE re-indexing is employed to eliminate artificial temporal ordering biases among retrieved historical observations. The generated observations are subsequently appended to the history bank for continuous rollout.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on DL3DV-Eval. Given the same input image and camera trajectory, we show frames generated with different methods along the roaming time. Explicit-3D baselines drift from the target trajectory or accumulate geometric distortions, and implicit baselines fail to follow the prescribed camera path, whereas SPARC preserves scene appearance and accurate camera control throughout the rollout. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of revisitation on WorldScore-Static. Each scene follows a closed-loop camera trajectory (top view), and frames are sampled along the roaming time. Baselines either distort the scene or fail to recover the originally observed content upon revisiting, whereas our SPARC faithfully restores the scene at both revisits. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 9. Additional long-horizon generation results. Without any degradation-aware augmentation, SPARC generates high-fidelity, minute-long videos with precise camera adherence and persistent scene consistency.

Figure 7. Ablation on attention pruning and historical RoPE indexing. Progressively incorporating geometric correspondence, local window attention, and correspondence bias improves camera adherence and reconstruction fidelity. The bottom rows visualize the pixel-wise difference |∆| between outputs generated using the original and shuffled history orders: sequential history RoPE yields discrepancies that grow along the trajectory, whereas our shared indexing remains invariant.

Figure 5. Camera alignment. SPARC achieves the best camera alignment on DL3DV-Evaluation.

Figure 10. Training-free dynamic scene generation. We segment the foreground object and shift its correspondence locations along a prescribed motion trajectory, allowing SPARC to synthesize natural object motion consistent with the specified trajectory.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces geometry-guided attention pruning for camera-controlled video generation, effectively combining video diffusion, efficient attention mechanisms, and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: SPARC: Geometry-Guided Attention Pruning for Long-Horizon Camera-Controlled Video Generation
papers.tldr: SPARC prunes video-transformer attention using scene geometry to enable precise camera control and long-term scene memory with over 50× faster inference when paired with four-step distillation.

papers.abstract: Departing from the paradigm of diffusion and autoregressive models, Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) enables high-quality image generation through iterative refinements. However, this repeated processing over the entire visual representations results in substantial computation overhead. Furthermore, the binary representations and global refinement mechanism in GRN disable the direct application of acceleration strategies developed for other generative models. To accelerate GRN model, we first observe several key properties by analyzing the entire generative process. That includes the stage characteristic, dual branch similarity and more importantly, the $\textbf{refinement redundancy}$. Motivated by the observations, we present $\textbf{FasterGRN}$, a training-free acceleration method for the Generative Refinement Network. $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ first divides the GRN into the semantic establishment stage and detail refinement stage according to its semantic establishment. For alleviating the refinement redundancy mainly resulting from the detail refinement stage, we propose Adaptive Retention Expansion ($\textbf{ARE}$) and Selective Token Freezing ($\textbf{STF}$) to shrink refinement steps and reduce token computations, respectively. In the experiments on GenEval and DPG-Bench benchmarks, our method $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ achieves a $2.03\times$ sampling speedup while largely preserving image generation performance. Our evaluation on COCO datasets additionally demonstrates that $\textbf{FasterGRN}$ even outperforms the original GRN in image fidelity.
authors: Ziqian Zhang, Pengcheng Wang, Yulong Chen, Yaxing Wang, Senmao Li, Kai Wang
bullets: GRNs incur high computation because they repeatedly refine entire visual representations.
The method identifies semantic establishment and detail refinement stages, with redundancy concentrated in detail refinement.
Adaptive Retention Expansion reduces refinement steps, while Selective Token Freezing reduces token computations.
FasterGRN is training-free and achieves a 2.03× sampling speedup on GenEval and DPG-Bench while largely preserving performance.
On COCO, it also surpasses the original GRN in image fidelity.

papers.abstract: Looped multi-view reconstruction refines scene features by repeatedly applying a shared transformer block. Making these updates cheaper requires knowing how an approximation at one step affects the rest of the refinement. We study this with paired interventions in D\'ej\`a View and stacked reconstruction transformers, separating the error an approximation injects, how that error propagates, and how it affects the output. In D\'ej\`a View, approximation errors are attenuated more strongly than matched random perturbations under a scale-adjusted state-error measure, and a local Jacobian decomposition separates the contribution of channel gating from the response to spatial error structure. Spatial approximations made early benefit from subsequent refinement, whereas cross-step reuse depends on which quantity is cached and how reuse steps are spaced. At equal final norm, approximation errors change the predicted rotations 1.55 times as much as random errors. These findings guide our proposed method, which reduces spatial resolution and pools keys and values early in refinement, then interleaves attention-output reuse with full attention, and is adapted through lightweight self-distillation. Across five reconstruction benchmarks, the balanced configuration runs $1.63\times$ faster than the official 16-step D\'ej\`a View model with a 1.86-point reduction in average pose AUC@$3^\circ$. At matched latency, it exceeds the interpolated curve of a trained baseline using full refinement blocks by 4.73 points in AUC@$3^\circ$ and improves the corresponding geometry metrics.
authors: Siyuan Zhang, Yuhan Chen, Yangyang Ning, Nan Wang, Jun Yan
bullets: Studies how approximation errors are injected, propagated, and translated into reconstruction outputs in Déjà View and stacked reconstruction transformers.
Finds that early spatial approximations are mitigated by later refinement, while cross-step reuse depends on the cached quantity and reuse spacing.
Shows approximation errors affect predicted rotations 1.55× more than matched random errors at equal final norm.
Proposes early spatial reduction and key/value pooling, interleaved attention-output reuse, and lightweight self-distillation.

Across five benchmarks, the balanced model is 1.63× faster with a 1.86-point average pose AUC@3° reduction; at matched latency, it improves AUC@3° by 4.73 points over an interpolated full-refinement baseline.

papers.title: Where to Approximate: Understanding and Accelerating Looped Multi-View Reconstruction
papers.tldr: The paper analyzes where approximation errors matter in looped multi-view reconstruction and uses the findings to design a faster model with modest pose-accuracy loss and better accuracy at matched latency.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are widely used for image segmentation. However, existing methods either use a decoder or use patch-based approach which trades boundary precision against the number of decisions as coarse grid cells mix foreground and background pixels, while finer grids require many more predictions, and autoregressive mask generation adds sequential decoding overhead. We propose SPiXSeg, which shifts the output from per-patch to per-superpixel label assignment, using superpixel tokens formed by aggregating patch-level visual features. An off-the-shelf model partitions each image into task-agnostic superpixels, so the partition is computed once and reused across tasks. A Spix-to-Mask (S2M) module scores each superpixel token in a single MLLM forward pass by directly comparing the MLLM's hidden representations, without autoregressive generation or a separate scoring network, and the selected superpixels are mapped directly to pixels without refinement. Without any trainable decoder head or post-hoc refinement, SPiXSeg achieves an average cIoU of 80.5 with LLaVA-1.5-7B and 81.9 with InternVL2.5-8B on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg and, when trained only on COCO-Stuff, extends to open-vocabulary semantic segmentation with mIoU of 29.0, 59.5 and 95.4 on ADE20K, PASCAL Context and PASCAL VOC, outperforming several SoTA MLLM baselines. Our results suggest that a fixed, query-agnostic superpixel partition is enough for accurate language-guided segmentation.
authors: Piyush Tiwary, Sohini Dutta, Prathosh A. P
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between coarse patch boundaries, costly fine-grained predictions, and sequential mask decoding.
Aggregates patch features into task-agnostic superpixel tokens using a fixed partition computed once per image.
Scores superpixels in one MLLM forward pass by directly comparing hidden representations, then maps selected regions to pixels.
Achieves 80.5/81.9 average cIoU with LLaVA-1.5-7B/InternVL2.5-8B on RefCOCO variants and supports open-vocabulary semantic segmentation when trained only on COCO-Stuff.
The approach omits a trainable decoder head and post-hoc refinement; its scope depends on the quality of the fixed superpixel partition.

papers.abstract: When a large language model (LLM) evicts prompt keys and values at the end of prefill, it must decide what to keep before it sees the queries from subsequent decoding steps. Generating a draft continuation can approximate those queries at the cost of extra autoregressive steps. Can we use the embedding of the first output token, already available from the final prefill logits, to construct low-cost pseudo queries that approximate future decoding queries? We start with FTQ-8, which places eight copies of the first token ID at consecutive future positions and reads their attention to the prompt in one causal forward pass. Each copy sees a different prefix, but a generic opening such as the offers a poor literal guess for seven successive tokens. Faster and Better Query (FBQ) preserves the first embedding and learns an additive offset at each of the seven remaining positions. We train these offsets to predict the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation. On LongBench, FBQ performs comparably to eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget, using a single forward pass to compute all probe queries.
authors: Jiankun Zou, Daixing Chen, Tongtong Yuan
bullets: Addresses cache-eviction decisions made before future decoding queries are available.
Extends FTQ-8 by adjusting seven repeated first-token embeddings with learned additive offsets.
Trains offsets to match the average prompt attention of a full-cache continuation.
Computes all eight probe queries in one causal forward pass, avoiding extra autoregressive drafting steps.
On LongBench, matches the performance of eight-step Lookahead Q-Cache at the same cache budget.

papers.abstract: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.
authors: Ahmed Alajrami, Ondrej Bohdal, Seokwoo Song, Taegeon Um, Peyman Hosseini, Savas Ozkan, Mete Ozay, Taha Ceritli
bullets: Addresses persona-attribute inference from a single day of mobile logs for personalization.
Introduces a synthetic benchmark containing 1,600 persona–log pairs.
Filters semantically similar logs while retaining behaviorally distinct events.
Reduces memory use by up to 39% across nine models and more than halves prefill time without hurting prediction quality.
Results suggest behavioral diversity matters more than retaining redundant log entries.

papers.abstract: High-resolution Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) preserve critical, fine-grained visual details by encoding a global thumbnail alongside multiple local crops. However, the resulting thousands of vision tokens introduce severe computational bottlenecks during Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Existing token pruning methods rely primarily on query-agnostic visual saliency, while current query-aware approaches either operate at a coarse crop-level resolution or compute token relevance too late, after vision tokens have already entered the heavy LLM layers. To address this, we propose a training-free, hierarchical token pruning framework that utilizes query guidance prior to executing any LLM blocks. Our top-down hierarchy first operates at the instance-level, dynamically scaling the vision token retention ratio of each sample based on its visual complexity. Next, at the crop-level, we distribute this sample budget across local crops using sentence-level cross-modal similarity. Finally, at the token-level, we exploit projected vision tokens alongside textual query token embeddings in the shared space to measure fine-grained alignment, applying a text-debiasing normalization to produce high-fidelity query scores. These query-guided budgets and scores are fused with local and global visual saliency metrics to select the most critical vision tokens. Extensive experiments on LLaVA-NeXT-7B demonstrate that our plug-and-play framework retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% vision token retention, respectively. Notably, at 25% retention, our method delivers a 2.0x inference throughput speedup and even surpasses the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.
bullets: Addresses the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of vision tokens from global thumbnails and local crops.
Dynamically allocates retention budgets across samples, crops, and tokens using visual complexity and query-aware cross-modal alignment.
Combines query-guided scores with local and global visual saliency to select critical tokens before any LLM blocks execute.
On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, retains 98.0% and 94.8% of unpruned performance at 25% and 10% token retention, respectively.
At 25% retention, achieves a 2.0× inference throughput speedup and exceeds the unpruned baseline on POPE by 0.7 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of our training-free token pruning framework for high-resolution LVLMs. An input image is processed into a full-image view and multiple sub-images, which are passed through a Visual Encoder and Projector to produce visual tokens (V ). A text query is tokenized into embeddings (E). The pruning process consists of three main stages: (1) Adaptive Budget Allocation: A two-level budget is computed. At the Sample-level, a token retention ratio (Rj) is dynamically set for each image based on its visual token diversity (Hj). At the Crop-level, this budget is distributed among the sub-images based on the query-crop relevance. (2) Query Score Algorithm: A fine-grained relevance score is computed between the query embeddings (E) and the visual tokens (V ). Raw cross-modal similarities are standardized using a text-debiasing z-score to produce a robust query score (qsi) for each token. (3) Fuse & Select: The final token selection score is calculated by fusing the Query Score with two visual saliency cues: a local score from the sub-image’s own [CLS] attention (ai) and a global score derived from the full-image view (gi). The top-bi tokens are selected and fed to LLM for inference.

Fig. 2: Adaptive per-sample budget allocation on POPE examples. Our query-aware framework dynamically scales token retention according to scene complexity. The visually redundant snow scene (left) retains only 516 of 2,880 visual tokens, whereas the cluttered baseball scene (right) dynamically allocates 860 tokens to preserve fine-grained details needed for accurate question answering.

Fig. 1: Pruning masks on a POPE sample at a 25% retention ratio. GlobalCom2 uses an image-only mask that is unchanged by the query; for the chair question shown here, it removes most chair evidence before the LLM and answers incorrectly. Our query-aware mask retains the relevant chair tokens and answers correctly.

TABLE I: Comparison with existing methods on LLaVA-NeXT-7B. The retention ratio R is defined with respect to the 2,880 token positions including padding. Avg. is the mean score relative to the unpruned model. Baseline results without a mark are taken from GlobalCom2 [11]; ∗ denotes results obtained by running the released code. The best and second-best results among pruning methods are in bold and underlined.

TABLE V: Inference efficiency of LLaVA-NeXT-7B on POPE at R = 25%. TFLOPs: LLM prefill FLOPs. Memory: peak GPU memory. Throughput: questions per second. Performance: average relative score in Table I.
TABLE II: Module ablation on LLaVA-NeXT-7B at R = 25%.
TABLE III: Ablation on α at R = 25% (β = 0.5). α = 1 uses only the global score; the default is underlined.
TABLE IV: Ablation on β at R = 25% (α = 0.7). β = 0 uses only the query score as the local score; the default is underlined. β = 1 removes the query score.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free hierarchical token pruning for high-resolution LVLMs directly targets token pruning/eviction efficiency and multimodal LLM inference.
papers.title: Hierarchical and Query-Aware Visual Token Pruning for High-Resolution LVLMs
papers.tldr: A training-free hierarchical method prunes high-resolution LVLM vision tokens using query relevance and visual saliency before LLM inference, substantially reducing computation while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: We present RenGen, a latent diffusion model that generates simple scenes from a few tokens and busy scenes from many, saving time and compute on simple scenes without losing realism. Most latent generators represent every image as a fixed grid of patch tokens, so a simple image costs as much to generate as a complex one. Prior methods that vary the token count through content-adaptive tokenization lose image quality as the count shrinks. RenGen instead trades scene complexity, rather than image quality, for fewer tokens. It does so by generating in the latent space of a pretrained region encoder, where each token represents one region of the image, and a decoder renders these region tokens back into pixels. Unlike patch tokens, region tokens cover areas of varying shape and position, so each token must capture both what its region contains and where it lies on the image canvas. We encode this spatial extent by adding positional embeddings to the encoder features before pooling, and we generate it by anchoring each token to a single randomly sampled point, from which the generator infers the region's shape, size, and content. At sampling time, the number of anchor points sets the trade-off between scene complexity and compute. On ImageNet $256{\times}256$, RenGen reaches a gFID of 1.34 with 88 tokens per image on average, the best among methods that vary their token count. It approaches the quality of RAEv2, a state-of-the-art patch-based model, at $2.5{\times}$ lower latency, advancing the Pareto frontier of generation quality versus compute. RenGen's gFID stays flat across scene complexity while latency varies by $2.4{\times}$ between simplest and busiest scenes, and its autoencoder reconstructs nearly as well as RAEv2 (rFID 0.32 vs. 0.30) with $2.9{\times}$ fewer tokens.
authors: Savya Khosla, Jay Mahajan, Akin Tuna Sakalli, Derek Hoiem, David Forsyth, Alex Schwing
bullets: Fixed-grid latent diffusion models spend similar compute on simple and busy images; prior adaptive tokenization can degrade quality.
RenGen represents images with variable-sized, spatially grounded region tokens from a pretrained region encoder.
The number of randomly sampled anchor points controls token count, scene complexity, and sampling latency.
On ImageNet 256×256, it achieves gFID 1.34 with 88 tokens on average and approaches RAEv2 quality at 2.5× lower latency.
Latency varies 2.4× by scene complexity, while gFID remains flat; reconstruction quality is close to RAEv2 with 2.9× fewer tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2. RenGen overview. (a) The region encoder partitions an image into N regions with Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher (FH) segmentation and pools frozen DINOv3 patch features within each region into region tokens, which the decoder renders back into an image. (b) For generation, P random anchor points fix the region positions. A DiT denoises one region token per anchor point, using the anchor coordinates as 2D RoPE positions, and the shared decoder renders the generated tokens into an image.

Figure 6. RenGen sets a new quality–compute trade-off. Left: gFID versus total TFLOPs per image on ImageNet 256×256. RenGen lies below the Pareto frontier of prior methods (dashed). Right: The source of this gain. At matched model size, RenGen generates 2.9× fewer tokens than RAEv2, which translates directly into 2.6× fewer TFLOPs and 2.5× less wall-clock time per image.

Figure 7. RenGen reconstructs fine detail as faithfully as RAEv2 with far fewer tokens. Each tile shows its token count; RenGen’s follows image complexity, from 31 tokens for the hairpin on a plain background to 103 for the crowded scene.

Figure 1. RenGen’s generation cost follows image content. Top: Wall-clock time and TFLOPs per image for end-to-end generation at different token counts for RenGen. Green values give the speedup over RAEv2, which always uses a fixed grid of 256 patch tokens (dashed line). Bottom: 256×256 samples from a single RenGen model. Each row uses the same class label, and each column uses the token count of the point above it, so fewer tokens yield simpler scenes at lower cost.

Figure 3. Image complexity varies, but patch tokenizers spend the same budget on every image. Top: ImageNet images of increasing complexity, overlaid with the 16×16 patch grid of patchbased latent diffusion models and with their region partitions. The simplest of the four scenes has only 22 regions, while the busiest has 130. Bottom: Regions per image across ImageNet validation set. The mean of 88 is 2.9× fewer than the 256 tokens of a patch grid (dashed line).

Figure 5. RenGen adapts its compute to scene complexity without losing quality. gFID stays flat across four complexity buckets, so in low-resource settings RenGen can generate simple, realistic scenes 2.4× faster and with 2.5× less compute than complex ones. Samples of the same class (bottom; anchor points in white) grow busier as the token budget increases.

Figure 4. Constructing DiT targets. During training, we place P anchor points on the image canvas, partition the canvas into their Voronoi cells, compute each cell’s coverage mask on the patch grid, and encode the image with the region encoder to obtain one target region token per anchor.

Table 3. RenGen achieves the best rFID and gFID among methods that vary their token count. It also reconstructs and generates nearly as well as RAEv2 with 2.6× fewer TFLOPs and 2.5× less wall-clock time (Fig. 6). The checkmark columns indicate whether a method’s token count varies with image content (content adaptive), whether a user can choose the token budget of a single model at inference (controllable complexity), and whether its latents come from a frozen pretrained representation encoder (frozen enc.). §Included as the closest prior generator that adapts its compute to image content; it operates in pixel space, so reconstruction metrics do not apply.

Table 4. RenGen scales to higher resolutions more efficiently than RAEv2. At 512×512, RenGen reconstructs slightly better than RAEv2 while using about a third of the tokens and DiT compute. Because its token count depends on image content rather than resolution, RenGen can also encode the full 512×512 image into the same 88 tokens, improving reconstruction further at no extra cost. A single RenGen model handles both 256×256 and 512×512 inputs here.

Table 2. Randomly fixing region positions with anchor points enables strong generation at low cost. Without any spatial prior, the DiT trains poorly. Conditioning on real layouts separately leads to memorization and requires real images at sampling time, while generating layouts roughly doubles sampling time and still degrades quality. Random anchor points avoid both and outperform held-out real layouts with a single DiT. At sampling, the DiT receives only the points; the training regions determine how the targets are partitioned around them. Sampling time is measured per image at batch size 64 on one NVIDIA GH200.

Table 1. Adding positional embeddings to patch features before pooling them into region tokens gives the best reconstruction and generation. REN tokens reconstruct poorly because their regions overlap and their features encode little position. Fine-tuning REN makes the number of tokens grow during training (∗mean token count at the start→end of training). Pooling patch features within fixed FH regions keeps the token count stable, but the tokens still encode little position. Adding an explicit mask code to each token improves reconstruction but hurts generation, because the DiT must generate these codes precisely.

papers.selection_reason: Content-adaptive token count in latent diffusion reduces compute for simple scenes; relevant to token-level efficiency.
papers.title: RenGen: Generating Images with as Many Tokens as the Scene Needs
papers.tldr: RenGen adaptively uses more tokens for complex scenes and fewer for simple ones, reducing generation cost while preserving image quality.

papers.abstract: Visual token compaction reduces inference cost by passing only selected image patches or video tokens to later layers. In sequence models with local convolutions, each removal changes which tokens are neighbors. Learning which tokens to keep therefore requires a training signal that accounts for the new neighborhoods. We introduce ProbConv, which computes the exact expected convolution before activation at a kept position under independent keep decisions. The operator is differentiable in the keep probabilities. With binary decisions, ProbConv and step gating reproduce the compacted Mamba block. Across image, vision--language and video backbones, ProbConv is strongest under strong compaction: its advantage over matched training controls grows as more tokens are removed. In Cobra, it also outperforms adaptations of published vision--language pruning methods at matched inference budgets. ProbConv also improves over matched zero-mask training in video frame selection and speech frame dropping. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/probconv
authors: Piotr Kubaty (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland), Mikhail Saladkou (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland), Jacek Tabor (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Centre for Credible Artificial Intelligence, Warsaw University of Technology, Poland), {\L}ukasz Struski (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland)
bullets: Token removal alters neighboring relationships in local-convolution sequence models, making standard training signals inaccurate.
ProbConv computes the exact expected pre-activation convolution at each kept position under independent token-keep probabilities.
The operator is differentiable, and binary decisions with step gating recover the compacted Mamba block.
It performs best under aggressive compaction and outperforms matched controls and several pruning adaptations across image, vision-language, video, and speech settings.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or discuss limitations beyond its evaluated application scope.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Different training rules retain different patches at the same budget. The ten evenly spaced ImageNet validation images use the Vim-Tiny models from Main Fig. 5a with 69 and 24 patches after the two cuts (seed 0). Dimmed patches are dropped. Green and red frames mark correct and incorrect predictions after the last cut. From the top: lorikeet, Bedlington terrier, coyote (Main Fig. 6), armadillo, bookshop, electric fan, mailbag, planetarium, spotlight and wok.

Figure 1. Keep probabilities in training, a hard mask at inference. Illustrative example with schematic probabilities. During training (bottom), the selector gives each patch a keep probability pt, drawn from gray (pt=0) to full color (pt=1), and ProbConv averages each convolution window over the keep decisions. At a high LapSum temperature τ many patches are partly kept; as τ decreases, few remain. At inference (top right), the top-k mask keeps the outlined patches, and later layers process only these.

Figure 3. Where each approach trains the selector. Keep probabilities with a fixed budget form a hypersimplex (L=3, k=2 shown); its vertices are binary masks. Rules choose a vertex and REINFORCE samples vertices. A zero mask is differentiable in the keep probabilities but computes a different network even at a vertex. ProbConv is differentiable and, with step gating, recovers the compacted Mamba block at each vertex (Proposition 2).

Figure 18. The full gallery pairs dense Cobra’s answers with ProbConv’s compacted answers. All 19 fixed examples show the original image beside the selection at a nominal 10% of LM FLOPs. The two labels give the model answers. Dimmed patches are dropped.

Figure 9. The zero-mask selector misses character emissions. Frames kept by each rule on one LibriSpeech test-clean utterance, below its log-mel spectrogram and its words, when subword units are decoded from a quarter of the frames without recovery. The zero-mask selector keeps long runs of frames. Statistics over 400 utterances: App. Fig. 5.

Figure 2. Removing a token changes the convolution window. Top: zero masking leaves the token’s slot in place. Bottom: ProbConv averages the keep and drop windows, and its gradient compares them (Eq. (5)). Step gating skips dropped updates, so the block matches physical compaction for binary decisions (Proposition 2).

Figure 5. The lead over zero-mask training grows as budgets tighten. Accuracy of (a) Vim-Tiny, (b) Cobra-3B and (c) VideoMamba-Ti at each budget (compute per budget: App. Tab. 1), for the selector trained with ProbConv or with zero masking and step gating, and for a fixed score with compacted fine-tuning (in Vim, the channel mean of the backward scan output, the unclipped token importance of ToP-ViM [68]; in VideoMamba, the token norm; none in Cobra, whose backbone stays frozen); every arm runs physically compacted at inference. DyVM (adapted): in Vim and VideoMamba, our selector, objective and schedule with DyVM’s training forward; in Cobra, DyVM’s predictor and objective (Secs. 3.1 and 3.2). Mean over three seeds (App. Tabs. 4, 9, 32 and 33).

Figure 8. ProbConv keeps frames like REINFORCE. Four of ten candidates kept by each rule (framed) on one ActivityNet-v1.3 validation video, Removing ice from car, which every rule classifies correctly. ProbConv and REINFORCE share three frames, the zero-mask policy at most one with either. The video is fixed by a rule that ignores the predictions: the most motion (MGSampler’s measure) among the single-label videos on which the four rules keep different frames.

Figure 7. ProbConv keeps the tokens around the moving person. VideoMambaTi at ρ = 0.5 on a Kinetics-400 validation clip (cartwheeling, correct for all three rules), six of its eight frames. Colored tokens reach the last block; gray ones are dropped. The cuts after blocks 6, 12 and 18 drop 784, 392 and 196 of the 1,568 patch tokens. The zero mask often keeps neighboring tokens along the scan, and the token norm keeps many sky tokens. More clips: App. Fig. 3.

Figure 6. With 24 patches left, only ProbConv classifies the coyote correctly. Patches kept by the Vim-Tiny networks of Fig. 5a at ρ = 0.35 (69 and 24 of 196 after blocks 10 and 20, seed 0); dimmed patches are dropped. Green and red squares mark correct and wrong predictions; the other arms predict timber wolf. The fixed score keeps mostly background, and DyVM (adapted) keeps more background than ProbConv. The zero mask also keeps patches on the coyote, but it trains on a forward that differs from the deployed network (Tab. 6). More images: App. Fig. 1.

Figure 21. ProbConv’s geometric-mean rank map is nearly flat, while the zero-mask convolution ranks the last raster positions first. The top rows show two POPE images. Bright positions enter the top-k set at smaller budgets. The bottom row gives the geometric mean of these ranks over 500 images.

Figure 8. ProbConv improves most Nucleotide Transformer tasks, with the clearest gains on splice sites and enhancers. The mean gain persists at matched compression. The plot gives the change in test MCC×100 relative to reproduced routing on 18 Nucleotide Transformer tasks, with 95% confidence intervals. Intervals use ten folds for individual tasks and variation across tasks for the overall means. For the matched-compression comparison, both methods use the pretraining ratio loss. Tables 26 and 27 give the task and group results.

Figure 20. ProbConv’s keep probabilities sharpen over training. At 10% of LM FLOPs, the upper panels show one POPE image and its LapSum temperatures at four checkpoints. Below, the left panel gives mean pi(1−pi) over 500 images, the middle panel tracks overlap with the final 46 tokens, and the right panel shows the probability histograms. The left panel includes only the three LapSum-trained rules; DyVM’s sigmoid probabilities carry no budget and are omitted.

Figure 23. After compaction, the short convolution reads beyond the three original predecessor offsets. ProbConv follows the observed distribution of these distances during training. At left, the white square marks a retained token. The rows show the ProbConv training window after 500 steps, the physically compacted window and the zero-mask training window. At right, curves give predecessor distances in raster positions over 500 POPE images. The solid curve shows deployment, the dashed curve shows training with ProbConv, and shading marks the zero-mask offsets.

Figure 22. Object coverage and conditional accuracy rank the selectors differently. The left panel shows retained object area across budgets on 4,053 POPE “yes” questions. The vertical line marks 46 tokens (10% of LM FLOPs), also shown in the middle panel with random selection as a dotted reference. The right panel shows accuracy with at least one retained token whose area is at least half covered by the queried object (solid), and without such a token (light). Objects come from COCO annotations rasterized onto the token grid.

Figure 19. At 10% of LM FLOPs, ProbConv’s gradient ranks the measured loss changes of single-token flips better than the gradients of the two zero-mask computations. For one POPE question, the first three panels compare predicted and measured loss changes for 729 token additions or removals on symmetric log axes. Colored points mark removals, and gray points mark additions. The fourth panel gives rank correlations over 48 questions, with bars at the medians. The right panel gives the absolute loss gap to physical compaction at the same mask. The example question is the one with the median ProbConv correlation. Only the training forward pass of ProbConv is the deployed network.

Figure 5. ProbConv retains more frames near character emissions than zero-mask training. Over 400 randomly sampled LibriSpeech test-clean utterances, the curves show the retained share of frames at each offset from the nearest character emission of the dense model’s intermediate CTC head. The plotted run decodes BPE from a quarter of the frames (seed 0).

Figure 4. A centered convolution is two causal ones. Taps of a convolution with two taps on each side of the output frame x4: a causal pass over the clip and a causal pass over the reversed clip, whose centre tap is zero, add up to the centered filter. With ProbConv in both passes the sum is the expected centered convolution of the compacted clip, because the kept frames before and after a kept frame are independent (App. Eq. (9) and App. Fig. 4).

Figure 11. The gap over zero masking increases as the language-model budget falls. The curves show the sixbenchmark mean for frozen Cobra-3B. Solid curves show learned selectors, dashed curves show training-free rules, and diamonds identify zero-mask training of the matched selector. Learned scores average three seeds. Values in Tab. 33.
Figure 2. Four per-image selections preserve the dense prediction with 4–22 patches. Panels show images 0, 2, 3 and 4 from Tab. 8, using 22, 13, 7 and 4 of 196 patches, respectively.

Figure 3. The three selection rules retain different subsets at each cut. VideoMamba-Ti uses ρ = 0.5 on eight randomly drawn Kinetics-400 validation clips. Yellow, pink and blue mark tokens dropped after blocks 6, 12 and 18, respectively. Tokens in their original colors survive all three cuts. Each clip shows the ground-truth class and each rule’s prediction.

Figure 16. The six fixed TextVQA examples compare retained patches and answers across Cobra selectors at a nominal 10% of LM FLOPs. Dimmed patches are dropped, and incorrect answers appear in red. These are examples 8–13 of the gallery introduced in Fig. 15.

Figure 17. The remaining TextVQA and GQA examples compare Cobra selectors at a nominal 10% of LM FLOPs. Dimmed patches are dropped, and incorrect answers appear in red. These are examples 14–19 of the gallery introduced in Fig. 15.

Figure 15. The same seven POPE questions reveal different selections and answers across rules. These are examples 1–7 of the 19 fixed Cobra examples. The nominal 10% LM FLOP budget retains 46 of 729 tokens at the projector, or 34 after layer 2 for DTP. Dimmed patches are dropped. Panel titles give each rule’s answer and p(yes). Incorrect answers appear in red. The evaluation harness scores an exact bf16 tie as “yes,” marked “tie” here.

Table 4. ProbConv reduces WER relative to zero-mask training. LibriSpeech test-clean WER (%, lower is better) for Mambabased HuBERT with greedy character CTC and no language model. Half the frames survive layer 6. The final CTC head sees the restored sequence. Learned rows share selector architecture, initialization and budget. Mean ± standard deviation over five seeds for causal scratch and three for the other columns. Bold: the lowest WER among the selection rules. Full results: App. 6.

Figure 9. Straight-through ProbConv with step gating agrees across H-Net’s two evaluations. Open markers show validation bits per base using the training computation, and filled markers show the deployed hard forward. The horizontal axis gives realized bases per chunk at target N=3. Points are means over three seeds. Values in Tab. 23.

Figure 24. DyVM’s recurring selection cluster overlaps the SigLIP outlier token at grid position (21,2), marked by the dotted square. The first two maps summarize feature norm relative to the median and cross-image cosine similarity over 300 POPE images. The remaining maps show selection frequencies at 10% of LM FLOPs for ProbConv, adapted DyVM and the layer-0 ∆ score on the images used in Fig. 14.

Figure 12. ProbConv scores higher on GQA and VQAv2 in every seed pair across the four comparisons shown. The plot gives ProbConv’s score minus the comparison score at a nominal 10% of LM FLOPs (11.3% for the benchmark prompts). Dots give the mean, and bars span the three paired differences.

Figure 10. ProbConv leads the plotted training-time comparisons at the tight Cobra budget. The figure gives the sixbenchmark mean at 10% of LM FLOPs against the cost of one GH200 run. Labels give optimizer steps, and bars span three seeds. The dotted line marks the cost of ProbConv with the CUDA kernel.

Figure 13. In the left example, ProbConv is the only one of the seven visualized selection rules to read the logo correctly. Each panel shows the answers from dense Cobra and ProbConv at a nominal 10% of LM FLOPs; on the left, the zero-mask arms answer “Ctas” and “Gcts” and DTP “Gcts”. The table gives retained tokens (of 196 patches in Vim-Tiny, 1,568 in VideoMamba-Ti and 729 visual tokens in Cobra-3B) and compute per image or video view. Each block reports mean test MCC×100. ∆ pairs folds against the first row in the block, which serves as the reference (dashes). The p-values use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over task–fold pairs. “Cont.” identifies the released checkpoint after 1,000 additional masked language modeling steps on hg38 with the specified router.

The Mamba-based HuBERT encoder retains half of the frames after layer 6 and restores dropped positions before greedy character CTC decoding. Results give LibriSpeech WER without a language model, as means and standard deviations over five seeds for causal training from scratch and three otherwise. “Fine-tuned from dense” adapts the trained dense model of the same seed for 20k steps.

Table 1. ProbConv leads at the tight budget, also at equal training time. Cobra-3B mean score (%) on GQA, VQAv2, TextVQA, POPE, VSR and VizWiz [13, 19, 23, 33, 38, 58]. Percentages in the headers denote remaining LM FLOPs (dense: 65.8% mean score). The upper block uses training-free rules. Lower rows train the selector on a frozen backbone (three seeds, mean ± standard deviation). DyVM predictor: DyVM’s predictor and objective, without or with its rearranged forward. papers.title: Train What You Run: Probabilistic Convolutions for Learning Token Compaction in State Space Models

papers.abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
authors: Ayush Barik, Fan Lai, Francis Y. Yan
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of selecting and compressing video evidence without modeling the value of additional tokens.
Formulates video retrieval-augmented generation as token allocation over frames and subtitles under a shared budget.
Uses an iterative water-filling algorithm with a provable convergence guarantee to optimize allocation.
Reuses tokens and VLM attention across multi-turn conversations without extra processing cost.
Improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points at comparable compute, and by up to 1.5 points with 1.7–17.3× fewer TFLOPs in multi-turn understanding.

papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $\sigma_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.
bullets: Across 58 open-weight LLMs from 14 families, FFN intrinsic dimensionality consistently follows a middle-heavy layer profile.
The profile is robust across calibration corpora and languages and remains largely preserved after post-training fine-tuning.
PCA-guided width pruning improves distilled students over uniform widths on four teachers, with gains depending on how unevenly dimensionality is distributed.
An inverted allocation performs worst, supporting the structural relevance of the measured dimensionality signal.
The advantage also persists after downstream supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines reconstruct a scene from images in a single forward pass, representing it as real-time-renderable 3D Gaussians. However, the resulting representations contain far more Gaussians than are needed to render the scene faithfully, especially when there are many input views. This drastically increases memory and storage requirements. Existing pruning methods either require costly re-optimization, which defeats the purpose of a single forward pass, or rely on simple strategies that do not exploit all the available information. We present AnyPrune, a transformer-based, optimization-free pruning module designed to work on top of any feedforward 3DGS pipeline. To remove unnecessary Gaussians, AnyPrune learns and exploits pipeline-specific redundancy patterns through a short single-GPU training on the frozen target feedforward pipeline. AnyPrune achieves better rendering quality than existing optimization-free pruning methods in most settings and generalizes to unseen datasets, as shown through extensive experiments across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input view counts. It prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about $5\,\mathrm{s}$ on a consumer GPU, faster than every method that merges Gaussians or re-optimizes the field. It can also be combined with the pruning built into feedforward pipelines, pruning further at moderate ratios while preserving or improving rendering quality. Finally, it can even suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that retains most of the quality.
authors: Nicola Leonetti, Federico Stella, Aoxiang Fan, Saqib Javed, Pascal Fua, Luigi Di Stefano
bullets: Addresses excessive Gaussian counts that increase memory and storage, particularly with many input views.
Uses a transformer-based pruning module trained briefly on a frozen target pipeline to learn pipeline-specific redundancy.
Works across multiple feedforward pipelines, datasets, and input-view counts, including unseen datasets.
Prunes a 1.6M-Gaussian field in about 5 seconds on a consumer GPU.
Can complement built-in pruning and suggest a scene-specific pruning ratio that preserves most quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of AnyPrune. A frozen feedforward 3DGS pipeline predicts the Gaussians G from the input views. G is rendered from the input poses and the render error Ev is used to compute a per-Gaussian feature vector fi which is encoded by an MLP and processed by the transformer together with the other features. As in SplatFormer, every head reads the per-Gaussian features computed by the backbone and, via a residual connection, the attributes of the input Gaussians. The residual heads predict adjustments to refine G into G′; the mask head predicts a log-space adjustment hi to be added to the Speedy-Splat sensitivity score Si to obtain each Gaussian’s keep logit zi (Eq. (3)). zi is used at training time to compute a factor mi = σ(zi/τ) by which to multiply the refined opacities of the Gaussians before rendering them. The masked field is rendered from the input and held-out views and supervised with Eq. (4), whose photometric term is denoted Lphoto. A sparsity term in the loss pushes the network to prune the redundant Gaussians. At inference, instead of using the soft mask, the user can either keep the k Gaussians with the highest zi to meet a budget, or those with zi > 0 for the model’s own budget.
