papers.abstract: We present VenusOCR2.0, a compact 1B-parameter vision-language recognizer designed for both high-accuracy and high-throughput document parsing across text, tables, and formulas. To continuously improve recognition quality without self-training collapse, we build a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) data engine where the model acts strictly as a weakness probe, while external multi-expert medoid consensus, VLM visual verification, and factorized synthesis supply reliable supervision across pretraining, curated SFT, and RLVR. VenusOCR2.0 couples a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder and 2x2 spatial token merging with a Qwen3-0.6B decoder, adopting compact atomic OTSL tokens to shorten table sequences and reduce structural errors. To further eliminate the autoregressive decoding bottleneck, we introduce PTPv2, a lightweight ($\sim$67M) decoupled parallel draft module that combines frozen multi-layer verifier conditioning, a standalone learned mask, and block-causal all-position next-token prediction. On OmniDocBenchv1.6, VenusOCR2.0 achieves an overall score of 96.45 and a state-of-the-art 98.57 formula CDM, substantially outperforming massive general-purpose VLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). Deployed in vLLM on a single H20 GPU, PTPv2 delivers a 2.96x single-request speedup and up to 2.36x higher batched throughput while guaranteeing lossless, token-for-token equivalence with standard autoregressive decoding.
authors: Lei Li, Zheng Wei, Yi Yuan, Qingbin Liu, Jiang Bian, Zang Li
bullets: Targets unified parsing of text, tables, and formulas with high accuracy and throughput.
Uses bounded recursive self-improvement with external expert consensus, visual verification, and factorized synthesis to create reliable supervision.
Combines a dynamic-resolution SigLIP2 encoder, spatial token merging, Qwen3-0.6B decoder, and compact OTSL table tokens.
Introduces PTPv2, a ~67M-parameter parallel draft module that preserves token-for-token equivalence with autoregressive decoding.
On OmniDocBenchv1.6, reports 96.45 overall and 98.57 formula CDM; PTPv2 provides up to 2.96× single-request speedup and 2.36× batched throughput on one H20 GPU.

papers.abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Jyotirmoy Nath, Neeraj Kumar, Brejesh Lall
bullets: Global freezing thresholds can prematurely remove small or slowly converging edits in multi-edit instructions.
TIDE localizes each instruction part using the editor’s attention and unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models.
It freezes tokens based on part-relative prediction drift, estimates their endpoints, and sparsely computes only active tokens.
On FLUX.2 Klein, TIDE reduces dropped edits by up to 77% at matched or higher speed and achieves up to 4.89× acceleration with 5.3× fewer TFLOPs.
It also performs fastest on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 across the reported benchmarks, though results are limited to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

papers.title: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
papers.tldr: TIDE accelerates multi-edit image generation without retraining by assigning each instruction part its own token-freezing budget, preserving edits while reducing computation.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models often retain only a limited set of past token positions for an attention query. A common strategy scores positions individually and keeps the highest-ranked K. Yet attention weights are renormalized over the chosen set: two individually important positions need not form the best pair. We ask whether independent ranking suffices even when each importance score measures the exact downstream change in next-token predictions caused by deleting that position alone. It does not. A four-position construction makes the ranked pair incur 133.2 times the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of the optimal pair, and a parametric family proves that this multiplicative gap is unbounded. An exact exchange identity and preference reversals for every K >= 2 explain the interaction. In exhaustive frozen-model audits of SmolLM2, Gemma, and Qwen, exact-singleton Top-4 leaves at least 10% relative improvement within a fully enumerated 24-position candidate pool in 55/60, 49/60, and 60/60 cases, respectively. SwapCert, a same-budget one-swap audit, detects 157/164 such cases and returns directly checkable improving supports. A KL-margin certificate relates support fidelity to next-token stability; larger-budget, multi-layer cached-decoding experiments measure predictive fidelity at K = 128 and 256. These results establish joint support quality as an essential object of analysis for sparse attention and motivate downstream-aware support selection under inference constraints.
bullets: Individually important positions may form a poor set after attention renormalization; optimal selection must account for interactions.
A four-position example yields a 133.2× KL-divergence gap, while a parametric family shows the gap can be unbounded.
Exhaustive audits find at least 10% improvement opportunities over exact-singleton Top-4 in 55/60 SmolLM2, 49/60 Gemma, and 60/60 Qwen cases.
SwapCert detects 157/164 such cases using a same-budget one-swap audit and provides checkable improving supports.
KL-margin certificates and larger-budget experiments connect support quality to next-token stability and predictive fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes top-K token selection and joint support quality in sparse LLM attention, directly relevant to token pruning and efficient attention.
papers.title: When Exact Token Importance Is Not Enough: Limits of Top-K Selection in LLM Attention
papers.tldr: Independent Top-K token selection can fail badly in sparse LLM attention—even with exact single-token importance—because token interactions make joint support quality essential.

papers.abstract: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth directly, LoopDVR reuses Transformer blocks across layers in both the ViT backbone and Transformer decoder, reducing the number of parameters while retaining the original computational structure. However, naively sharing parameters can disrupt the distinct transformations learned at different depths. To address this challenge, we identify suitable sharing groups based on inter-layer representation dissimilarity and keep the final backbone block independent for multi-scale feature construction. We then initialize each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its group's terminal layer to better preserve the learned representations. An independent Loop Adapter at each layer further helps retain depth-specific transformations within shared blocks. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone and integrate it with a looped decoder for task-specific training. Experiments demonstrate that LoopDVR achieves the best accuracy--parameter trade-offs across dense recognition tasks. Compared with the reference models, it reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy. Notably, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 box AP with only 7.0M parameters, highlighting its effectiveness in compact models.
authors: Sirui Liang, Xuanlong Yu, Longfei Liu, Xiaodong Cun, Xi Shen
bullets: Targets parameter reduction in dense visual recognition without directly shrinking network width or depth.
Shares Transformer blocks across selected layer groups in both the ViT backbone and decoder, while keeping the final backbone block independent for multi-scale features.
Uses representation-dissimilarity-based sharing groups, terminal-layer initialization, and per-layer Loop Adapters to preserve depth-specific transformations.
Applies visual representation distillation before task-specific training with the looped decoder.
Reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy; LoopDet-S reaches 50.9 box AP with 7.0M parameters.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $\tau$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $\tau$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.
authors: Yifeng Lin, Liuxiang Qiu, Yunfeng Chen, Tiesong Zhao
bullets: Fixed-scale token pruning can miss information needed at different manipulation stages and adds computational overhead.
The training-free method uses a single perception temperature, τ, to control the scale of retained visual representations.
τ is updated online from semantic trends, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating adaptation strength.
Stable semantics across consecutive frames enable asynchronous reuse of token-retention indices during inference.
Evaluations across VLA models, simulation benchmarks, and two real robots show effective speedups with near-baseline success rates.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are a predominant architecture for computer vision, with token reduction emerging as a popular paradigm to improve their efficiency. Prior work compares reduction algorithms, but not how models respond to them, nor how their response changes with model depth. We propose Monte Carlo Token Pruning (MCTP), which estimates each token's impact on the prediction when tokens are explicitly removed during the forward pass. Applying MCTP to recent pretrained models, we observe that most, such as DINOv3, maintain a similar ranking of token importance at every depth (high Coherent Aggregation), while SigLIP 2 does not. This coherence requires predictions to survive pruning, which depends on keeping high-norm "sink" tokens: prefix tokens are kept by design, while prefix-free SigLIP 2 forms them on patch tokens, which pruning may remove. We show that in removing DINOv3's prefix tokens, its predictions and coherence collapse, while protecting only 5 tokens for SigLIP 2 cuts the token impact outside the object's bounding box by up to 62%. Beyond this, MCTP offers a post-hoc method to evaluate how a pretrained ViT responds to pruning, and suggests that token reduction methods should keep "sinks".
bullets: Introduces Monte Carlo Token Pruning (MCTP), which measures token importance by explicitly removing tokens during inference.
Most tested pretrained models, including DINOv3, preserve similar token-importance rankings across depth; SigLIP 2 does not.
DINOv3’s prefix tokens act as protected sink tokens, while prefix-free SigLIP 2 forms sinks on patch tokens that pruning can remove.
Removing DINOv3 prefix tokens collapses prediction quality and coherence; protecting five SigLIP 2 tokens reduces out-of-object token impact by up to 62%.
MCTP provides a post-hoc way to assess pruning responses and motivates protecting sink tokens during token reduction.

papers.selection_reason: Token pruning analysis with protected sink tokens for ViTs; directly relevant to efficient token reduction.
papers.title: Token Pruning Needs a Protected Sink Token: Coherent Spatial Aggregation in Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Token pruning in ViTs requires preserving high-norm sink tokens to maintain coherent spatial aggregation and reliable predictions.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometry models such as VGGT recover camera parameters, depth maps, and point maps from one to hundreds of views in a single forward pass, making them powerful backbones for multi-view 3D perception. However, VGGT's global attention is quadratic in the number of frames and dominates end-to-end runtime on long sequences, which has motivated a range of training-free efficiency methods such as token merging. These methods, however, come with a drop in accuracy that makes them hard to use in place of VGGT. We propose GPA-VGGT, a training-free acceleration method that replaces global attention in early blocks with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set. In the remaining blocks, we merge only keys and values while preserving all queries, restore the attention mass of the tokens each merged key represents, and randomly project the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching cost. Across diverse multi-view geometry tasks, GPA-VGGT provides training-free acceleration at speedups comparable to prior work while preserving the information required for precise geometric estimation, retaining over 99% of VGGT's pose accuracy under AUC@3.
bullets: Targets VGGT’s quadratic global-attention runtime on long multi-view sequences.
Uses frame attention with shared cross-frame keys/values in early blocks.
Later merges only keys and values, preserves all queries, and restores represented-token attention mass.
Randomly projects the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching overhead.
Achieves speedups comparable to prior training-free methods across multi-view geometry tasks while preserving precise estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of GPA-VGGT. Early blocks 0–8 replace global attention with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set containing special tokens and content-adaptive pooled image-token summaries. Later blocks 9–23 preserve all queries and merge only K/V tokens, using a weaker merge ratio in the core blocks 13–16. (a) Pooled summaries are constructed by assigning patch tokens to stride-8 seeds according to cosine similarity and averaging the K/V tokens within each content-adaptive cluster; the summary size determines the + log s correction. (b) K/V matching is computed after a 128-dimensional Gaussian projection, while all queries are retained for global attention.

Figure 5. Qualitative reconstruction under estimated camera poses. Each column shows the point cloud produced by the corresponding method, and red boxes indicate the enlarged regions below. GPA-VGGT most closely matches the geometry reconstructed by vanilla VGGT.

Figure 2. Two sources of accuracy degradation in existing token-merging methods. Top: Query merging collapses the block-12 outputs of 83 tokens into 12 shared outputs, whereas retaining all queries while merging only K/V preserves the output diversity of the unmerged model. Bottom: Omitting the + log s correction disproportionately allocates attention to the first frame. Restoring the correction recovers an attention distribution close to that of the unmerged model.

Figure 1. Accuracy and runtime scaling with the number of input frames. Although existing acceleration methods substantially reduce end-to-end runtime, they incur pronounced camera-pose degradation under the strict AUC@3 metric. GPA-VGGT achieves comparable runtime while maintaining camera-pose accuracy close to that of vanilla VGGT.

Figure 3. Effect of cross-frame context in the early blocks. Top: Replacing global attention with frame attention substantially displaces the block-8 output field from the full-global-attention reference, whereas the shared cross-frame K/V set largely preserves it. Bottom: Pairwise alignment of per-frame drift directions. Cross-frame special tokens partially align the drift, and image-token summaries further reduce its variation, preserving a coherent geometric reference across views.

papers.abstract: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.
authors: Boyang Wang, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Oindrila Saha, Matheus Gadelha, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Condition tokens from modalities such as identity, scribbles, depth, and motion videos create substantial computation and memory costs.
A codec-based pruning method removes redundant spatiotemporal conditioning tokens.
On-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter to reproduce the codec’s pruning pattern without degrading quality.
Scaled to 16 conditioning modalities, it prunes 66% of condition tokens on average, makes denoising 2× faster, and reduces KV-cache memory by up to 73%.
Benefits extend to pretrained image and video generators and increase with more conditions, longer videos, and higher resolution.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based view synthesis models render each target viewpoint from the source images, without an explicit 3D representation, which lets them reproduce fine detail and view-dependent effects. However, their decoder attends to every source token for every frame, so rendering slows with each source image. Rasterization avoids this by culling primitives that the viewpoint does not see, but source tokens cannot be culled this way, as they have no explicit position or extent. Our key insight is that source tokens are nonetheless spatial anchors: each encodes a local region of the scene, so the decoder's attention for any viewpoint concentrates on a few of them. A lightweight router predicts these tokens from the source tokens and the viewpoint, and the decoder attends only to a fixed budget of top-ranked tokens, so its cost no longer depends on the number of source tokens. We supervise the router with the decoder's attention, using non-maximum suppression to demote redundant tokens. With 24 source images and two views' worth of tokens, our model renders 6.4 times faster than LagerNVS, at a PSNR only 0.68 dB lower. One ranking serves every budget, so the budget can change at render time.
bullets: Source tokens act as local spatial anchors, enabling viewpoint-dependent token culling without explicit 3D geometry.
A lightweight router ranks tokens using source features and the target viewpoint; the decoder attends only to a fixed top-token budget.
Router training uses decoder attention supervision and non-maximum suppression to reduce redundant selections.
With 24 source images, rendering is 6.4× faster than LagerNVS while achieving PSNR only 0.68 dB lower.
A single token ranking supports changing the compute budget at render time.

papers.abstract: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.
authors: Chaofan Li, Qihan Ding, Shihan Wang, Zhehao Shen, Boyu Shen, Quanyu Chen, Haoyu Wu, Lan Xu, Xin Lou
bullets: Targets the challenge of streaming feed-forward 3D Gaussian human reconstructions under strict bandwidth and lightweight-client constraints.
Splits the reconstructor before its Gaussian head and uses multi-rate token streaming with server-side compression and client-side restoration.
Combines opacity-guided pruning, PCA reduction, lossless anchor geometry coding, and a feature-reconstruction hypernetwork.
Neural Session Calibration fine-tunes the Gaussian head during warm-up to handle novel cameras and changing capture conditions without per-frame overhead.
Achieves 32.2 FPS at 50 Mbit/s, 22.1 ms decoding on an RTX 3050 Ti, 22.8× less data than float32 Gaussians, and a 1.050 dB PSNR gain after calibration.

On the server (blue), each frame undergoes eight-view matting, PointSplat up to its head, opacity-guided token pruning, PCA to rank r with b-bit quantisation, and lossless anchor coding. papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $\pi_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.
bullets: Token approximation error is a poor routing signal: it can be 1.3–1.7× worse for action deviation than input novelty.
Novelty is measured by whether a token falls outside the calibration subspace, favoring action-relevant views such as the wrist camera.
The training-free method routes each token once per layer to either a low-rank or original MLP, enabling static-shape CUDA-graph execution.
On LIBERO, it accelerates the π₀.₅ prefix by up to 1.61× and remains 2.7–2.9× closer to the original policy than competing compression methods at equal compute.
Closed-loop task success is preserved.

(b) Eager execution, same score and exact fraction: deciding once per token and layer instead of once per product moves the whole front to the right.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the cost of long-context decoding, but token selection introduces additional scoring and ranking overhead. Moreover, uniform page scoring overlooks differences in relevance between near and far context. We propose Near-Far Attention (NFA), which adapts retrieval to regional attention patterns while keeping candidate scoring lightweight. During prefill, the Lightweight Gate Estimator identifies regions that can be skipped during decoding, adding less than 1% to dense-prefill time. For the remaining regions, the Calibration-Free Subspace Extractor supplies compact features shared by page-level and token-level scoring without offline calibration. The Distance-Aware Two-Level Selector then scores near and far pages differently and jointly ranks candidate tokens under a shared budget. Evaluations across model families, parameter scales, and GQA/MLA architectures show aggregate task quality comparable to full attention. On Qwen3-8B at 512K context length, NFA achieves up to $5.49\times$ operator speedup and $2.97\times$ whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.
authors: YuanShuo Wang, Jianchao Tan, Lei Gong, Teng Wang, Wenqi Lou, Xuehai Zhou
bullets: Addresses retrieval overhead and the limits of uniform page scoring in sparse attention.
Uses a Lightweight Gate Estimator during prefill to skip low-value regions with under 1% added dense-prefill time.
Extracts compact, calibration-free features for both page- and token-level scoring.
A distance-aware two-level selector ranks near and far pages and candidate tokens under a shared budget.
On Qwen3-8B at 512K context, achieves up to 5.49× operator and 2.97× whole-model decoding speedup over FlashInfer, including selection overhead.

(b) Compact query and key representations are shared by both selection levels. papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. However, existing compression methods on selective context risk losing global information, recursively rewriting summary leads to semantic drift, while repeatedly recompressing the full history shifts the growing cost to the compressor. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. DMC-5 maintains the raw trajectory as an Append-only Canonical View, preserving global access while allowing the compressor to reuse a stable historical prefix instead of recursively rewriting or recomputing prior context. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. DMC-5 further incorporates YAMATO (integritY-Aware Memory Abstractions for Tool Operations) to preserve execution-critical information during lossy compression. Experiments on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA show that DMC-5 reduces agent model input by 38.5-57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5-28.0% with 78.0-85.0% compressor cache-hit rates, while improving task performance by 1.0-5.8% over the uncompressed baseline.
authors: Haochen Li, Xiaobing Tu, Yinggui Wang, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang
bullets: Addresses growing trajectory context, irrelevant history, semantic drift, and repeated recompression costs.
Uses an Append-only Canonical View for stable full-history access and a compact Decision View for action generation.
Combines dual-model collaboration with YAMATO to preserve execution-critical tool information during lossy compression.
On AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA, reduces agent input by 38.5–57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5–28.0%.
Reports 78.0–85.0% compressor cache-hit rates and 1.0–5.8% higher task performance than the uncompressed baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of DMC-5. (a) A general compressor V integrates Append-only Canonical View, while a specialized agent Urizen acts on compact Decision View. (b) Each compression round reuses the stable historical prefix and only prefills new suffix. (c) YAMATO restores executioncritical records through pointers from raw records and combines them with recent raw turns.

Figure 1: Motivation and overview of DMC-5. (a) Long-horizon agents repeatedly reread a growing trajectory, increasing cost while decision-relevant information is sparse. (b) Existing compression patterns trade off global information, semantic stability, and repeated compressor processing. (c) DMC-5 separates full-history integration from action generation: an Append-only Canonical View enables stable prefix reuse for the general compressor, while a compact Decision View retains recent and execution-critical information for the specialized agent. (d) DMC-5 improves the cost– performance trade-off over the uncompressed specialized agent and existing compression baselines.

papers.title: DMC-5: Dual-Model Collaboration with Cache-aware Context Compression for Long-horizon Agents
papers.tldr: DMC-5 compresses long-horizon agent histories using cache-aware collaboration between a general compressor and a specialized action model, reducing input and cost while improving task performance.

papers.abstract: Dense feed-forward networks are unaffected by how their neurons are grouped: every neuron is evaluated. Sparse execution makes this grouping consequential, because each input can access only a few experts. An arbitrary partition can therefore retain pretrained weights while separating computations that an input needs together. We argue that upcycling should organize neurons according to their responses to similar inputs. To establish this correspondence, we introduce a context-guided upcycling approach REACT, Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories, that uses frozen denoising trajectories to connect input contexts with pretrained neuron responses. We first identify contexts after timestep-wise centering to account for distribution shifts across noise levels, then use their associated responses to allocate intact neurons to routed experts. The same contexts initialize the corresponding router entries, aligning expert contents with their intended inputs, while global activation statistics select an always-active shared expert. Layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation refine this initialization for sparse execution. On ImageNet-1K, our approach achieves better generation quality while activating only 37.5% of the original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activated parameters by 27.6%.
authors: Hesen Yang, Yuxue Liu, Yanzhe Chen, Weibo Zhao, Junwei Su, Dan Hu, Shenggan Cheng, Xuanlei Zhao, Wenchao Zhou, Junhua Wang, Lansong Diao, Yang You
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between arbitrary neuron partitioning and the input-dependent computation required by sparse execution.
Uses frozen denoising trajectories to identify timestep-normalized contexts and associate them with pretrained neuron responses.
Allocates intact neurons to routed experts, initializes router entries from the same contexts, and adds a globally active shared expert.
Refines the initialization through layer-wise reconstruction and end-to-end adaptation.
On ImageNet-1K, achieves better generation quality while activating 37.5% of original FFN parameters and reducing total per-token activation by 27.6%.

(a) Frozen trajectories define timestep-centered token clusters whose responses assemble routed experts and whose centroids initialize same-index router rows; pooled co-activation selects shared units. (b) Only the router input is centered at run time; experts receive the original state. (c) Stage I matches sparse FFNs to dense teachers, and Stage II adapts the full denoiser.

Figure 1: Why grouping matters under sparse execution. Orange marks the eight of 32 pretrained units needed by one token. Dense execution reaches all units, whereas a random partition leaves only four accessible through top-2 routing. REACT groups units by response and initializes each router row from the matching context, restoring access to all eight. This is a conceptual illustration, not a measurement.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes REACT for sparse execution in feed-forward networks using 'contextual trajectories' to route experts. The concept of using trajectories for routing and efficiency is transferable to World Models (Latent Action Models) and Embodied AI (memory/trajectories).
papers.title: REACT: Response-based Expert Assembly from Contextual Trajectories
papers.tldr: REACT upcycles dense feed-forward networks into sparse routed experts by grouping neurons according to their responses to similar input contexts.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting renders photorealistic views in real time. However, a single scene often needs millions of Gaussians, so these models are costly to store and render. Pruning reduces this cost by keeping a subset of the Gaussians. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when a Gaussian alone is removed. At high pruning ratios, many Gaussians are removed together, so Gaussians that are redundant alone but essential together are lost. We present LMnOP (Leave-Many-Out Pruning), which estimates the importance of each Gaussian under the removal of the other Gaussians. This leave-many-out importance is the average loss increase when a Gaussian is removed while the others are also removed at random. We compute the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form, and approximate the importance from them without sampling removal patterns. We refine each Gaussian's probability of remaining with its importance and prune once at the end. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics on three datasets at 90% and 99% removal. It improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.
authors: Sunjae Jeong, Jaeseung Kim, Hyoseok Hwang
bullets: Targets the storage and rendering cost of scenes containing millions of 3D Gaussians.
Addresses the limitation of leave-one-out scores, which can miss Gaussians that are redundant individually but important together.
Computes exact per-pixel color mean and variance under random Gaussian removal in closed form, avoiding sampled removal patterns.
Updates each Gaussian’s retention probability from its estimated leave-many-out importance and prunes only once.
Without fine-tuning, achieves the best result on 16 of 18 metrics across three datasets at 90% and 99% removal; improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LMnOP. Every Gaussian starts with the keep probability K/N , and the histograms show the keep probabilities after r updates. µ-σ rendering gives the mean and variance of each pixel’s color under the current keep probabilities, and we compute the LMO importance of every Gaussian from them. We then move each keep probability halfway toward bi and compute the importance again. Here bi is 1 for the K Gaussians with the highest importance and 0 for the others. After R importance computations, we keep these K Gaussians and prune the rest in one final step.

Figure 3. Quality of pruned models on the 3DGS training curve. Bicycle, without fine-tuning. Top: the original model and LMnOP at 90% removal, with the PSNR / LPIPS of the view. The zoomed region in the red box shows slight white artifacts in the pruned model. Bottom: test PSNR and LPIPS of 3DGS during training. Each marker places a pruned model where 3DGS reaches the same value. The markers indicate quality, not training time.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. (a) Treehill and Playroom at 90% removal and (b) Bicycle and Garden at 99% removal, without fine-tuning. Red boxes mark high-frequency regions, and green boxes mark low-frequency regions.

Figure 5. PSNR and LPIPS across pruning ratios. MipNeRF360, without fine-tuning. Each point is a separate pruning of the original model. The horizontal axis is spaced by the logarithm of the kept fraction.
Table 3. Pruning models trained with different methods. LPIPS (↓) on Mip-NeRF360 at 90% and 99% removal, without finetuning. The first row is the original model.
Table 4. Fine-tuning after pruning. Mip-NeRF360 at 90% removal. All methods use the same 5,000 steps with a fixed number of Gaussians. Each block is ranked separately.

Table 2. Importance of paired Gaussians in the original and the pruned model. Each pair has the same leave-one-out importance. LMnOP keeps one Gaussian of each pair and removes the other. Values are medians (×10−6). Bars show each pair on a common scale.
Table 5. Ablation. Mip-NeRF360 without fine-tuning. The first row is the baseline, leave-one-out importance under the squared error in a single pruning stage, and the last row is LMnOP.

papers.selection_reason: Pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives via leave-many-out importance is a token-level pruning/eviction method for efficient rendering.
papers.title: LMnOP: Pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting via Leave-Many-Out Importance
papers.tldr: LMnOP prunes 3D Gaussian Splatting models more effectively at extreme removal rates by estimating each Gaussian’s importance in the presence of other simultaneous removals.

papers.abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
authors: Ce Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jinxi He, Xiyuan Yang, Pan Wang, Han Liu, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful evidence in a single pass under bounded frame storage and unknown future questions.
Groups recurring failures by cause and searches papers, model cards, and code for adaptable methods or pretrained perception models.
Can jointly add perceptual capabilities and revise how their evidence is stored and retrieved.
Selects accuracy-improving revisions on validation streams, then optimizes for faster revisions within a quality tolerance.
Across three benchmarks, it achieves the best accuracy within frozen-backbone comparisons; on OVO-Bench, it reaches 75.1% accuracy with 0.30-second average response time using Qwen3-VL-8B.

figures.caption: Figure 1. From manual design to open-world harness evolution. (a) Researchers design and revise the memory and retrieval pipelines of streaming systems [8, 54, 57, 63]. (b) Video recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods [22, 24, 26] automate harness revision from execution feedback within a preconfigured set of models and tools. (c) MORSE makes online research part of this loop. An LLM-based Editor investigates observed failures through papers, model cards, and code, then adapts existing methods and requests missing perception tools. Host-reviewed tool acquisition lets the harness and its available capabilities evolve together around a frozen answering VLM.

Figure 4. Inference efficiency on OVO-Bench. Measured mean answer latency and streaming write cost, using Qwen3-VL-8B for all methods. Each bar separates VLM calls from calls to other models. The direct VLM uses at most 128 frames at 1 fps without memory; H0, HS7, and HS11 are the seed, the harness after the accuracy rounds, and the final harness.

Figure 2. The MORSE optimization loop. Left: the harness Hk writes observations to memory through WH and retrieves evidence through RH for the frozen VLM F . Middle: the LLM-based Editor diagnoses errors and costly operations from training traces, researches solutions, proposes executable revisions, and validates them on private streams. Right: papers, model cards, and code inform program edits and tool requests; approved tools become callable after host integration. Below: accuracy rounds improve answer quality; efficiency rounds reduce latency with bounded quality loss relative to both the parent and the stage-entry harness.

Figure 5. Memory of the final harness at question time on three OVO-Bench test questions (tasks EPM, ASI, and FPD). Questions and options are reproduced verbatim. Each panel gives the question, its options (green: correct; red: the seed’s choice), and both answers with the probability P (gold) of the correct option. The timeline shows what the write path stored from the start of the video to the question (black marker). Notes: captions every 16 s, chapter notes over four captions, and a step log of who does what (purple outline: steps cited in the answer prompt). Index: ViCLIP vectors of 16-s segments and 4-frame windows, darker when closer to the question and options. Frames: the 64-frame store (tall ticks: segment key frames; pale ticks: frames since forgotten). Tools: OWLv2 detections, dark if the noun is named in the question or options. Read: the frames sent to the VLM, retrieved key frames in purple and the 4 most recent frames in gray. Thumbnails show six of them with the selector that chose each: similarity to the question (CLIP, ViCLIP index), temporal coverage (recency, gap fill, caption gap), or the last strong scene change (visual change). The seed sends only the captions and the 4 most recent frames.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces MORSE, a framework for optimizing the memory harness of a frozen video-language model (Qwen3-VL-8B). It addresses the problem of selecting evidence to retain in a streaming video system, which aligns with both Multimodal Foundation Models (VLMs) and Efficient AI (token eviction/pruning). The use of open-world auto-research to adapt the system is a novel approach to memory optimization.
papers.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
papers.tldr: MORSE improves streaming video memory by using recurring failures to search for and integrate external research, achieving strong accuracy and efficient querying with frozen video-language backbones.

papers.abstract: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.
authors: Fu Dai, Haodi Quan, Kamal Taha
bullets: Short-sequence failures are mainly attributed to rotary positional encoding rather than content matching.
Random gaps in position IDs let the indexer and frozen teacher learn long-range positions without processing long sequences.
An 8K-distilled indexer nearly matches 32K- and, on one model, 64K-distilled quality; the reported training-cost reduction is about 6× per token.
3–4-bit key quantization requires no retraining; 4-bit keys change perplexity by at most 0.05 and yield 1.6–2.2× faster scans.
Benefits vary by model and serving setting: position compression can be competitive, and decoding speedups appear mainly for long contexts with multiple streams.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. Top, training. Left: an indexer distilled on 8K tokens sees only a small arc (blue) of a slow rotary pair, so at 64K it meets unseen rotations. (1) Position-skipped distillation lets the ids of T contiguous tokens jump by a random offset u after a cut point, so every distance up to the range R occurs. (2) The frozen model computes dense attention under the same ids, and each layer’s indexer matches its head-summed attention pt,s with a KL loss; only the indexer receives gradients. (3) Each token keeps one b-bit key, an integer scan scores all keys, and attention reads the k best (orange). Bottom, serving: in every layer H query heads are scored against the b-bit keys by a fused integer scan; beyond R the ids are scaled by ρ = R/L. Blue: our components.

Figure 2: ∆PPL over DENSE at k = 2048 as a function of the evaluation length, on a logarithmic axis; the values are those of Table 2. SHORT-8K fails beyond 8K and LONG-32K degrades beyond 32K. SKIP-64K, distilled on 8K sequences, stays at or below 1.23% up to 64K.

Figure 3: Jaccard overlap Jℓℓ′ of the top-2048 sets of all pairs of layers of DeepSeek-V2-Lite at the same query, at 32K, averaged over the last 1024 decoding steps of four PG-19 documents. Left: ORACLE selection. Right: SKIP-64K at native positions. The diagonal is 1 and is clipped by the colour scale.

Figure 4: Left: Jaccard overlap of the top-2048 sets of each layer and the previous one on DeepSeek-V2-Lite (four PG-19 documents, last 1024 decoding steps, indexer SKIP-64K). Orange ticks: the five retrieval layers. Right: SKIP-64K in all 27 layers (All) or in 8, the others reusing the nearest earlier selection; the passcode probe is in-sample for GAPFILL-8, the RULER tasks are held out (all seven in Table 18).

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods degrade substantially under aggressive pruning, especially on visual grounding (VG). We analyze the sources of this degradation from the perspective of the output shift that pruning causes in decoder layers, and decompose this shift in closed form into two terms, an image summary error and an attention allocation error. The summary error stems from the loss of visual information, and the allocation error from the drop in the share of attention assigned to visual tokens. To reduce both errors, we propose CAR (Coverage selection and Attention Reallocation), a token pruning framework that restores attention share while maintaining information. Specifically, to minimize the summary error, whose upper bound tightens as the retained tokens better cover all visual tokens, our coverage selection retains tokens that are both salient and non-redundant, with saliency from encoder heads chosen by a label-free probe. To minimize the allocation error, our attention reallocation reassigns the attention of the discarded tokens to the retained ones through a closed-form logit bias. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B with $90\%$ of the visual tokens pruned, CAR retains $93.0\%$ of the unpruned accuracy on visual question answering (VQA) and $77.9\%$ on VG, against $26.5\%$ for the best existing method on VG; the logit bias alone raises the VG accuracy of existing methods by up to $24$ points. Experiments on multiple MLLMs across VQA, VG and video understanding show that CAR generalizes well and consistently outperforms existing methods.
authors: Xixi Jiang, Pingcheng Dong, Chen Yang, Xin Yang, Kwang-Ting Cheng
bullets: Visual token pruning accelerates MLLMs but can sharply hurt performance, especially visual grounding, due to decoder output shift.
The shift is decomposed into image summary error from lost information and attention allocation error from reduced visual-token attention.
Coverage selection keeps salient, non-redundant tokens using a label-free encoder-head probe.
Attention reallocation transfers discarded-token attention to retained tokens via a closed-form logit bias.
With 90% pruning on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, CAR retains 93.0% of unpruned VQA accuracy and 77.9% of visual-grounding accuracy; results generalize across MLLMs and tasks.

papers.abstract: Adaptive visual token routers aim to save computation while preserving the image detail needed to answer each question. A higher average score could reflect better choices for individual images or more frequent use of high resolution on tasks that need it. We distinguish the two by keeping action counts fixed within each task and comparing the router's assignments with random pairings of the same actions and images. On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B gain from matching but lose more from their action frequencies relative to a task table, with a 1.71-point gain and a 3.95-point loss on 7B. Exchanging the continuous resolutions chosen by the external selector CARES also lowers quality on 7B. When requests arrive with task labels, the table outscores the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.
bullets: The study separates routing quality into action allocation and image–action matching while holding per-task action counts fixed.
On equally weighted ChartQA and TextVQA, both Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B benefit from matching, but deviate more from task-optimal action frequencies.
For Qwen2.5-VL-7B, matching adds 1.71 points, while its action-frequency choices cost 3.95 points relative to a task table.
Randomly exchanging CARES-selected continuous resolutions also reduces 7B quality, supporting the value of image–resolution matching.
With task labels, a task table beats the discrete router by 1.92 points and saves 31.76 ms per complete 7B request on average.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning can reduce the inference cost of vision language models, but its effectiveness depends on preserving complementary visual information under a limited token budget. A central challenge is to quantify the additional information a candidate token contributes beyond the retained set, a contribution that conventional scores based on attention or similarity struggle to capture directly. In this work, we revisit visual token pruning from the perspective of information gain and use mutual information to characterize the incremental value of candidate tokens. We further establish theoretically that frame potential serves as an effective surrogate for mutual information. Building on this observation, we propose FP-Prune, a training-free visual token pruning method that iteratively removes tokens with low information gain to preserve as much complementary visual information as possible. Experiments on three widely used VLMs and eight datasets demonstrate that FP-Prune outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and inference efficiency. Further analysis shows that the surrogate objective closely aligns with model performance. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an effective method for visual token pruning.
authors: Haozhe Zhao, Junxiang Zhang, Junxin Wang, Yuan Ge, Xiangchen Song, Dingyang Zhang, JingBo Zhu, Tong Xiao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of measuring a candidate token’s additional information beyond retained tokens.
Uses mutual information to characterize incremental token value and theoretically links it to frame potential.
Introduces a training-free, iterative pruning method that removes tokens with low information gain.
Experiments across three VLMs and eight datasets show improved accuracy and inference efficiency over baselines.
Analysis finds strong alignment between the surrogate objective and model performance.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence inference in large language models is constrained by the high cost of prefilling, where dense attention scales quadratically with context length. Exploiting similarity across attention heads offers a way to reduce redundant computation. Prior approaches in this direction have relied on localized query observations to determine head-level computation reuse or budget allocation. However, inter-head similarity does not imply uniform query requirements, leaving adaptation to varying budget needs and selection preferences across query regions a key challenge. We introduce QASparse, a Query-Adaptive Sparse attention mechanism with hardware-efficient execution. QASparse preserves the efficiency of shared cross-head importance estimation while adapting computational budgets and token selections to query requirements, and it executes these dynamic sparse decisions through dedicated kernels. Its query adaptivity stems from two complementary innovations: Local Budget Regression models local variations in computational demand along query positions to estimate budgets for different query regions and attention heads; Boundary Voting lets queries within each head vote over candidates near the selection cutoff using actual query/key scores, refining the retained set while preserving the initial selection size. To reduce the execution overhead of dynamic budgets, we further design length-specialized selection kernels that efficiently support query-adaptive sparse patterns across context lengths. Together, these designs efficiently combine shared estimation with local decisions while adapting both how much attention is computed and which interactions are retained. Experimental results demonstrate improved benchmark scores and faster prefill attention computation compared with existing sparse attention baselines.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Zihao Yang, Quanjiang Li, Haijiang Li, Jiancheng Pan, Qichao Zhao, Zihan Dong, Qiushi Shi, Jinshi Liu
bullets: Targets the quadratic cost of dense attention during long-sequence prefill and the limitations of uniform head-level sparsity.

Length-specialized kernels reduce the overhead of executing dynamic sparse patterns; experiments report better benchmark scores and faster prefill attention than prior sparse-attention baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) tokenize images using fixed spatial grids, so visual token count grows with pixel area rather than scene content. We propose to group neighboring patches based on their visual appearance, allowing tokens to represent coherent image regions rather than fixed spatial windows. We introduce RVLM, a VLM trained to use regions rather than patches as its visual units. Analyzing region construction for general-purpose VLMs, we find that regions must cover the full image, stay spatially connected during end-to-end training, and preserve fine structure such as small text, while semantic grouping adds little. RVLM therefore partitions images using training-free Felzenszwalb-Huttenlocher segmentation, assigns each ViT patch to a region, and pools patches within each region into a variable-length sequence of visual tokens. The patch-to-region assignment is retained to support spatially precise prediction through coarse-to-fine decoding. Across tasks spanning VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation, RVLM matches or improves example-weighted task performance while using 21.5% fewer visual tokens than an identically trained patch baseline. The advantage grows with image resolution, reaching a 5.3-point gain while using 51.8% fewer visual tokens at the highest-resolution setting. The gains are largest on spatially demanding tasks, where prior token-reduction methods degrade most sharply. RVLM adds no model parameters and improves inference throughput by up to 35.9%. On unseen pathology and satellite images and on video benchmarks without any video training, RVLM performs on par with the patch baseline while using 2-3$\times$ fewer visual tokens. These results establish regions as a scalable alternative to patch-based visual representations while preserving the spatial precision required for grounded prediction.
authors: Savya Khosla, Chris Dongjoo Kim, Alex Schwing, Derek Hoiem, Christopher Clark, Sangho Lee
bullets: Uses training-free Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher segmentation to group patches into variable-length, spatially connected regions.
Preserves full-image coverage and fine structure, including small text; semantic grouping is not essential.
Retains patch-to-region mappings for coarse-to-fine spatial prediction.
Matches or improves performance across VQA, pointing, counting, segmentation, and depth estimation while using 21.5% fewer tokens overall.
At higher resolutions, gains reach 5.3 points with 51.8% fewer tokens; inference throughput improves by up to 35.9%, with strong transfer to pathology, satellite, and video benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of RVLM. We generate content-adaptive regions using FelzenszwalbHuttenlocher segmentation and assign each ViT patch to a region. The retained patch-to-region correspondence enables coarse-to-fine spatial grounding, where the LLM selects a region, then a patch within it, and finally a precise point within the patch.

papers.abstract: A diffusion language sampler makes two choices for every position in its denoising window: where the next token comes from, and when the position is committed to the KV cache. Using the entropy-bound sampler in DiffusionGemma, we study two extremes of the second choice. Committing each token as soon as it is accepted removes the chance to revise it, which hurts when the entropy bound is relaxed to trade accuracy for speed. When accepted tokens are frozen, macro accuracy falls from 73% to 20% as the bound is relaxed, while the unfrozen sampler stays near 70%. Committing a whole block at once wastes computation, since tokens converge in a largely left-to-right order and more than half of the window holds already-final tokens by twenty denoising steps. These findings motivate the Rolling Entropy Sampler (RES), which commits a contiguous accepted prefix once it reaches a minimum length and keeps positions farther ahead open to revision. Unlike earlier rolling samplers, RES runs on uniform diffusion, where accepted tokens can still change, and it needs no training. Across seven benchmarks, RES increases tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, while macro accuracy goes from 80.7% to 78.8%, and it extends the speed-quality Pareto frontier beyond what tuning the entropy bound alone reaches.
authors: Patrick Pynadath, Nicolas Perez-Nieves, Bobak Shahriari, Jean Tarbouriech, Ruqi Zhang, Ivan Lobov
bullets: Immediate commitment harms quality when the entropy bound is relaxed, whereas leaving tokens revisable maintains accuracy.
Committing entire blocks wastes computation because tokens typically converge in a left-to-right order.
RES commits a contiguous accepted prefix after it reaches a minimum length and keeps later positions open for revision.
Across seven benchmarks, RES raises tokens per forward pass from 19.3 to 25.5, with macro accuracy decreasing from 80.7% to 78.8%.
RES requires no training and extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier beyond entropy-bound tuning alone.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Columns in the top and middle rows show LiveCodeBench, GPQA Diamond, and Natural2Code. Top row: Spearman 𝜌 and Kendall 𝜏 between the acceptance order of the DiffusionGemma EB sampler and the AR generation order; across all tasks the sampler is strongly biased towards left-to-right order. Middle row: Percentage of wasted denoising slots averaged across canvases for LCB v6, GPQA Diamond and Natural2Code. For a given sampling step, a slot is wasted if it belongs to a contiguous prefix that has already converged to its final token. By denoising step 20, the mean fraction of wasted canvas slots exceeds 50% on all three tasks. Bottom row: Accepted tokens are revised more often at higher entropy bounds (in both argmax and sampled-token stability), independent of renoising.

Figure 4 | Three passes of the rolling sampler. Every pass spends a fixed budget of ten positions (dashed frame), split between an encoded prefix of the tokens committed on the previous pass and the remaining denoising window; the mask panel on the right is exactly that block of ten. Left: positions keep their column, so each slot can be read down its column. Out-of-order acceptances wait for a contiguous prefix (w at 𝑡) and unaccepted slots stay mutable (column ten: r→ o). The prefix completing at 𝑡+1 is four slots long, so four slots must be encoded at 𝑡+2: the block advances by however many positions graduated into the KV cache, and the split is 0+10, then 2+8, then 4+6. Right: rows are queries, columns are keys; a coloured cell means the query attends to the key. The encoded prefix is causal, so its KV-cache entries depend only on committed tokens and are never revised, while denoising positions are bidirectional among themselves and attend fully to the prefix. Committing more positions per pass therefore moves the KV cache forward faster, but leaves fewer positions to denoise on the next pass. Every query additionally attends to the whole KV cache (white cells), which the panels omit for space.

Figure 1 | (a) The unified stopping criterion matches the original at a slight speedup. (b) Simulation of per-position commitment in DiffusionGemma: freezing each token upon acceptance removes the chance for later revision. Frozen variants degrade much faster than unfrozen variants as the entropy bound is relaxed, showing the cost of losing this sampler flexibility.

Figure 2 | Where the denoising slots go. Both samplers denoise a width-8 window per pass in the same order, and the colours are those of Figure 4: teal = still denoising, amber = accepted on this pass, white = already encoded and in the KV cache, gray = not yet admitted. Brick marks a slot spent re-denoising a position that was already accepted but is still waiting for its prefix, that is, wasted work. (a) The block sampler appends only once the block is fully resolved, so converged positions idle and each block re-pays warm-up. (b) The rolling sampler appends the accepted prefix immediately and admits fresh positions in its place, wasting far fewer slots.

papers.abstract: The decay exponent $\alpha$ in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as $s_i = A_i \cdot (t-i)^{-\alpha}$, where $A_i$ is cumulative attention and $\alpha$ controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to $\alpha=0$ and $\alpha\to\infty$, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of \citet{xiang2026nohair} bounds the admissible range of $\alpha$, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields $[0.556, 0.822]$ for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. \textsc{NoHairCache} achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM ($p < 0.05$ on all three datasets, with $0.06$--$0.10$ PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget $512$). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining $98.2\%$ of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at $25\%$ retention versus $91.1\%$ for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.
bullets: Frames H2O and StreamingLLM as endpoints of a shared score: cumulative attention weighted by token age via exponent α.
Calibrating α on WikiText produces model-consistent ranges that also align with perplexity-based optimal regions across five models.
Achieves the lowest perplexity on WikiText, PG19, and arXiv without per-dataset tuning, outperforming H2O and StreamingLLM.
Matches or exceeds StreamingLLM on all evaluated QA task–budget cells; QA results are treated as corroborating because per-cell tests are not significant.
The approach is scoped to calibrated model-specific exponent ranges and is accompanied by a calibration script and drop-in scorer.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Vision-Language Models solve multimodal reasoning tasks by retaining hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, allowing every generated token to attend to the visual tokens at any time during the generation process. However, whether continuous access to these visual tokens is necessary remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how visual token influence evolves along two dimensions: generation time and transformer depth. Using long-form visual reasoning benchmarks and multiple model scales, we first analyze the attention dynamics across generation time and transformer depth. We identify a temporal and depth-wise structure in the use of visual information. Visual attention peaks during the initial generation steps and then rapidly declines as attention shifts toward previously generated reasoning tokens. Across depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and becomes very weak in the final layers. We further verify these observations with causal intervention that removes all visual tokens across generation time and model depth. These interventions confirm that visual-token dependence in multimodal reasoning is neither temporally persistent nor uniformly distributed across transformer depth. Thus, retaining the complete visual context at every layer and decoding step may be unnecessary. Our experiments demonstrate that we can remove up to 59\% of tokens from the full input prompt across generation time and 11\% across all transformer layers, while incurring only a very small performance drop. On video benchmarks, up to 65\% of the input prompt tokens can be removed during generation without affecting performance.
bullets: Visual-token influence declines rapidly after the initial generation steps as models rely more on previously generated reasoning tokens.
Across transformer depth, visual influence is concentrated in intermediate layers and is weak in final layers.
Attention analyses and causal interventions show that visual dependence is neither temporally persistent nor uniform across depth.
The approach removes up to 59% of input-prompt tokens during generation and 11% across all layers with only a very small performance drop.
On video benchmarks, up to 65% of prompt tokens can be removed without affecting performance.

papers.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.
authors: Nurlan Nazaraliyev, Elaheh Sadredini, Nael Abu-Ghazaleh
bullets: Top-$p$ selection adapts computation to attention distributions, avoiding top-$k$’s fixed-budget waste or context loss.
Integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM with scheduler-decoupled block selection and a two-stream pipeline that overlaps selection with layer computation.
Uses a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel to reduce selection cost.
Relocates tokens based on prefill attention scores to reduce intra-block sparsity and inflated selection budgets.
Reports 1.17×–1.80× faster sparsity analysis, negligible accuracy loss, and up to 8× larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

papers.abstract: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.
authors: Yiyu Qian (Cornell University), Xing Wu (Shanghai University)
bullets: Targets experimental details distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and discussion—beyond the reach of text-only extraction.
Builds a heterogeneous graph linking schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content.
Combines semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to assemble multimodal evidence packages.
Applies visual interpretation only to graph-selected figures rather than the entire document.
On the SOFC-Exp corpus, retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of evaluated field instances and reduces average input tokens by 73.40% versus full-context processing.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.
authors: Jintao Cheng, Yipu Zhang, Haozhe Wang, Lin Jiang, Jiang Xu, Wei Zhang
bullets: Targets high latency and memory use that hinder VLA deployment on edge devices.
Combines trajectory-aware token propagation, contiguous spatial token selection, and flow-conditioned action-block refresh.
Aligns computation with both scene motion and hardware locality to reduce wasted compute and KV-cache fragmentation.
Closed-loop LIBERO evaluations report a 2.13× end-to-end speedup over dense inference with 30% visual-token retention and essentially unchanged success rate.
