papers.abstract: Query-based 4D reconstruction models such as D4RT encode a video once into a global scene representation and obtain outputs by decoding independent point queries. However, inference is often influenced by dense outputs and long videos. Although D4RT separates encoding from decoding, a dense output still requires one decoder query for every pixel of every frame, and a long video is still encoded as many overlapping segments. In this work, we analyze the inference cost of D4RT and show that a large part of it is redundant. In particular, we find that the later decoder blocks attend to a small set of tokens shared by all queries. Based on these findings, we propose FastD4RT, a training-free framework that accelerates D4RT. By exploiting the smoothness of the outputs over time and across pixels, FastD4RT encodes and decodes only at sparse anchors and recovers the remaining outputs via interpolation. It decodes the remaining queries against a shared token set selected once per segment. We further characterize the errors introduced by both components. Experimental results show that FastD4RT accelerates D4RT by about 5 times on average across all its tasks with competitive accuracy, and further improves accuracy on long videos. Our code is available at https://github.com/Lycheemeng/fastd4rt.
authors: Meng Bi, Yili Jin, Kaiyuan Hu, Xize Duan, Jiaxin Huang, Hong Huang, Xue Liu
bullets: Targets redundant computation from dense pixel-frame queries and overlapping long-video segments in D4RT.
Uses sparse spatial-temporal anchors and interpolation to recover remaining outputs.
Decodes queries against a shared token set selected once per video segment.
Analyzes the errors introduced by sparse interpolation and shared-token decoding.
Reports competitive accuracy across D4RT tasks and improved accuracy on long videos.

papers.abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
authors: Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, Sheng Zheng, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets the long visual token sequences created by multi-view 3D inputs.
Formulates pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget.
Uses local prototype initialization followed by global cross-region refinement via minimax hierarchical clustering.
Evaluated across three 3D VLMs and five 3D scene-understanding benchmarks.
With 10% of visual tokens retained, preserves 93.2% of Video-3D LLM performance and delivers 2.04× faster inference.

papers.abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.
bullets: Fixed, uniform Transformer architectures may be inefficient for individual tasks.
Learnable scalar gates remove attention or MLP sublayers during training, creating a heterogeneous subnetwork in one run.
Evaluated on standard and looped Transformers ranging from 140M to 2.7B parameters.
Carved models achieve lower validation loss at equal compute and outperform size-matched pruning or distillation models.

papers.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
papers.tldr: Model Carving jointly learns Transformer weights and topology, producing smaller, faster models that can outperform dense and post-hoc compressed alternatives.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained recognition benefits from high resolution, but not every image region needs it. We study a foveated Vision Transformer (FoVT) that uses last-block class attention from a 224-pixel glance to select regions for refinement. Fine patches from the 448-pixel image replace the selected coarse cells, and the same backbone classifies the mixed-resolution input. We evaluate FoVT on five benchmarks with two seeds and 26 configurations per dataset. Attention beats random selection on all five benchmarks, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points on the smallest objects. At equal transformer cost, Holm-corrected tests detect no FoVT deficit relative to a port of the official CF-ViT, but no dataset shows a corrected FoVT advantage in both seeds. FoVT requires no feature reuse, distillation loss, or selection schedule. Reusing coarse features shows no significant benefit and costs 1 to 3 points when the reuse module is trained at the head learning rate. Skipping refinement for the most confident 19 to 24 percent of images leaves accuracy unchanged to two decimal places. At the transformer cost of uniform 336-pixel inference, gated FoVT improves accuracy on four benchmarks, with the largest gains on NABirds and FGVC-Aircraft and no significant gain on Stanford Dogs. Foveation primarily saves computation: relative to a uniform 448-pixel model trained with the same auxiliary glance loss, ungated FoVT uses 44 percent fewer transformer operations, with no significant accuracy difference on four benchmarks and a 0.53-point deficit on FGVC-Aircraft. Wall-clock savings are smaller than the reduction in transformer operations.
bullets: A 224-pixel glance uses last-block class attention to select regions for 448-pixel refinement within the same backbone.
Attention-based selection consistently beats random selection, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points for the smallest objects.
At equal transformer cost, FoVT shows no corrected accuracy deficit versus ported CF-ViT, but also no consistent corrected advantage.
Gating refinement for the most confident 19–24% of images preserves accuracy; at uniform 336-pixel cost, gated FoVT improves four of five benchmarks.
Ungated FoVT reduces transformer operations by 44% versus uniform 448-pixel inference, but wall-clock savings are smaller and FGVC-Aircraft shows a 0.53-point deficit.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. FoVT: glance, look, zoom, re-classify. Stage 2 re-embeds the top-K cells from the full-resolution image as 4K fine tokens (orange), which replace the corresponding coarse input embeddings. The same backbone processes the mixed sequence ZK and produces ℓf . Selection indices are detached. At inference, K fixes the per-image cost, and an optional confidence gate returns ℓg and skips Stage 2 for confidently classified images.

papers.title: When Does Looking Closer Pay Off? Simple Foveated ViTs for Fine-Grained Recognition
papers.tldr: A simple attention-guided foveated ViT can improve fine-grained recognition efficiency by refining only selected image regions, though accuracy gains are inconsistent.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.
authors: Anqi Li, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high cost of rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences for each decision.
Probes a few candidates at multiple token budgets and selects the smallest budget that maintains their ranking.
Requires no training or task labels; the first observation-processing step remains exact and context frames are cached.
Across seven navigation and manipulation tasks, matches dense planning success at 2.3× speedup and retains 98% at 2.5×.
Evaluated in a closed-loop study spanning more than 80,000 episodes with frozen checkpoints.

papers.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.
authors: Xu Yuan, Liangbo Ning, Yujuan Ding, Qing Li, Wenqi Fan
bullets: Targets the loss of local multimodal evidence and high overhead in text-centric and earlier Vision-RAG systems.
Builds semantically complete regions with Content-Adaptive Regionalization.
Represents each page with local region vectors plus a global vector, trained using multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning.
Uses late-interaction matching to estimate region relevance, then rearranges selected regions into a compact visual context.
Across five benchmarks, it improves retrieval and generation over corresponding baselines while reducing visual tokens and computation.

papers.selection_reason: Region-level Vision-RAG with compact multi-vector retrieval; relevant to multimodal LLMs and visual token efficiency.
papers.title: When Visually Rich Documents Meet Multi-Vector Retrieval for Region-level Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: MV-VisRAG improves Vision-RAG by retrieving and assembling only the most relevant document regions instead of using redundant full-page visual contexts.

papers.abstract: Understanding how spiking neural networks (SNNs) efficiently process data streams is key to (i) studying how biological brains conserve energy for lifelong predictions and (ii) enabling efficient continuous AI inference. In this work, we propose a theory on how an SNN incrementally tracks its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued neural network (ANN). We prove that the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output implicitly determined by the SNN input. Based on this principle, we develop LIF-Stream, a conversion framework for efficient SNN inference over unbounded data streams. It enables the converted SNN to reuse its prior activation state and compute only the activation updates between frames, thereby reducing the average number of time steps needed per frame. Specifically, LIF-Stream controls the SNN to continuously track the reference ANN output, which gives a high-accuracy prediction for every frame. Evaluation on three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks with distinct modalities shows that LIF-Stream achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to high-accuracy SNN techniques.
bullets: The work addresses energy-efficient, lifelong prediction over continuous data streams.
It proves that a discrete SNN can continuously track the instantaneous output of its corresponding firing-rate ANN.
LIF-Stream converts ANNs into SNNs that reuse prior activation states and compute only frame-to-frame updates.
The method reduces the average number of time steps per frame while maintaining high-accuracy predictions.
Across three large-scale streaming benchmarks and distinct modalities, it achieves the best reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off among high-accuracy SNN methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Conceptual overview and empirical trajectory analysis of LIF-Stream. (Left) Conceptual diagram of our LIF-Stream framework for streaming SNN inference. (Right) Empirical validation on MOT17 video sequences (Milan et al., 2016) evaluated as a streaming pedestrian detection task. LIF-Stream efficiently tracks the continuous ANN output by updating only inter-frame delta, whereas standard reset-based IF and LIF-SNNs suffer from re-convergence latency overhead for every frame.
Figure 3: Efficiency via inter-frame redundancy (post-hoc analysis; Table 1 uses a fixed number of ticks).
Figure 4: Finer temporal resolution benefits ours (post-hoc analysis).

Figure 7: Stream encoders (τ = 8). (a,b) The decoded input x̃ of one coordinate on a staircase of six frames with T = 8 ticks each (grey lines mark frame boundaries). (c) Input readout error |x− x̃| at the last tick of each frame against the tick budget, on a correlated random stream; values are clipped at 10−6. (d) AP50 of the converted detector streaming one Argoverse-HD sequence (901 frames) against the tick budget; the dotted line is the dense ANN.
Figure 5: SNNs on egocentric driving perception. Figure 6: Prior IF-conversions fail to stream.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a framework for efficient SNN inference by reusing activation states and reducing time steps, contributing to computational efficiency in AI systems.
papers.title: Spiking Neural Networks Incrementally Track Firing-Rate Networks
papers.tldr: LIF-Stream lets spiking neural networks continuously track ANN outputs while reusing activation states, enabling efficient high-accuracy inference on unbounded data streams.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models rely on large pretrained encoders, yet typically process every modality to its full depth, regardless of its computational cost or predictive contribution. This raises a fundamental question: how should limited computation be allocated across modalities to preserve predictive performance? We reveal a substantial mismatch between the computational cost of modality encoders and the predictive benefit of processing them more deeply, suggesting that different modalities require different encoding depths. However, enabling heterogeneous depths introduces a key challenge: representations extracted at different depths must still be effectively fused. To address this, we propose $\textbf{DepthMSA}$, a budget-aware framework that supports flexible modality depths within a single MSA model. Specifically, we introduce combinatorial anytime training, which supervises the fusion head across all cross-modal depth combinations using a single full-depth encoder pass. At inference, a training-free, cost-aware allocator selects the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a sample-specific FLOPs budget. On CMU-MOSEI, DepthMSA maintains accuracy within one percentage point of the full-depth model while reducing measured FLOPs by 45\%, or by 82\% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. When a CLIP visual encoder dominates computation, the allocation shifts toward reducing visual depth, achieving 56\% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy. Compared with ADMN, an adaptive layer-allocation method that trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant reaches its accuracy with 3.2$\times$ fewer FLOPs and lower latency, without any per-budget training. Our project is available at https://pwang322.github.io/DepthMSA/.
authors: Pan Wang, Jie Peng, Zhimin Li, Jingxian Chen, Hui Ji, Huanrui Yang, Pengfei Zhou, Tianlong Chen, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between modality encoder cost and the predictive value of deeper processing.
Uses combinatorial anytime training to supervise fusion across all cross-modal depth combinations in one full-depth pass.
A training-free, validation-calibrated allocator selects the lowest-error depth configuration within each sample’s FLOPs budget.
On CMU-MOSEI, it stays within one percentage point of full-depth accuracy while reducing measured FLOPs by 45%, or 82% with skip-enabled training.
When vision dominates computation, it reduces visual depth for 56% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy; scope is demonstrated on CMU-MOSEI.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DepthMSA. (a) Each modality encoder provides J = 4 shared-weight exits and an optional skip level. (b) Combinatorial anytime training supervises all cross-modal depth configurations using a single full-depth encoder pass. (c) Validationtime calibration estimates the prediction error of each configuration and constructs a utility table. (d) For each test sample, the allocator computes configuration costs, selects the lowest-error feasible configuration, and executes the corresponding encoder depths.

Figure 3. Accuracy–efficiency trade-offs on three MSA datasets. Each DepthMSA or DepthMSA-skip curve is obtained from one trained model evaluated at multiple budgets, whereas ADMN uses a controller for each budget. The skip-enabled model extends the feasible operating range to lower measured FLOPs. Lines connect operating points. Mean over three seeds.

The horizontal axis shows encoder GFLOPs saved; the vertical axis shows the change in validation MAE relative to full depth (symmetric log scale). Larger savings with smaller error changes indicate greater depth redundancy. The modality offering this trade-off changes from audio with pre-extracted visual features to vision with CLIP. Mean over three seeds.

One DepthMSA and one DepthMSA-skip model each serve all budgets. ADMN uses the same backbone with a budget-specific controller. Bold: lowest GFLOPs and latency at each budget. Mean over three seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DepthMSA, a budget-aware framework for multimodal sentiment analysis that allocates different encoding depths to different modalities to reduce FLOPs while maintaining accuracy. This is a direct technical contribution to efficient resource allocation in multimodal models.
papers.title: DepthMSA: Combinatorial Training and Budget-Aware Depth Allocation for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.tldr: DepthMSA adaptively allocates encoder depth across modalities to substantially reduce MSA computation while preserving sentiment accuracy.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.
authors: Chris Gu, Marco Andono Sie, Nathan Zhou, Christopher Potts, Julie Kallini
bullets: VLMs often process hundreds of visual tokens, creating unnecessary inference cost when only part of an image matters.
DTM uses a lightweight delete gate to score contextualized tokens, trains deletion differentiably, and physically removes tokens during inference.
The framework is extended to bidirectional multimodal encoders and decoder-only models, producing V-MrT5Gemma2 and V-MrGemma3.
With 80% visual-token deletion—about 60% fewer FLOPs—DTM outperforms FastV on ChartQA and TextVQA while retaining 90–96% of unpruned performance.
Benefits increase at higher deletion rates and are strongest for document, chart, and scene-text reading tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dynamic Token Merging (DTM) in encoder–decoder and decoder-only VLMs. (a) V-MrT5Gemma2 deletes selected visual tokens before encoder layer k, retaining all text tokens. The shortened encoder output feeds the decoder’s merged self- and cross-attention. (b) V-MrGemma3’s prefill uses bidirectional attention within images and causal attention for text, caching the full prompt before the gate and the compacted prompt after it; decoding reuses these caches and appends generated K/V without further deletion. Both diagrams show hard deletion at inference. The gate and deletion rule are the same in both architectures; only where the gate takes effect differs.

Figure 2: One 60%-trained T5Gemma 2 1B–1B checkpoint (V-MrT5Gemma2) across inference budgets, deletion after layer 5. Each curve holds one task- and method-specific checkpoint fixed and evaluates it at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate, 60%, is highlighted. DTM’s advantage widens as the inference budget tightens beyond the training target.

Figure 6: T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 language-backbone architectures. Visual tokens enter after SigLIP encoding, pooling, and image projection. (a) T5Gemma 2 uses a bidirectional encoder and a decoder with merged self- and cross-attention. Each decoder block projects the final normalized encoder states H into its own keys and values. (b) Gemma 3 uses a decoder-only backbone. Here Le and Ld denote encoder and decoder depths: both are 26 for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B and 18 for 270M–270M; Gemma 3 4B has L = 34 decoder blocks.

Figure 7: Matched-rate evaluation on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (V-MrT5Gemma2), deletion after layer 5. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 60% and 80% deletion; at 20–40%, the methods are close.

Figure 8: Matched-rate evaluation on Gemma 3 4B (V-MrGemma3), deletion after five decoder layers during prompt prefill. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. DTM leads on nine benchmarks at 80% and six at 60%; at 20–40%, the methods are close.

Figure 4: Spatial evidence retention at matched 80% visual token deletion after layer 5. Bars show the mean percentage of evidence patches retained on the same eligible questions for each model–dataset pair; dashed lines mark the expected retention of random deletion. T5 1B, T5 270M, and G3 4B denote T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, and Gemma 3 4B. DTM retains the most evidence in 22 of 24 comparisons.

Figure 3: One 60%-trained Gemma 3 4B checkpoint (V-MrGemma3) decoder-only across inference budgets, deletion after five decoder layers during prefill. Each curve holds one checkpoint fixed across deletion rates from 10% to 90%, with 60% highlighted. V-MrGemma3 shows the same widening advantage at 80–90% deletion.

Figure 5: Soft and hard visual token deletion in DTM. Vision and text tokens, denoted as svi and sti , are processed normally from layers 1 through k − 1. The hidden states before layer k are entered into the deletion gate, producing a score for each token. During hard deletion, hidden states with gate scores less than τ are pruned; the gate scores are applied as biases to only the remaining pre-softmax attention scores. Soft deletion adds gate scores to key columns; hard deletion removes sv1 and sv3 and retains the text tokens.

Figure 22: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for Gemma 3 4B on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%); shading marks L5. The attention-based selectors improve with later deletion on this backbone, while DTM stays nearly constant and is highest at 40–80%.

Figure 23: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for T5Gemma 2 270M–270M on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%); shading marks L5. The smallest backbone benefits most from later deletion, especially at 80%.

Figure 21: Deletion-depth sensitivity across budgets for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B on DocVQA. Panels show individual methods; line colors indicate matched training and evaluation deletion rates (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%). The horizontal axis gives the number of layers before deletion; shading marks L5. DTM is nearly flat across depth, whereas FastV and φ-R peak at L5 and fall at L6 at every rate.

Figure 16: Checkpoint reuse across deletion budgets at L5. Rows specify training targets; grouped columns specify inference deletion. Gray diagonal cells show matched scores, with the strongest method in bold and underlined. Off-diagonal cells show St(e) − Se(e); negative values favor training at the evaluation rate. All cells average the same ten benchmarks equally. Red shading deepens with the size of the penalty. A 60%-trained DTM checkpoint used at 80% costs at most 0.6 points on average, and on Gemma 3 even a 20%-trained DTM checkpoint loses less at 80% than any baseline.

Figure 9: Matched-rate evaluation on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, deletion after layer 5. Each point uses a model trained and evaluated at the deletion rate δ on the horizontal axis. The advantage emerges at higher deletion rates on the smallest backbone: DTM leads on 1, 3, 7, and 8 benchmarks at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%.

Figure 27: Randomly sampled ChartQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (1 of 2). Each row shows the input with its question and gold answer, then the 52 of 256 visual tokens kept by each method in full contrast (outlined), with deleted patches washed out. Below each panel: the prediction and its relaxed-accuracy score. Blue: DTM; gold: FastV; magenta: φ-R; green: Random. DTM concentrates its budget on labels, tick values, and bar ends.

Figure 29: Randomly sampled TextVQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (1 of 2). Each row shows the input with its question and gold answer, then the 52 of 256 visual tokens kept by each method in full contrast (outlined), with deleted patches washed out; below each panel, the prediction (long answers truncated) and its VQA-accuracy score. Blue: DTM; gold: FastV; magenta: φ-R; green: Random. All three informed selectors keep much of the scene text; they differ in which words remain.

Figure 26 shows one way the attention-based selectors spend budget that DTM does not. On Gemma 3, FastV and φ-R keep the four corner patches of the image at median rates of 0.50 and 0.42, above the uniform rate of 0.20 on nine of ten benchmarks, whereas DTM keeps them at 0.02–0.12 on every model and benchmark. The two attention-based selectors also agree with each other far more than either agrees with DTM (median Cohen’s κ of 0.59, against 0.29 and 0.30), while DTM’s keep-sets agree across the three separately trained backbones (median κ 0.63, against 0.34 for FastV and 0.29 for φ-R). Gates trained on different models thus converge on similar selections.

Figure 20: Sensitivity to deletion depth on DocVQA. Models are separately trained and evaluated at 40% (dotted) or 80% (solid) deletion with the gate after each layer. The horizontal axis gives the number of layers before deletion; shading marks L5, the setting used in our main experiments. On T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, the attention-based selectors drop when they read the first global-attention layer (L6), whereas DTM does not.

Table 2: Matched-rate evaluation at 40% and 80% visual token deletion for T5Gemma 2 (1B– 1B) and Gemma 3 (4B), deletion after layer 5. Each score comes from a model trained and evaluated at the given deletion rate δ; Base is the unpruned model fine-tuned in the same way. Bold marks the best method per column within each model; each task uses its own metric (Section 5). The gray row gives the percentage of language-model FLOPs saved, which is the same for every method. Figures 2 and 3 include 60%, and Figures 7–9 (appendix) show 20–80%. DTM’s lead grows with the deletion rate on both architectures and is largest on DocVQA, ChartQA, and TextVQA.

Figure 10: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B trained at 20% (a) and 40% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 40%, DTM leads on nine benchmarks at 80% inference deletion; checkpoints trained at only 20% transfer less well, and DTM leads on half.

Figure 11: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B trained at 60% (a) and 80% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 60% or 80%, DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 80% and 90% inference deletion.

Figure 12: Fixed checkpoints on Gemma 3 4B trained at 20% (a) and 40% (b) deletion, deletion during prefill. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Figure 13: Fixed checkpoints on Gemma 3 4B trained at 60% (a) and 80% (b) deletion, deletion during prefill. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 60%, DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 80% and 90% inference deletion; trained at 80%, on nine.

Figure 14: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M trained at 20% (a) and 40% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. The smallest backbone transfers less well from low training targets: DTM leads on five or six benchmarks at 80% and 90% inference deletion.

Figure 15: Fixed checkpoints on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M trained at 60% (a) and 80% (b) deletion. Each curve evaluates one checkpoint at deletion rates from 10% to 90%; the training rate is highlighted. Blue diamonds: DTM; gold triangles: FastV; magenta crosses: φ-R; green circles: Random; dotted line: unpruned Base, fine-tuned the same way. Trained at 60%, DTM leads on all ten benchmarks at 80% inference deletion (eight at 90%); trained at 80%, on eight and six.

Figure 19: Query aggregation for FastV and φ-R on T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, matched deletion after layer 5. Variants and line styles as in Figure 17. On the smallest backbone, text queries help φ-R on DocVQA and TextVQA but not FastV; neither reaches DTM at 60–80% deletion on these tasks.

Figure 18: Query aggregation for FastV and φ-R on Gemma 3 4B, matched deletion after five decoder layers during prefill. Variants and line styles as in Figure 17. FastV again prefers all-query scoring (35 of 36 settings against text last), whereas φ-R gains from text queries on DocVQA and InfoVQA at 80%.

Figure 17: Query aggregation for FastV and φ-R on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, matched deletion after layer 5. Each selector ranks visual tokens by attention averaged over all valid queries (all mean, used in the main results), over text queries only (text mean), or from the final text query (text last); each variant is separately fine-tuned. Dashed: DTM; dotted: unpruned Base. Allquery scoring is the strongest FastV variant almost everywhere, by up to 17 points on DocVQA.

Figure 16 separates the loss associated with a tighter budget from the additional cost of checkpoint reuse. For DTM, moving from matched 60% to matched 80% deletion lowers the mean score by 3.3, 3.5, and 3.6 points for T5Gemma 2 1B–1B, Gemma 3 4B, and T5Gemma 2 270M–270M, respectively. Reusing the 60%-trained checkpoint at 80% incurs only a further 0.6, 0.2, and 0.2 points. Matched training is not uniformly best: at 60% inference deletion, Gemma 3’s 40%-trained DTM checkpoints average 0.7 points above their 60%-trained counterparts. These means summarize heterogeneous task metrics and are descriptive comparisons of the selected checkpoints.

Figure 28: Randomly sampled ChartQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (2 of 2). Presented as in Figure 27: kept tokens in full contrast, predictions and relaxedaccuracy scores below each panel; blue DTM, gold FastV, magenta φ-R, green Random.
Figure 30: Randomly sampled TextVQA questions at matched 80% deletion on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B (2 of 2). Presented as in Figure 29; blue DTM, gold FastV, magenta φ-R, green Random.

Table 10: Normalized area over inference deletion rates 10–90%. All checkpoints are trained at 60% deletion and evaluated at nine deletion rates; the area is the trapezoidal integral divided by the 0.8-wide interval, so values remain on each task’s 0–100 metric scale. The final row weights tasks equally. Bold marks the strongest method within each model. Table 1: Three instances of the DTM framework. All share the delete gate, soft-to-hard deletion, and controlled deletion objective (Section 3.2). Table 4: PI versus PID deletion-rate control on T5Gemma 2 1B–1B at all four training targets. Each DTM arm is retrained with the derivative term disabled (kd = 0), changing nothing else (L5, c = −22, τ = −7). Scores are best in-training validation scores at the trained deletion rate; tracking error |et| and overshoot above the target are in percentage points of training-time deletion. The derivative term tightens tracking at every target (lower mean |et| in 19 of 20 pairs, one tie) but improves accuracy only at the 80% target, where PID wins on all five tasks by 0.81 points on average.

Table 13: What each method keeps on ChartQA and OCR-text benchmarks at matched 80% deletion. Recall is the percentage of patches in each category that a method keeps; uniform selection keeps 20.3%. The default intercept starts training at 84–99.6% deletion regardless of the target, whereas calibration starts within 1.5 points of the target in all 16 configurations. Each saving is computed from summed theoretical forward costs at the recorded input and generatedoutput lengths; the vision encoder and image projector are excluded. The final row weights tasks equally. Savings are nearly constant across benchmarks except RefCOCO+, whose longer prompts and outputs are never deleted.

Table 15: Per-dataset input and output lengths and FLOPs savings for Gemma 3 4B at L5. FLOPs savings are presented in the same way as Table 14. Gemma 3 saves slightly more than T5Gemma 2 1B–1B at every deletion rate.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamic token merging for vision-language models directly targets token-level efficiency.
papers.title: Dynamic Token Merging for Efficient Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Dynamic Token Merging removes unimportant visual tokens in vision-language models, substantially reducing computation while preserving strong performance, especially for document and text-heavy image understanding.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
authors: Zirui Zhao, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong
bullets: Long-video token pruning and merging can lose accuracy because sparse frames may span unrelated scenes, causing 3D patch tokenizers to blend them before token selection.
The method analyzes frame similarity and tokenizer behavior across 16 open models to guide budget allocation.
A closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and tokenizer class to choose token grids and the reduction dimension before encoding.
Across five accelerators and three video LLMs, ESSENCE is more accurate in 58 of 60 matched-TTFT comparisons.
Using 80% of tokens, it matches full Qwen-model accuracy with 1.6× faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it improves accuracy by up to 3.4 points.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free method to accelerate video LLMs by tokenizing 'moments' (segments of frame similarity) rather than individual frames, addressing tokenization inefficiencies.
papers.title: Tokenize Moments, Not Frames: Tokenizer-Aware Budget Allocation for Training-Free Video LLM Acceleration
papers.tldr: ESSENCE accelerates video LLMs without training by allocating tokens to temporally coherent moments instead of uniformly sampled frames.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of knowledge transfer when visual token compression creates mismatched teacher and student token counts.
Reconstructs teacher visual states after the final LLM layer and before an important intermediate layer.
Uses response-level supervision at the intermediate layer instead of direct token-wise KL or MSE matching.
Adds an attention-readout loss to align contextual information integration during response prediction.
Evaluations across diverse benchmarks show improved performance for token-compressed students while retaining inference efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Knowledge distillation with visual token compression for MLLMs; addresses efficiency and multimodal model improvement.
papers.title: DVTR-KD: Distilling Vision-Language Models via Intermediate Visual Token Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DVTR-KD distills vision-language models by reconstructing dense teacher visual tokens from compressed student tokens, improving compressed-student performance while preserving token-efficiency benefits.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) encode each frame into hundreds of visual tokens, making video inference expensive. Existing methods reduce this cost through similarity-based merging or attention-based selection but face two challenges: Hierarchy-blind Pruning, which overlooks regional compressibility and can discard critical evidence, and Attention Drift, where positional effects and attention sinks shift text-to-vision attention away from task relevance. We propose FoveaTree, a two-stage, training-free visual-token pruning framework. First, Merge-Gain Density Estimation measures the feature distortion caused by regional merging and constructs a quadtree-derived density map to guide token dropping, merging, and retention. Second, Attention Tree Pruning uses the surviving units and inherited tree topology to refine text-to-vision attention in intermediate LLM layers, preserving relevant regional evidence while removing low-relevance content. We evaluate FoveaTree on InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B across five video question-answering benchmarks and one captioning benchmark at 50%, 30%, and 10% visual-token retention. FoveaTree consistently achieves overall state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated settings, offering a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
bullets: Targets hierarchy-blind pruning and attention drift in Video LLMs.
Estimates regional merge distortion to build a quadtree-based density map for token dropping, merging, and retention.
Refines intermediate-layer text-to-vision attention using surviving tokens and inherited tree structure.
Evaluated on InternVL3.5-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B across five video QA and one captioning benchmark at 50%, 30%, and 10% retention.
Reports consistent overall state-of-the-art performance across evaluated settings, with a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

papers.title: FoveaTree: Information-Density Trees for Query-Guided Visual Token Pruning in Video Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FoveaTree is a training-free, two-stage method that prunes video visual tokens using regional information density and topology-aware attention to reduce inference cost while preserving task-relevant evidence.

papers.abstract: Preference training is the standard recipe for reducing object hallucination in vision-language models, and each new method reports a lower CHAIR score. We ask what that reduction consists of. Every trained system is compared with its base model's caption truncated to the same object recall, which removes the part of the gain that comes from saying less; the remainder is compared with what a deliberately weak, frozen, eleven-feature post-hoc probe fitted on 500 annotated images can reproduce. All criteria were specified in the analysis code and frozen before the outputs they judge existed. For eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B, the probe reproduces at least two thirds of what training removes beyond saying less for 7 of 8 methods on COCO, 8 of 8 on AMBER and 6 of 8 on Object HalBench, with RLAIF-V the consistent exception; a later public method released for both LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL (SENTINEL) meets the same bar on both. On our own DPO checkpoints the accounting holds on Qwen2.5-VL but fails on InternVL2.5 on COCO (2 of 4 training designs). At matched recall, the base model plus the probe beats truncation for 8 of 9 LLaVA-1.5 systems on COCO and 9 of 9 on AMBER, on the two newer backbones, and when realized as actual sentence deletion. The same measure prices training signals: DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or by an object-level CLIP score recovers 0.70 and 0.87 of the beyond-brevity gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO on Qwen2.5-VL (the probe 0.73 on InternVL2.5), both beat length-matched random labels, and CLIP labels buy more than probe labels on COCO. Human judgements show that the sentences the probe deletes are wrong more often than those truncation would delete; a human check of the CHAIR evaluator's precision falls below our pre-set bar, which we report as a limitation.
bullets: The study separates CHAIR improvements into reduced verbosity versus genuine hallucination reduction by matching object recall with truncated base-model captions.
A frozen, 11-feature probe trained on 500 annotated images reproduces at least two thirds of beyond-brevity gains for most evaluated methods, with RLAIF-V as the main exception.
At matched recall, the base model plus probe generally outperforms truncation across LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, COCO, and AMBER evaluations.
Probe- or CLIP-based preference labels recover substantial portions of ground-truth-labelled DPO gains, while outperforming random labels; CLIP labels perform better on COCO.
Human checks support the probe’s deletions, but also identify insufficient precision in the CHAIR evaluator as a limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'cheap pruning' techniques in vision-language models (VLMs) to reduce object hallucinations, directly addressing efficiency (token pruning) and VLM robustness.
papers.title: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest
papers.tldr: Much of anti-hallucination training’s apparent benefit comes from shorter captions and can be replicated by a cheap post-hoc probe, though some methods and backbones retain gains beyond brevity.

papers.abstract: Extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from images to videos faces substantial memory and latency challenges due to the massive number of visual tokens. These challenges have driven the development of numerous visual token compression methods and more efficient LLM architectures. However, existing compression methods are often evaluated with different training setups, tasks, and models, making fair comparison difficult. Meanwhile, the growing use of hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures raises questions about whether compression strategies transfer across backbones. We present VidToC, a controlled evaluation framework for representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time encoding strategies, covering training-free and fine-tuned settings on three complementary video understanding tasks. Our results reveal task-dependent compression behavior and characterize the effects of compression placement, time encoding, and backbone choice. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing and selecting video token compression strategies across tasks and training settings.
authors: Zihan Xiao (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Boshen Xu (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China), Pei Fu (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jianzhong Ju (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Zhenbo Luo (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Jian Luan (MiLM Plus, Xiaomi Inc), Qin Jin (AIM3 Lab, Renmin University of China)
bullets: Video MLLMs face major memory and latency costs from large numbers of visual tokens.
Existing compression methods are difficult to compare fairly because evaluations use different setups, tasks, and models.
VidToC provides a controlled framework spanning representative compression algorithms, LLM backbones, and time-encoding strategies.
Experiments across three video-understanding tasks show that compression behavior depends on the task, compression placement, time encoding, and backbone.
The study offers empirical guidance for selecting compression strategies, including across hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models process large numbers of visual tokens, making token pruning important for efficient inference. Training-free pruning methods differ in whether and how they use the user query, and the value of query conditioning remains unclear. We present a controlled study of training-free, pre-LLM video token selection. Using a shared Qwen-3-VL backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings, we compare 21 pruning principles spanning query-agnostic, shallow query-conditioned, structured query-conditioned, and holistic strategies. To instantiate the last two categories, we introduce Structured Query Pruning, which decomposes the question into semantic anchors, and a Pareto variant, which combines anchor relevance with query-agnostic visual diversity. Across Video-MME, MVBench, and LongVideoBench, relevance computed from the raw question embedding is unreliable (8--16 points below the best methods), whereas anchors derived from query decomposition avoid this failure. However, query access is not inherently advantageous: strong query-agnostic coverage methods remain competitive or superior in the full-field comparison. Relative to a redundancy-only baseline, structured selection helps most on evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; on broad tasks, the holistic selector improves over either relevance or redundancy alone. Further, pruning reduces cost and memory. These results support a practical design rule: preserve visual coverage by default, and add structured relevance when the task and token budget demand selective evidence retrieval.
authors: Divya Kothandaraman, Timo Kumkel, Jaclyn Pytlarz
bullets: Compares 21 training-free video token pruning strategies under shared backbone, token budgets, and decoding settings.
Raw question-embedding relevance is unreliable, performing 8–16 points below the best methods across evaluated benchmarks.
Structured query decomposition avoids this failure by selecting tokens linked to semantic anchors.
Query access is not always beneficial: strong coverage-based, query-agnostic methods can match or outperform query-conditioned approaches.
Structured selection helps evidence-specific and long-context tasks at tight budgets; holistic selection helps broad tasks, while pruning reduces cost and memory.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression often treats salience or similarity as a proxy for transcription importance. Complete document OCR breaks this assumption: small symbols and repeated entries can be indispensable to the transcript despite being visually inconspicuous. We present Select and Compensate, a two-stage framework built on a simple idea: choosing where to retain a token need not determine all the evidence it carries. Selection combines adaptive encoding resolution with global importance and local contrast to choose which tokens to retain as anchors. Compensation enriches these anchors with nearby discarded content and its relative position, without adding tokens. The OCR backbone remains frozen, and native coordinates and structural tokens are preserved. We evaluate complete page transcription across five backbones on OmniDocBench and document reconstruction on MPDocBench. With half the original visual tokens, our input-adapted configuration reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall on Ovis versus 96.09 for the uncompressed model, and paired evaluations show gains over simply reducing the input resolution on both benchmarks. With the original input grid, our method stays within 0.17 points of the uncompressed model at 75% retention and exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points at 25%. On a fixed 200-page Ovis workload at the same 50% visual-token budget, only 3 of its outputs hit the length limit, versus 30-34 for the evaluated RTPrune, DivPrune, and HiPrune adaptations, and it finishes the batch 35-40% sooner. Code will be made publicly available.
authors: Yixuan Huang, ShengFan Zhang, Jiawei Chen
bullets: Targets a key OCR limitation: visually subtle symbols and repeated entries may be essential despite low salience.
Selects anchor tokens using adaptive resolution, global importance, and local contrast.
Compensates retained anchors with nearby discarded content and relative positions without adding tokens; the OCR backbone remains frozen.
At 50% of the original tokens, Ovis reaches 95.42 OmniDocBench Overall versus 96.09 uncompressed, and paired evaluations outperform simple input-resolution reduction.
At 25% retention, it exceeds a learned global selector by 4.70 points; at a 50% budget, it also reduces length-limit hits and finishes a fixed workload 35–40% sooner.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.
authors: Payman Behnam, Elaheh Sobhani, Saad Amin, Yahya Hassan, Daniyal Khan, Biswadeep Chakraborty, Tanish Patwa, Souvik Kundu, Alexey Tumanov
bullets: Targets redundant, low-utility tokens in long reasoning traces, which can nevertheless receive high attention scores.
Uses uncertainty-guided pruning: retains more cache during uncertain phases and prunes more aggressively when confidence is high.
Uses redundancy-aware selection to favor informative and diverse tokens over content similar to recent reasoning.
Co-designs the method with vLLM through fused CUDA decode kernels while preserving paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture.
Across three benchmarks and two reasoning models, improves accuracy under constrained cache budgets; for one 8B model, reports up to 1.43× speedup and 45% higher throughput versus Full-KV.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
authors: Zhengbo Zhou, Dooman Arefan, Shandong Wu
bullets: Addresses the risk that visual-token compression removes contextual information needed to interpret subtle mammographic lesions.
Uses a bilateral-guided token selector to prioritize lesions and their local and contralateral-breast context within a shared token budget.
Applies a bilateral reward to encourage diagnostic reasoning that benefits from preserved cross-image evidence.
Experiments on datasets built from CBIS-DDSM and VinDr-Mammo report better evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained token budgets.
Inference benchmarking shows reduced prefill latency.

papers.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context LLM inference.
Propagates token importance across attention-induced transition graphs beyond recency or immediate attention.
Evaluated on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning across multiple LLM families.
Maintains competitive task performance under moderate to aggressive compression, including up to 90%, with low end-to-end overhead.
Scope: performance is demonstrated across the reported tasks and model families, with a favorable accuracy–memory trade-off rather than universal superiority.

papers.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: PRKV uses Personalized PageRank to estimate globally important tokens for training-free KV-cache eviction, enabling substantial memory savings while preserving long-context performance.

papers.abstract: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.
authors: Zhen Huang, Shuwei Li, Ruizhe Yao, Xinrui Chen, Danyi Liu, Haoyuan Liang, Zhiyu Ye, Qiuyan Sun, Bingwei Chen, Yiyuan Li, Xu Zhou, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Clustering queries and keys together limits sparse-attention accuracy because queries in a cluster share key selections.

It efficiently executes per-query routing by grouping queries with identical selections and merging results with a carried softmax offset.
Evaluated on four Wan and HunyuanVideo text-to-video and image-to-video models, it achieves 1.66–2.10× end-to-end speedup.
It reports 28.9 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and 35.4 dB on HunyuanVideo, while remaining closest to dense attention among evaluated sparse methods.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.
authors: Xiaolin Lin, Kai-Chiang Wu, Bing Li, Grace Li Zhang
bullets: Targets the high first-token latency caused by prefill on roughly 100K-token interleaved image-text inputs.
Uses an early attention head in a small hybrid model, with images at half resolution, to rank whole input units.
Keeps the top 10% of tokens/units and feeds them to the target VLM as a shorter ordinary prompt.
A single untrained selector transfers across different target model families.
On MMLongBench at 128K tokens, it maintains average accuracy while reporting 3.7×, 11.6×, and 8.2× prefill speedups for three target models.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.
authors: Siqi Xiang, Zhipeng Xu, Shengrui Liu, Zulong Chen, Chunyan Miao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets inefficient perception of long interaction histories in LLM-based agents.
Renders past interactions as images and allocates resolution according to relevance to the next decision.
Uses a lightweight, teacher-guided relevance estimator optimized to preserve decision consistency.
Works across multiple tasks and backbones and can complement existing memory management methods.
Scope: focuses on adaptive perceptual granularity rather than deciding what memories to retain or retrieve.

papers.abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.
bullets: Splits history into blocks and uses a fast yes/no selector to reveal relevant blocks while masking others in one key-value cache.
On a synthetic lookup task with Qwen3-1.7B, selective context improved accuracy from 93/120 to 119/120; masking was comparable to deletion.
Context selection is the main weakness: a supervised linear probe reached 110/120, while keyword search achieved perfect task performance.
The probe did not transfer to a second task, limiting evidence for general-purpose selection.
Block switching also supports undoing failed attempts and running subagents without creating a new context.

papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/
authors: Yuze Wu, Mo Zhu, Xingxing Li, Yuheng Du, Zhaoqi Wang, Yuxin Fan, Wenjun Li, Kenghou Hoi, Zhichao Han, Xin Zhou, Fei Gao
bullets: Separates multimodal reasoning from low-level control by predicting 3D poses and navigation intentions that are converted into dynamically feasible actions.
Uses an automated 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline to generate scalable, photorealistic UAV navigation data and address data scarcity and domain gaps.
Employs progressive three-stage training for improved grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation.
Adds a memory-aware cognitive agent for long-horizon task decomposition and onboard optimizations such as token sparsification and model lightweighting.
Reports 7.1×–9.4× speedups while maintaining high navigation performance, with improvements demonstrated in simulation and real-world UAV experiments.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates can cause irreversible evidence loss. In this paper, we study this problem from the perspective of assessing the spatiotemporal distribution of query-specific evidence and propose a novel and training-free approach termed NULLTOK. For every patch across all frames, we construct an empirical-null distribution from 64 group-matched irrelevant control queries, capturing the scores expected in the absence of target-specific evidence. Target affinities are calibrated against these same-position references into right-tail Monte Carlo p-values, which are discrete super-uniform under a conditional exchangeability assumption. Calibrated screening and a high-recall semantic guard produce candidate tokens for deterministic visual deduplication and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation. To validate NullTok, we apply it to two representative MLLMs and conduct extensive experiments on a set of video benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness under a bounded visual token budget. For example, it achieves 65.81% and 68.85% on Video-MME using frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones, respectively, at a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents (FFE), without subtitles or audio. These results outperform all evaluated baselines on Video-MME under the same budget for both backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/potato-kitty/NullTok.
authors: Zhang Ziyue, Juwei Jian, Baiyang Song, Yunshan Zhong, Jun Peng, Yiyi Zhou, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses evidence loss caused by selecting frames before pruning tokens in long videos.
Builds position-matched empirical-null distributions from irrelevant control queries and converts affinities into Monte Carlo p-values.
Combines calibrated screening with a high-recall semantic guard, deduplication, and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation.
Evaluated with frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on video benchmarks without subtitles or audio.
On Video-MME at 64 full-frame equivalents, achieves 65.81% and 68.85%, outperforming evaluated baselines for the respective backbones.

Figure 4. MLVU accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B at a cap of 16 Full Frame Equivalents (FFE). NULLTOK exceeds both OTPrune and ReDiPrune by 1.38%. The vertical axis starts at 60%.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free token selection for long-video MLLMs; directly fits video understanding and token pruning efficiency.
papers.title: NullTok: empirical-null token selection for training-free long video understanding
papers.tldr: NullTok is a training-free method that selects query-relevant video tokens using empirical-null calibration, enabling long-video understanding within a fixed visual-token budget.

papers.abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Xiyue Zhang, Bing Hu, Guangmin Song, Chenyi Zhang, Li Wang
bullets: Problem: KV-cache pruning lets growing reasoning tokens evict image tokens, causing larger accuracy losses in later conversational turns.
Method: Keep all visual entries in CPU memory and dynamically swap query-relevant visual entries into slots occupied by low-scoring text entries.
Training-free and compatible with existing retention policies, including DBTrimKV.
Across four benchmarks, two retention policies, and two reasoning VLMs, ShelfKV improves DBTrimKV by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory and 8.7 points when DBTrimKV has twice the memory.
It outperforms a fixed visual reserve in conversational settings without reducing standalone-question accuracy.

A sketch proposes candidates, and the current query swaps those that outscore text entries onto the desk on the GPU. Displaced text entries are parked, not deleted, so the desk keeps the host’s entry count.

Figure 2. Reasoning crowds out visual KV; protection beats extra shared capacity. (a) Cache composition during the first-turn output under DBTrimKV (B = 256). (b) Follow-up accuracy gains (percentage points) over the same host (61.3%); the dashed line marks the unconstrained full-cache gain.
