papers.abstract: Classification of lung adenocarcinoma into poorly differentiated (PD) and well-to-moderately differentiated (WMD) subtypes plays an important role in patient survival; however, consistent classification is difficult due to inter-observer variability among pathologists. Collecting data from multiple hospitals is also challenging due to patient privacy concerns. This study proposes a web-based federated learning system that shares only locally trained model weights without sharing patient data between institutions. The UNI2 foundation model and CLAM-SB were used to classify pathological whole slide images. A four-client federated learning system was constructed, and the NLST cohort was reserved exclusively for external validation. In centralized evaluation, joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperformed single-institution training on external validation, confirming the necessity of multi-institutional data integration. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedNova were compared as federated learning algorithms under identical experimental conditions. Test AUC ranked as FedBN, FedProx, FedNova, and FedAvg. FedNova showed the most balanced classification performance between PD and WMD. L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity was applied to reduce model transmission size. FedAvg, FedProx, and FedBN showed a tendency of decreasing Test AUC under pruning, while FedNova achieved improved Test AUC across all sparsity levels. A web-based application was developed supporting slide upload, local training, AI classification, and attention heatmap-based visualization. The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning was confirmed as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification performance while protecting patient privacy.

bullets: Addresses inter-observer variability and the difficulty of sharing pathology data across hospitals.

The platform supports slide upload, local training, classification, and attention-heatmap visualization; NLST was used for external validation.

papers.abstract: Query-based segmentation models achieve strong performance even under real-time inference on workstation GPUs. On edge devices, however, we show their transformer decoders are deeply memory-bandwidth-bound, a bottleneck invisible to standard FLOP analysis that worsens with input resolution and limited DRAM bandwidth. An FP16 roofline analysis with tensor-core GEMMs active and hardware DRAM counters shows that the non-tensor-core aggregates of FastInst and Mask2Former reach only $2.5\%$ to $6\%$ of the CUDA-core ridge yet account for $53\%$ to $70\%$ of decoder time and $61\%$ to $71\%$ of decoder bytes. The largest individual kernels sustain up to $90\%$ of nominal peak DRAM bandwidth, effectively saturating the memory bus. The bottleneck is therefore not primarily low GEMM intensity, but cross-kernel activation traffic. CompactInst addresses this bottleneck using parameter-free spatial pooling at $4{\times}$, which reduces the bytes moved within the transformer decoder, while a two-convolution refinement head recovers spatial detail. Under TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano, CompactInst delivers decoder speedups from $2.35{\times}$ to $4.74{\times}$ and model speedups from $1.57{\times}$ to $2.62{\times}$ as input resolution grows, while closely matching accuracy ($-0.4$ AP on COCO val2017, $+0.2$ AP on Cityscapes test). A heavier variant with $2.57{\times}$ more decoder FLOPs still runs its decoder $1.74{\times}$ faster on the most bandwidth-constrained device, confirming at the deployment level that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, govern latency.
bullets: Roofline analysis identifies DRAM bandwidth as the dominant decoder bottleneck, especially at higher resolutions and on bandwidth-limited devices.
Non-tensor-core decoder operations consume most decoder time and bytes despite low CUDA-core utilization, with large kernels nearing peak DRAM bandwidth.
CompactInst uses 4× parameter-free spatial pooling plus a two-convolution refinement head to reduce activation traffic and recover detail.
On Jetson Orin Nano with TensorRT FP16, it achieves 2.35–4.74× decoder speedups and 1.57–2.62× end-to-end model speedups as resolution increases.
Accuracy remains close to baseline on COCO and Cityscapes; a higher-FLOP variant further supports that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, determine latency.

papers.abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) imposes substantial computational overhead on vision-language models (VLMs), motivating model-agnostic input reduction methods that can be readily applied across diverse VLMs, including in black-box settings. Simply enforcing a visual-token cap reduces computation, but it can discard information needed to answer the question. A single reduction strategy also struggles to accommodate different scenarios. Our key observation is that cropping and compression are complementary: cropping highlights small targets and local details, whereas whole-image compression better preserves context for large targets or distributed evidence. Based on this observation, we propose C$^2$-Routing, which adaptively selects cropping or compression according to the input image and question. Since both strategies may still discard key information, we further design a safety gate that uses the predicted joint correctness distribution under original and reduced inputs to guide fallback and protect accuracy. To accommodate consumer GPU resource constraints, all training and evaluation experiments run on RTX 3090 GPUs. To measure gains beyond token capping, we use full-image baselines with the same cap of 1,024 visual tokens. We conduct extensive evaluation on three VLMs and 18 datasets spanning local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents. With the visual budget already capped, C$^2$-Routing further reduces end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36% on average, with a mean relative task-score decrease of only 0.77%.
bullets: Addresses the information loss and limited flexibility of using a single visual-token reduction strategy for VQA.
Routes each image-question pair to cropping for local details or compression for broader context.
Uses a safety gate based on predicted correctness under original and reduced inputs to trigger fallback when needed.
Evaluated across three VLMs and 18 datasets covering local details, global scenes, scene text, and documents.
With a 1,024-token visual cap, reduces average end-to-end FLOPs by 36.53% and visual tokens by 42.36%, with a 0.77% mean relative task-score decrease.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 presents C2-Routing, a model-agnostic frontend that selects and protects visual information before VLM infer-

Fig. 1(a,b). When question-relevant information is concentrated in a small region, whole-image downsampling leaves fewer pixels to represent that region, potentially making answer-relevant details unrecognizable. Cropping removes irrelevant background and increases the key region’s relative prominence, helping the model attend to and recognize the evidence. It can therefore reduce visual tokens and computation while improving accuracy. Conversely, when relevant information spans a large area or is distributed across multiple locations, a crop that retains all relevant content typically removes little background and offers limited computational savings; a tighter crop can discard necessary evidence and context. Moderate whole-image downsampling can instead preserve recognizable evidence and spatial relationships, reducing visual tokens and computation while largely maintaining task performance.

papers.abstract: Establishing dense correspondence between high-resolution 3D shapes remains challenging due to the spatial--spectral coupling at the core of many functional-map methods, which grows quadratically with mesh resolution. We observe that this coupling is equivalent to a scaled dot-product attention formulation, with learned descriptors serving as queries and keys and spectral basis functions as values. This connection makes efficient attention implementations directly applicable to shape matching and an effective mechanism for scaling spatial-spectral coupling. We show that optimized quadratic attention implementations can scale modern deep functional map pipelines to large mesh sizes, improving both runtime and memory consumption, while sub-quadratic methods introduce errors, particularly for non-isometric shape pairs, where an exact coupling proves most necessary. These insights motivate \textit{Geo-FlashAttention}, which restricts the exact softmax to geometry-selected surface patches and achieves near-linear empirical scaling while preserving correspondence accuracy of exact implementations. Across six standard benchmarks and three functional-map pipelines, rigorous analysis shows that efficient couplings preserve correspondence accuracy. At $60k$ vertices, these insights reduce peak training memory from 106.08 to 5.67\,GiB, with Geo-FlashAttention being $1.5\times$ faster per training step than FlashAttention. This enables end-to-end learning for correspondence problems on large meshes such as cortical surfaces, where high resolution is required to preserve disease-relevant intricacies of the surface geometry. Project page available https://spatial-spectral-attention.github.io/
authors: Bence Demeter, Kilian Ehrenreich, Amelie Kleber, Ioana Oprisiu, Philipp Spohn, Christian Wachinger, Fabian Bongratz, Lennart Bastian
bullets: Functional-map coupling scales quadratically with mesh resolution, limiting dense correspondence on large surfaces.
The paper identifies this coupling with scaled dot-product attention, enabling optimized attention implementations for shape matching.
Sub-quadratic approximations can introduce errors, especially for non-isometric shape pairs requiring exact coupling.
Geo-FlashAttention applies exact softmax attention only to geometry-selected surface patches.

Across six benchmarks and three pipelines, efficient couplings preserve accuracy; at 60k vertices, memory drops from 106.08 to 5.67 GiB, and Geo-FlashAttention is 1.5× faster per step than FlashAttention.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2.Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.
authors: Senhao Liu, Yuheng Zhang, Chunyu Wei, Yueguo Chen, Xinran Zhang
bullets: Addresses the context-length and information-loss tradeoff in textual RAG compression.
Renders documents as images and encodes them with a frozen vision encoder.
Uses Encoder-Bridged Retrieval to match text queries with visual tokens without contrastive training.
Applies Query-Driven Distillation to reduce retrieved visual tokens to as few as 16 injected tokens.
Achieves the best compression-aware accuracy across LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, with a 5.17-point LongBench-v2 improvement over the closed-book backbone.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.
authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Chun-Mei Feng, Anthony Cohn, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke Nandi
bullets: Addresses high inference latency caused by dense visual-token processing in robotic manipulation.
Uses a lightweight Decision Influence Estimator conditioned on visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception.
Trains token selection with action supervision plus an auxiliary objective predicting future visual features from demonstrated actions.
Performs one hard token-selection and packing step at deployment, then uses the VLA policy’s native action generation.
Across five real-world tasks, reduces mean latency from 137.25 ms to 93.25 ms (1.47× speedup) while achieving 61% average success versus 60% unpruned.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
authors: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Targets the indexer bottleneck, which can exceed half of prefill GPU time at long context lengths.
Uses layer-wise calibration to handle heterogeneous cross-query retrieval overlap across layers.
Trains adaptive layer-wise group indexers through group-level distillation while retaining query-specific refinement.
Reduces repeated full-prefix scans via token-bank sharing within query groups.
On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1, reports up to 6.22× prefill, 3.40× decoding-kernel, and 1.54× end-to-end serving speedups while maintaining near-lossless LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER performance.

papers.abstract: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. Existing checks compare the reader model's answer or its most likely words, and thus miss a frequent failure, silent evidence loss: key evidence is removed while the answer stays the same, leaving the answer unsupported and risky for other models that reuse the context. To address this challenge, we propose SELD (Silent Evidence Loss Detector), which needs no training and no labels. Its principle is that when evidence is lost, a reader model's preferences among the answers it leaves unsaid shift even if its answer does not, so comparing these preferences before and after compression reveals losses that answer checks cannot see. We also build SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of length-matched evidence and control deletions from three question-answering datasets. Quantitative and qualitative experiments with five reader models on it show that SELD consistently outperforms strong and recent baselines across compressors, compression rates and models, identifying the evidence-removing edit in 83% of matched pairs with unchanged answers, against 70% for the strongest baseline. These results show that evidence loss in compressed contexts can be detected even when the answer is unchanged.
bullets: Silent evidence loss can make compressed contexts unsafe for reuse because answers may remain correct but unsupported.
SELD compares shifts in a reader model’s preferences among unchosen answers before and after compression, requiring no training or labels.
The authors introduce SEL-Pairs, a benchmark of matched evidence-removal and control deletions from three QA datasets.
Across five reader models, compressors, and compression rates, SELD identified the evidence-removing edit in 83% of unchanged-answer pairs, versus 70% for the strongest baseline.
The method targets evidence loss beyond answer-preservation checks; its evaluation scope is the benchmark’s datasets, models, and compression settings.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Test 1: single-sentence deletion on 2,414 new questions. (a) How often each check scores the keysentence deletion above its equal-length control, among pairs whose answer did not change (50% is chance; LUMINA-ECU is post hoc). (b) The two main tests (pooled over reader models) and eight per-reader tests. (c) Post-hoc checks: SELD minus JS divergence by answer group and SELD minus six text-only scores among unchanged answers. Intervals are Bonferroni-corrected within each family (Section A).

Figure 1: Silent evidence loss and how SELD detects it (illustrative; bars: gray for the original context, blue for the compressed one). (1) Compression removes the only sentence that states the answer. (2) With the full guide, both reader models answer the right. After compression, reader model A still answers the right from its default, so an answer check passes; reader model B, reading the same compressed context downstream, falls back on a different default and answers the left. The loss was silent for A, so nothing stopped the context from reaching B. (3) Checks that look at the top answer (answer agreement, JS divergence, answer-likelihood drop) see almost no change; in our tests they change less than when an equally long, harmless sentence is deleted. SELD compares the reader model’s preferences among all the answers it leaves unsaid, which shift when the evidence is gone. A real case with measured scores is given in Section I.

Figure 2: SEL-Pairs and SELD (schematic). (1) For each input, an evidence edit (red) removes evidence and a control edit (gray, dashed) removes other text of exactly the same token length: single-sentence deletion from the original context on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA (denoted S and C in the text); swaps inside LLMLingua-2 outputs at 25, 50 and 75% and inside Provence outputs (B and C, with the output as input A; LLMLingua-2 swaps are refilled to equal length); and MuSiQue’s official unanswerable context against a control that keeps the key paragraphs (U and T ). (2) SELD (step 1) reads the reader model’s scores for every possible next word under O and X , so that the answers left unsaid count; (2) centers them and ignores their scale, so that a mere change in confidence does not count; and (3) measures the angle between the two patterns. A check passes a pair when it scores the evidence edit above its equal-length control.

papers.abstract: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare nine dense detectors, eight YOLO models of four generations and FCOS, on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.
bullets: The study evaluates nine dense detectors, including eight YOLO models and FCOS, on VisDrone and DOTA with controlled tuning and held-out testing.

On VisDrone, training a single detector at higher resolution outperforms tiled inference with box fusion whenever that resolution is feasible; higher resolution also beats a larger model at equal compute.
SCAHI combines dense outputs from tiles using coverage-aware weighting and a fine peak grid, avoiding information loss from decoded-box fusion.
With identical tiles, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS.
On DOTA, where full-image resolution is infeasible, SCAHI improves over the best single pass and replacing SAHI's merge step yields substantial gains.

Figure 2. Why dense fusion removes tile-border fragments. (a) Box fusion sees two decoded boxes for one object that straddles a tile seam: the fragment predicted by tile A overlaps the full box from tile B too little to be suppressed. papers.selection_reason: Introduces SCAHI, a method for efficient small object detection using dense fusion and coverage-aware inference, which is relevant for perception in embodied systems.
papers.title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection
papers.tldr: Slicing helps mainly when full-image resolution is insufficient, and SCAHI improves tile fusion by preserving dense, complementary predictions.

papers.abstract: As long-video understanding gains increasing attention, augmented reality (AR) devices are emerging as a compelling deployment platform. However, egocentric videos exhibit significant temporal redundancy, imposing substantial memory and computational burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware. To address this challenge, we introduce UTOPI, a plug-and-play pre-compression module designed specifically for egocentric long videos on AR platforms. First, we leverage user motion signals to estimate inter-frame overlap and propose a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm. Second, we exploit eye-tracking sensors to identify user fixations, enabling the separation of attended foreground content from background and its preferential retention via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism. Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance. Code and project page are available at https://sai-lab-nyu.github.io/utopi/.
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of temporally redundant egocentric videos on resource-constrained AR hardware.
Uses user motion to estimate inter-frame overlap and perform viewpoint-shift-invariant token pruning.
Uses eye tracking to distinguish attended foreground content from background and preferentially retain it.
Works as a plug-and-play pre-compression module across multiple benchmarks and model backbones.
Achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Block-diffusion drafters propose a whole block of tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees built from their position-wise marginals increase the expected accepted length of speculative decoding. Every tree node occupies a query row in target verification, so under concurrent serving low-yield branches compete with other requests for verification capacity. Existing tree methods select verified nodes by draft probability under a fixed or cost-selected per-request budget, and thus always retain a prefix of the drafter's ranking. We present D3Tree, which learns which nodes of a block-diffusion draft tree are worth verifying. A tree-size head with 2H+2 parameters predicts each candidate's conditional survival from the draft state, the candidate embedding, and its draft log-probability. Thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains yields an ancestor-closed subtree whose size adapts to each request and decoding round. The head is trained on a frozen drafter with conditional labels on the full candidate tree; an optional joint mode also steers the drafter toward the retained reference path. At serving time, D3Tree verifies whole trees under light load and, under heavy load, allocates one batch-wide node budget by predicted survival, sized to the target's matrix-multiplication tiles. Retained trees share one ancestor-masked target pass, while construction, pruning, and scheduling run on the GPU and overlap with the host. Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings, with 3.2-4.0x speedup over autoregressive decoding for one request and 1.3-1.8x at 64 concurrent requests, where fixed-budget trees fall below autoregressive speed. Under a time-varying arrival trace, it has the lowest mean end-to-end latency in every arrival phase.
bullets: Fixed probability-ranked trees waste verification capacity on low-yield branches when requests compete for resources.
D3Tree predicts each candidate’s conditional survival and retains an ancestor-closed subtree with request- and round-adaptive size.
It supports whole-tree verification under light load and batch-wide, tile-aligned node budgeting under heavy load.
Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 benchmarks, it is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings.
Reported speedups are 3.2–4.0× for one request and 1.3–1.8× at 64 concurrent requests; it also achieves the lowest latency across all phases of a time-varying arrival trace.

papers.selection_reason: Learns to prune draft-tree nodes for efficient speculative-decoding verification, directly relevant to token/candidate pruning for efficient inference.
papers.title: D3Tree: Learning to Prune Block-Diffusion Draft Trees for Efficient Verification
papers.tldr: D3Tree learns to prune block-diffusion draft trees according to predicted node survival, improving speculative-decoding efficiency—especially under high concurrency.

papers.abstract: Adaptive tokenization aims to reduce the compute spent on uninformative image regions while preserving accuracy. Existing work relies on (i) fixed or frozen scoring rules, which cannot be trained toward the task loss, or (ii) discrete masks trained with straight-through estimators, which yield noisy gradients, while fully differentiable alternatives instead leave the pre-trained regular grid. We revisit adaptive tokenization from a regular-grid perspective and ask: can a two-scale quadtree be learned end-to-end without deleting a single token during training? We show that one coarse token and its four fine children can be made the two endpoints of a single continuous interpolation. We introduce Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning (\dvsp{}), which keeps four \emph{virtual slots} per $2{\times}2$ region and blends their token features and attention mass with a single weight $α$, exactly reproducing the discrete grid at $α\in \{0,1\}$. On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, \dvsp{} retains $97.9\%$ of dense Box AP while removing $64.2\%$ of visual tokens, giving a $1.61\times$ end-to-end speedup, and it outperforms entropy-based APT, DART, and uniform lower-resolution dense adaptation at matched budgets; these gains depend on the conserved attention mass, whose removal costs $1.59$ Box AP. On a frozen Segmenter it also improves Cityscapes mIoU, and on frozen DeiT backbones it exceeds entropy selection at identical per-image token counts.
bullets: Addresses fixed scoring rules, noisy straight-through masks, and differentiable methods that abandon the pre-trained regular grid.
Uses four virtual slots per 2×2 region and a single interpolation weight to blend coarse and fine token features and attention mass.
On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, removes 64.2% of visual tokens while retaining 97.9% of dense Box AP and achieving a 1.61× end-to-end speedup.
Outperforms entropy-based APT, DART, and uniform lower-resolution adaptation at matched token budgets.
Improves Cityscapes mIoU on a frozen Segmenter and exceeds entropy selection on frozen DeiT backbones; conserving attention mass is important.

papers.selection_reason: Differentiable adaptive tokenization removes a large fraction of visual tokens in ViTs, directly relevant to token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning for Adaptive Tokenization in Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning learns adaptive quadtree tokenization end-to-end while preserving regular-grid training, substantially reducing vision-token compute with limited accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Video fusion aims to integrate complementary cues from heterogeneous sources, producing visually informative videos with coherent spatio-temporal structures. Jointly learning cross-modal complementarity and temporal dependencies typically relies on large-scale, high-quality video datasets, whose storage and repeated use during optimization incur substantial costs, making data-efficient learning highly desirable. To address this challenge, we rethink video fusion from the perspective of dataset condensation and propose STAR-VF, the first framework that condenses spatio-temporal representations for data-efficient video fusion. STAR-VF condenses the original training set into a compact set of learnable spatio-temporal representations, which are decoded into synthetic video clips and optimized using feature-level supervision provided by a frozen proxy model. The resulting condensed data preserves fusion-relevant spatial and temporal cues without requiring ground-truth fused videos as supervision. To adapt fusion learning to condensed representations, we equip the final fusion model with flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation, enabling direct temporal interaction and adaptive selection of fusion-relevant information in representation space. Extensive experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-VF, trained with only approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training set, achieves fusion quality comparable to methods trained on the full data. Further analyses validate the contributions of learned condensation and flow-free temporal modeling, and demonstrate the robustness of the condensed supervision across different proxy encoders and downstream fusion models. Project page: https://zju-xyc.github.io/STAR-VF-Project-Page/.
bullets: Targets the storage and optimization costs of large video-fusion training datasets.
Learns compact spatio-temporal representations, decodes them into synthetic clips, and optimizes them with feature-level supervision from a frozen proxy model.
Uses flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation for fusion directly in representation space.
Supports infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion without requiring ground-truth fused videos.
Using approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training data, it achieves fusion quality comparable to full-data training; robustness is shown across proxy encoders and downstream fusion models.

In Stage II, the learned condensed set is decoded into synthetic temporal samples to train the final fusion model 𝐹𝜃 with flow-free temporal alignment and query-driven intra-frame aggregation. During inference, only the trained fusion model is used, without the condensed set or proxy model.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.
bullets: Long sessions can exceed one GPU’s KV-cache capacity, requiring aggressive token eviction.
Even when over 99% of later-needed tokens remain cached, accuracy drops as their rotary-position distance from the query grows.
PACE uses the agent’s plan to retain future-relevant context and bounds rotary distances by renumbering retained tokens.
On 100K-token Qwen3-8B coding tasks with a 2,048-token budget, PACE passes 97% of hidden-unit tests versus 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV.
The method scales to 1M–2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with 9% added wall time and no measurable perplexity cost.

papers.selection_reason: KV-cache engine for long-horizon LLM agents directly targets cache memory efficiency, token retention, and long-context processing.
papers.title: PACE: Keeping the Right Tokens in the KV Cache Is Not Enough for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.tldr: PACE shows that retaining the right KV-cache tokens is insufficient for long-horizon agents unless their positional distance remains retrievable, and combines plan-aware retention with position renumbering to preserve long-context performance.

papers.abstract: Context selection can reduce input length during long-input inference but can remove evidence required to answer a query. We introduce CoRA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating evidence preservation under shared token budgets. We compare head and tail truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, dense retrieval with reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across BABILong, LOONG Financial Spotlight, a custom NoLiMa diagnostic, and LongMemEval. Evidence-preservation results reveal task-dependent tradeoffs: BM25 achieves 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong at 128K, dense retrieval and dense reranking each achieve 0.908 needle recall on NoLiMa at 64K, and dense retrieval achieves 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval at 64K. Evidence, token retention, and complementary reader evaluations use the same selected contexts. Reader evaluations use dataset-native answer metrics and three runs on the same questions, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. At a 32K budget, BM25 achieves 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval achieves 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy. The results show that method rankings vary across evidence types and between evidence recall and downstream accuracy.
bullets: Compares truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across four long-context benchmarks.
Evaluates evidence recall, token retention, and downstream reader accuracy using the same selected contexts.
Reports strong but task-specific recall: BM25 reaches 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong, while dense retrieval reaches 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval.
At 32K tokens, BM25 obtains 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval obtains 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy.
Finds that evidence-recall rankings do not consistently predict downstream answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Sparse attention addresses this bottleneck by restricting each query to a subset of the context, but its effectiveness hinges on identifying relevant regions both cheaply and reliably. Existing training-free methods primarily rely on runtime relevance estimates, with selection dimensionality and granularity typically governed by fixed heuristics rather than the intrinsic interaction structure of pretrained attention heads. We take a different perspective: the query-key operator of each pretrained head defines a characteristic response structure that determines the resolution needed for sparse selection, both across feature directions and across context tokens. Building on this insight, we propose Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention (HASA), a training-free sparse attention framework that jointly adapts selection resolution along these two dimensions. Along the feature dimension, the singular spectrum of each head's query-key operator determines an effective rank, yielding a compact, head-specific response space. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. HASA captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass and, compared with UNIQUE, a strong recent sparse-attention baseline, improves accuracy by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points on RULER and LongBench-Pro, respectively, and accelerates self-attention by up to 1.32x, while achieving up to 14.07x speedup over dense attention.
authors: Wajih Hassan Raza, Ahsan Bilal, Yidan Shen, Renjie Hu, Xin Fu, Yu Wen
bullets: Targets the computational and KV-memory bottleneck of attention as context length grows.
Uses each head’s query-key operator to determine an effective feature rank and compact response space.
Merges neighboring token regions when their responses are directionally coherent, while preserving heterogeneous regions separately.
Computes exact attention with original full-dimensional KV states for selected regions.
Captures 88.1% of dense-attention mass, improves reported RULER and LongBench-Pro accuracy over UNIQUE by up to 3.47 and 2.57 points, and reaches up to 14.07× speedup over dense attention.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HASA. (1) Each head’s pretrained query–key interaction structure determines its effective rank, yielding a compact head-specific response space. (2) In this compact response space, neighboring regions with coherent token responses are progressively merged, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. (3) Relevant regions are selected using compact region summaries, followed by exact attention over their original full-dimensional KV states.

papers.title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.
authors: Siyuan Yan, Shen Gu, Xiaoxing Ma, Chun Cao, Jingwei Xu
bullets: Targets two inference costs: growing historical-prefix attention and repeated processing of mostly unchanged generation positions.
Uses prefix KV sparsity by selecting a compact, cross-step-stable subset of historical keys and values.
Uses early query sparsity to predict which positions will update, then runs only their queries through deeper Transformer layers.
Training-free and evaluated at 32K context length.
Reports end-to-end/per-step speedups of 1.34×/2.83× on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41×/4.72× on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Duet. (A) Block-level prefix selection: After the first dense step, Duet selects a compact historical prefix subset for each sparse suffix layer and reuses the resulting KV cache within the generation block. (B) Step-wise query selection: in subsequent denoising steps, Duet identifies active query rows at an early selection layer and propagates only these rows through the remaining Transformer layers, reducing redundant computation in both attention and FFN/MoE. Active and bypassed states are then recombined for the next denoising step.

Figure 4: Inference speedup across context lengths. End-to-end and stable-step speedups over dense inference on LLaDA2.1-mini and SDAR-8B at 8K, 16K, and 32K context lengths. Stable-step latency averages all denoising steps except the first step, highlighting the execution efficiency of sparse decoding. Duet achieves increasingly larger speedups as the context grows and consistently provides the strongest stable-step acceleration among the compared methods.

Figure 3: LongBench quality–throughput trade-off. Five-task Macro-F1 relative to each model’s dense score (100%) versus 32K end-to-end throughput. Absolute Macro-F1 scores are reported in Table 1; task-wise results appear in Appendix Table 4.

Our method is designed around the two orthogonal computation dimensions, selectively reducing both the query rows propagated through deep layers and the historical prefix KV states they attend to.

Figure 5: Two sparsity opportunities in BDLM inference. (a) A compact prefix subset selected at the beginning of a generation block continues to cover most of the prefix-attention mass throughout denoising. (b) Intermediate representations can identify, with high recall, the positions selected by the final-layer decoding policy. Results are shown on LLaDA2.1-mini as a representative example.

papers.abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.
authors: Qijia Zhuang, Rui Liu, Yuxiang Ren
bullets: Long-horizon tool use creates growing context overhead from structured outputs and intermediate artifacts.
Existing text-importance and truncation methods may discard information needed by later workflow steps.
WAAC models successful trajectories to learn reusable compression experience and performs online backward dependency analysis.
It combines historical experience with current dependency constraints to choose compression strategies for different information types.
On PinchBench and Odysseys, WAAC reports an overall score of 87.6, a 19.0% perfect completion rate, and execution-cost reductions of 19.7% and 29.1% versus the strongest baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WAAC. Offline processing converts verified development trajectories into canonical workflow fragments and field-level policy records. Before each online model invocation, WAAC derives requirements from outstanding obligations, retrieves compatible historical policies, and combines them through a conservative join. The resulting projection changes the model-visible history while retaining original events and artifacts in runtime storage.

papers.tldr: WAAC compresses long-horizon agent trajectories by preserving workflow-critical information, improving task performance while reducing execution costs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.
authors: Sungwon Moon, Minji Kim, Hyemin Boo, Daeun Song, Jiyoung Lee
bullets: Targets slow closed-loop robot response caused by expensive visual processing.
Training-free pruning uses the predicted prior action as a geometric prior before the vision encoder runs.
In the fixed third-person view, it keeps patches along the projected end-effector path and semantic anchors.
In the wrist view, it removes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for action-induced camera motion.
Evaluated in LIBERO, VLABench, and four real-robot tasks, achieving up to 1.61× speedup and 59.5% FLOPs reduction with negligible success-rate degradation.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.
authors: Zanting Ye, Yunrui Lin, Shengyuan Liu, Jing Hao, Chen Hu, Yefeng Zheng, Lijun Lu
bullets: Addresses the high cost and redundancy of processing hundreds of volume slices in medical vision–language models.
Separates visual-content selection from token-budget allocation instead of coupling them.
Groups contiguous slices into ordered units and uses Lorentz distance for token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement.
Uses visual-encoder attention entropy to assign more tokens where attention is more dispersed.
Across nine settings, retains 22.78% of tokens on average while achieving 121.68% mean relative quality and robust performance at a 10% budget.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of VoluCompose. A frozen visual interface converts an ordered volume into visual tokens. The hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units, allocates tokens across units, selects distinctive anchors with the Lorentz distance, and refines them with related context while preserving source order. The attention-calibrated capacity control module determines the total budget 𝐵 from a prescribed retention fraction or normalized attention entropy. The compact token sequence is supplied to the language decoder for downstream tasks.

papers.abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Zixuan Wang, Weisong Shi
bullets: Dense BEV grids waste computation on regions the vehicle will not traverse.
A coarse scene encoding predicts path-related heat, then selectively refines high-heat cells under a fixed budget.
The mixed-resolution BEV covers the full scene and requires neither an HD map nor a navigation command.
With 10% refinement, it uses 28% of BEV queries and 66% of encoder time versus a full fine grid, while achieving lower reported errors on nuScenes and NAVSIM navtest.
The approach is evaluated on two benchmarks and is intended for path-focused, efficient end-to-end driving.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of BEVCast at the 10% refinement budget. Both encoders read the shared image features and the ego motion embedding and the coarse memory of the previous keyframe. The full grid baseline encodes 10,000 cells of 1.024 m in one pass with the same encoder architecture.

Figure 2. Learned selection at the 10% refinement budget on three validation frames. The bottom row shows the heat in pale blue on the coarse grid over the whole 102.4 m range with the 62 refined cells outlined in orange and subdivided into 1.024 m cells and the annotated agents in grey.

papers.title: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: BEVCast reduces BEV computation by refining only cells near the predicted driving path while maintaining or improving planning performance.

papers.abstract: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
bullets: Targets DiTs’ inefficient uniform processing of mostly sparse visual content.
Routes tokens independently through MLP and self-attention operations, adapting compute by token, image, and denoising timestep.
Processes as few as 12.5% of tokens, substantially reducing training and inference costs.
Higher sparsity and model depth improve generation performance over unrouted baselines.
Token allocation is interpretable, correlating with visual content, noise level, and video motion.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive. Each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.
bullets: Targets high VLA inference cost and distraction from redundant visual tokens, especially across multiple cameras and under distribution shift.
Uses segmentation-guided pruning to remove irrelevant patches, followed by saliency-guided attention biasing over retained visual tokens and language instructions.
On LIBERO-Spatial, removes 85% of scene-camera tokens while essentially matching unpruned success and improves OOD success by up to 7 percentage points.
Adds 7.8 ms per inference call for refinement and achieves up to 3.3× LLM-forward speedup at higher input resolutions.
Across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones, benefits are strongest in multi-camera settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-stage T3R pipeline. Stage 2 (biasing): Integrated Gradients over the instruction identifies salient words; an additive attention bias (𝛽=2.0) is injected into the middle decoder layers for action-token queries, steering attention toward salient text tokens and retained visual patches before the action chunk is decoded.

The crossover is consistent with pruning reducing misleading background context.

papers.abstract: LiDAR is a critical sensor for autonomous driving and robotics, yet it remains vulnerable to adverse conditions such as fog, rain, transparent objects, and low-reflectance surfaces. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL) addresses these limitations by capturing the complete return waveform as a histogram, preserving rich reflection characteristics including multi-path echoes and weak signals. While recent Transformer-based approaches have demonstrated promise on FWL data, two fundamental bottlenecks remain: high computational cost from redundant tokens in low-intensity background regions, and limited generalization due to scarce annotated training data. We address both bottlenecks by exploiting the physical structure inherent to FWL data. First, we propose FWL-ToPM, a token pruning and merging mechanism that leverages intensity distributions to selectively reduce tokens while retaining critical waveform content. Second, we introduce FWLAug, a data augmentation framework designed as a regularization method that preserves waveform structure, retaining the Time-of-Flight waveform of each ray and the frustum geometry, to improve generalization to unseen scenes. Evaluated on the Ghost-FWL benchmark, FWL-ToPM achieves over 8 times speedup at real-time throughput alongside a nearly 9-point F1 gain over the prior state of the art, establishing the first real-time FWL Transformer that simultaneously improves accuracy. FWLAug further improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution test set of unseen scenes. Together, these methods push FWL-based perception toward practical deployment. The code and the OOD dataset are publicly available and can be accessed via the project page: https://keio-csg.github.io/FWL-ToPM
bullets: Addresses Transformer inefficiency from redundant low-intensity background tokens and limited labeled data in full-waveform LiDAR.
FWL-ToPM prunes and merges tokens using intensity distributions while preserving important waveform content.
FWLAug augments data while retaining each ray’s Time-of-Flight waveform and frustum geometry.
On Ghost-FWL, FWL-ToPM delivers over 8× speedup and nearly 9-point higher F1 than the prior state of the art.
FWLAug improves performance on both the standard benchmark and an out-of-distribution set of unseen scenes; code and the OOD dataset are public.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (Top) During training, FWLAug augments FWL samples while preserving ToF waveform structure and frustum geometry. High-intensity patches are selected by pruning, spatially reordered along a space-filling curve, and processed by the FWL-ToPM Encoder, which merges redundant tokens before self-attention and unmerges afterward across L Transformer blocks. (Bottom Left) Pruning removes low-intensity background tokens, and merging aggregates the remainder, concentrating computation on object-relevant waveform content. (Bottom Right) Proportion of pixel classes across intensity bins in FWL data. Most regions in FWL data correspond to noisy background, and our pruning strategy removes these dominant low-intensity regions.

Figure 3: (Left) F1-mean vs. FPS trade-off for all compared methods. (Right) Comparison of F1-mean and FPS without additional training. For pruning and merging, ρlow and ρm are varied from 0 to 0.9, respectively. For pruning+merging, ρlow is fixed to 0.7 while ρm is varied. All models are trained without FWLAug.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of classification results with existing FWL-based recognition methods.

Figure 2: Illustration of FWLAug. FWLShiftMix (top): an object in Sample 1 is shifted away from the LiDAR, creating a blank region Ωblank. A glass-containing region Ωsrc is then selected from Sample 2 and pasted into the blank, producing an augmented scene in which the waveform structure of each ray is preserved. FWLCutMix (bottom): a crop region Ωsrc containing minority class (glass) is selected from a source frame and pasted into a destination frame at a random location. Both methods prioritize glass-containing regions to mitigate class imbalance.

Figure 1: Our OOD Test Set. Based on the dense 3D maps as shown in Scene, we annotated FWL data with 4 labels: Ghost (red), Object (green), Glass (blue), Noise. Blue crosses indicate the LiDAR positions during data acquisition. The RGB images show the scenery of the capture locations.

After pruning low-intensity background tokens, the remaining high-intensity tokens are merged by aggregating similar-feature source tokens into destination tokens, reducing the total token count while preserving object-relevant content. The zoomed-in regions show that merged tokens retain the spatial structure of reflected objects across diverse scenes.

Markers indicate annotated Object (green), Glass (blue), and Ghost (red) bins, labels indicate the Top-3 highest-intensity peaks of each ray, and the dashed line indicates the intensity threshold below which patches are pruned at ρlow = 0.7. The photographs show the corresponding scenes, with the red marker indicating the observed ray. Top-3 peak extraction discards the Object and the Glass return, whereas our intensity-based pruning retains both because they lie above the pruning threshold.

papers.abstract: KV cache eviction must decide which entries carry information that the rest of the cache can no longer supply. A natural way to estimate this is a learnable gate: give each cached entry a gate on its attention weight and train the gate on the model's own objective. The gate belongs inside the normalizing softmax, where suppressing one entry hands its mass to the others rather than discarding it. That same normalizer absorbs any per-query constant, so a constant gate cancels and reproduces the frozen model exactly. Trained on the language-modeling loss the gate stays near a constant score while its loss falls throughout: optimization succeeds, but a frozen backbone was fit for dense attention, so its loss prefers the no-op, and a near-constant score ranks nothing. The no-op is not a floor the gate improves from but what its objective asks for. A second obstacle survives once the gate moves, since the same gradient charges the gate for errors the frozen model already makes, which no reweighting of positions separates out. Much of the machinery in learnable eviction, from sparsity penalties to relaxations of the discrete decision, works around the first obstacle rather than removing it; both are removed by putting dense attention beyond the gate's reach and making the dense model's predictions its target. Under these two conditions capacity is never the missing ingredient: neither a larger scorer, nor explicit access to the past, nor a trainable backbone helps. The same holds for what eviction unavoidably discards, which is recovered by parameter-free centroids read inside the same softmax far better than by any memory read outside it, since the mass they must return is a share of that normalizer and available nowhere else. At 75\% KV cache compression, this gate reaches 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, 3.72 and 1.36 points below full-cache inference.
bullets: A gate inside the attention softmax reallocates suppressed entries’ probability mass instead of discarding it; constant gates exactly reproduce dense attention.
Language-modeling loss on a frozen dense model favors this no-op, leaving gate scores nearly constant and unable to rank entries.
Even after gates move, gradients conflate eviction decisions with errors already present in the frozen model.
The proposed setup gives the gate a target beyond dense attention and uses parameter-free centroids inside the softmax to recover discarded information.
At 75% KV-cache compression, it scores 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, within 3.72 and 1.36 points of full-cache inference.

The three history variants add one branch that is summed into the MLP’s pre-activation: (c) a depthwise causal convolution over the previous eight tokens, (d) a gated recurrence carrying a fixed-size state 𝑆𝑗−1, and (e) a single-head causal attention over the prefix up to 𝑗. papers.title: The Gating Mechanism of KV Cache Eviction
papers.tldr: Learnable KV-cache eviction fails when trained only against a frozen dense-attention model, but succeeds when dense attention is kept outside the gate and discarded information is restored within the same softmax.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk and have made efficient video generation practical. However, further accelerating these models toward real-time generation remains challenging, as few-step distillation leaves little cross-step redundancy for existing training-free caching methods to exploit. We revisit this regime and identify two token-level redundancy patterns: cross-frame redundancy from static content shared across adjacent frames, and cross-step redundancy from tokens that converge early during denoising. Crucially, we find that early clean estimates along the model's own denoising trajectory provide an effective online signal for locating both patterns, requiring no retraining, auxiliary predictor, or reference video. Based on these findings, we propose PreSTP (Predictive Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning), a training-free framework that constructs a unified token-wise redundancy mask from cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence. Tokens marked as redundant skip subsequent computation under a consistent last-computed-value restoration rule, and a content-adaptive mask reuse strategy further reduces dense probing cost. On 5-second generation, PreSTP achieves 1.52x-3.20x speedups and a better efficiency-fidelity trade-off than coarse-grained caching baselines such as TeaCache and FlowCache. On 30-second generation, it reaches up to 1.96x speedup while improving VBench-Long and suppressing long-horizon drift. Notably, it continues to reduce inference cost even in the extreme one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy vanishes entirely and coarse step-wise caching is no longer applicable.
bullets: Targets limited cross-step redundancy in few-step autoregressive video generation.
Uses early clean denoising estimates to detect cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence online.
Applies a unified token mask, last-computed-value restoration, and adaptive mask reuse without retraining or auxiliary predictors.
Reports 1.52×–3.20× speedups for 5-second videos and up to 1.96× for 30-second videos, with improved long-horizon fidelity.
Remains effective in the one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy and step-wise caching are unavailable.

papers.abstract: AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.
bullets: Token waste is measured by normalizing full agent trajectories, identifying removable spans with an LLM judge, and mapping them to token-level costs.
The framework validates waste through interventions that remove marked spans and observe task outcomes and subsequent actions.
Online pruning removes 41–46% of model reasoning while largely preserving performance across two agent benchmarks.
Waste varies more by task and agent setting than by model, with distinct patterns in reasoning, execution, and harnesses.
The framework turns token waste into an actionable signal for improving models, reasoning strategies, and agent harnesses.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at https://pranjal2041.github.io/vtr
bullets: Targets the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of visual tokens accumulating across long interaction histories.
Jointly trains a vision-language model with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that selects action-relevant, nonredundant image-region tokens.
Uses an adaptive loss to minimize token count while limiting performance degradation.
Matches the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video-game action prediction using 2.5–5.8× fewer visual tokens.
Reduces inference cost by up to 3.3× and prefilling time by up to 2.9×; outperforms resolution reduction and other token-dropping baselines on OSWorld.

papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting recurring shell-output structure alongside execution-specific content without running commands.
