bullets: Targets lower computation without sacrificing semantic understanding.
Uses semantic, variable-resolution token merging guided by object and text localization.
Preserves spatial coverage and finer distinctions at object boundaries and literal text.
Learned [REL] registers perform additional relevance pruning after early decoder processing.
Across 3 backbones and 13 benchmarks, retains 86.10–92.33% of full-token performance using 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image tokens, outperforming 15 baselines at every evaluated budget.
papers.selection_reason: Image-token compression via semantic merging and relevance pruning directly targets token-level efficiency for vision-language models.
papers.title: Just Respect the Semantics: Image-Token Compression via Pre-LLM Semantic Variable-Resolution Tokenization and In-LLM Relevance Pruning
papers.tldr: Varest compresses image tokens by preserving fine detail for objects and text while coarsening redundant regions, then pruning less relevant tokens inside the LLM.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Fengyu Zhou, Yijuan Liang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Existing pruning methods can retain strong overall performance but substantially harm OCR and visual grounding.
Bifocal uses mixed-granularity pruning with separate query-focused and image-intrinsic token budgets plus a pooled whole-image representation.
It matches question words to regions, balances this with norm-debiased image saliency, maximizes coverage, and applies density-adjusted text-to-image attention pruning inside the LLM.
Using roughly one-quarter of the visual tokens, it retained over 90% of unpruned performance in every evaluated ability group across three MLLM families.
The method was evaluated across ten pruning methods, five ability groups, and nine model-budget settings; code is publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free visual token pruning for MLLMs, directly relevant to efficiency and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Bifocal: Training-Free Mixed Granularity Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Bifocal is a training-free visual-token pruning method that preserves fine-grained and general MLLM abilities by combining query-focused, image-intrinsic, and coarse image evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.
authors: Vatsal, Soumil Malhotra, Priyanshu Chahal, Sanjeev Kumar
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of token interactions and limited understanding of robustness in training-free token reduction.
Uses class-attention pruning to remove less-important tokens and similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy.
Introduces Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) to assess robustness under image transformations.
Evaluated on pretrained ViT and DeiT models, it achieves competitive compute reduction with better accuracy than existing token-reduction methods.
Finds that hybrid token reduction preserves prediction stability and does not produce hallucination-like behavior for common transformations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes training-free token pruning and merging for Vision Transformers, directly matching token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
papers.tldr: A training-free prune-and-merge strategy compresses Vision Transformer tokens while reducing computation and preserving accuracy and prediction stability.

papers.abstract: We propose a unified spatial-density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full-pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM-Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill-probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM-Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity.Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL-3.5, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-1.5) and three full-pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three-way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density-based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top-k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM-Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL-3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM-Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full-pipeline validation for any decode-phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/TwinPrune
authors: Kai Liu, Anqi Li, Junxian Li, Zhixin Wang, Zhikai Chen, Renjing Pei, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Prefill-only probes can hide severe decode-phase quality degradation, so pruning claims require full-pipeline evaluation.
Method: Apply density-based scoring for bipartite visual-token merging during prefill and top-k visual KV eviction during decode.
Contribution: Establishes separate benchmarks and evaluation guidance, recommending MM-Vet or DocVQA for decode-pruning validation.
Results: Prefill selection is up to 100× faster at high resolution; decode pruning outperforms H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM across tested retention ratios.
Scope: Evaluated across seven model variants and multiple vision-language benchmarks; performance gains are reported for both stages.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes density-aware token pruning and KV eviction for vision-language models, directly addressing efficiency in both prefill and decode phases.
papers.title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: TwinPrune uses spatial-density-aware token pruning separately for prefill merging and decode KV eviction, improving the compute–memory–accuracy trade-off while exposing pitfalls in phase-specific evaluation.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers incur high computational costs when processing long visual token sequences. Existing reduction methods typically rank tokens independently and discard those deemed unimportant or redundant. We propose a reconstruction-guided framework for visual token condensation (ReConV), which summarizes the complete visual sequence with a compact Summary Bank (SMB) and retains tokens whose information is not adequately captured by the SMB, as indicated by their reconstruction residuals. At each compression layer, a lightweight position-conditioned decoder reconstructs the current tokens, leaving shared information compressed in the SMB while explicitly preserving poorly reconstructed details. Experiments on image classification and multimodal understanding demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs: ReConV surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48\% fewer GMACs on ImageNet and enables reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference. Code is available at TokenDrop.
authors: Xiaoya Tang, Shilong Liu, Daniel Smolyak, Xiwen Li, Quynh Nguyen, Tolga Tasdizen
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of Vision Transformers on long visual token sequences.
Uses a position-conditioned decoder to reconstruct tokens from a Summary Bank at each compression layer.
Retains tokens with large reconstruction residuals, rather than ranking tokens independently.
Achieves favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs in image classification and multimodal understanding.
On ImageNet, surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48% fewer GMACs and supports reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes reconstruction-guided visual token condensation, directly fitting token pruning/eviction for efficient vision and multimodal inference.
papers.title: Bottlenecked semantic compression by representation reconstruction
papers.tldr: ReConV compresses long visual token sequences by reconstructing shared information in a compact summary bank and retaining tokens with unrecovered details, improving efficiency while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Video language models represent a video as a long sequence of visual embeddings in a decoder's input. Every visual embedding is processed by every decoder layer during prefill, stored in the key value cache, and attended by every generated token, so a long video raises prefill, memory, and generation cost at once. We present WIRE (Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding), which reduces this recurring cost by moving part of the video conditioned computation of a frozen video language model from its input activations into a temporary low rank update of its weights. WIRE keeps a short explicit visual context, so the update acts as a correction rather than a replacement of the video. WIRE first compresses the full resolution embeddings of each frame into a small set of carrier tokens using a question conditioned bidirectional selective scan, and physically contracts the decoder input so every decoder layer, cache entry, and decoding step operates on the shorter sequence. Hypernetworks at selected decoder layers read the compressed forward pass together with a readout of the full resolution features removed by contraction and generate LoRA updates to the attention and feedforward projections. The updates are merged after prefill, so autoregressive decoding runs the unmodified frozen backbone. On Qwen3-VL-8B, WIRE with 16 carrier tokens per frame contracts the visual stream by $3.5\times$, reduces decoder prefill time by $3.35\times$ at 256 frames and $4.14\times$ at 1024 frames, shrinks the key value cache proportionally, and keeps per token decoding latency approximately constant. Across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames, it obtains the highest average accuracy among efficient video language models we evaluate under a common 256 frame budget.
authors: Ameen Ali, Tamim Zoabi, Lior Wolf, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Addresses the rising prefill, KV-cache, and attention costs caused by long video embedding sequences.
Compresses each frame into carrier tokens using a question-conditioned bidirectional selective scan, then contracts the decoder input.
Uses hypernetworks to generate LoRA updates from compressed features and removed full-resolution information at selected decoder layers.
Merges updates after prefill, allowing autoregressive decoding to use the unmodified frozen backbone.

On Qwen3-VL-8B with 16 carrier tokens per frame, achieves 3.5× visual-stream contraction, 3.35–4.14× faster prefill, proportional KV-cache reduction, and top average accuracy across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a method to compress visual tokens and reduce KV cache/prefill cost in frozen video LLMs, directly targeting efficiency in multimodal inference.
papers.title: WIRE: Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding of Frozen Video LLMs
papers.tldr: WIRE makes frozen video LLMs more efficient by replacing most long visual inputs with a short context plus temporary low-rank weight updates that preserve video information.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.
authors: Shengzhen Li, Yongkang Li, Hao Gao, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited representation quality and high latency caused by generic visual pretraining and dense patch processing.
Distills complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models.
Adapts the encoder to multi-frame driving and stores spatiotemporal context in register tokens for planning.
Uses register-guided token compression to reduce redundant patch computation while improving planning performance.
Reports 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Builds a knowledge-dense, token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving, improving planning and achieving 2x speedup via register-guided token compression.
papers.title: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: ConDenseDrive distills diverse visual knowledge into a token-sparse encoder that improves planning while delivering 2.0× faster inference for end-to-end autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
authors: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
bullets: Fixed relevance–diversity weights vary substantially across tasks and even among samples within the same benchmark.
SAVER infers a sample-specific weight from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens using a Geometric Intent Prior.
It combines Weighted Text Centroid relevance scoring with Visual Marginal Coverage Gain diversity selection.
The training-free method retains 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B while using 11.1% of the original visual tokens.
It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
papers.selection_reason: Sample-aware visual token reduction for VLMs balancing relevance and diversity at inference time.
papers.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
papers.tldr: SAVER improves visual token compression by adapting the relevance–diversity trade-off to each input sample at inference time.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Dohyeon Kim, Bedionita Soro, Bruno Andreis, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: MoE models reduce computation but retain all expert parameters, creating substantial memory overhead.
Existing merging methods may produce poor function interpolation and depend on calibration data.
SLEM uses a VAE-based latent representation, grouping experts by latent similarity within and across layers.
It derives merge coefficients from expert weight spectra and applies geometry-aware latent interpolation.
The method achieves comparable or better general-knowledge performance and higher average performance on math-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory efficiency in Mixture-of-Experts models through expert merging in a latent space, relevant to efficient AI and LLMs.
papers.title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
papers.tldr: SLEM compresses Mixture-of-Experts models without calibration data by merging experts in a spectrum-aware latent space.

papers.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.
authors: Shuo Gao, Chenhao Zheng, Zhongzheng Ren
bullets: Addresses the linear memory and latency growth caused by encoding every video frame as visual tokens.
Uses a training-free, inference-only strategy that ranks frames by prompt relevance and diversity, then packs them at varying resolutions.
Works with off-the-shelf VLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
Experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME report consistent improvements over full-resolution, token-reduction, and keyframe-selection baselines.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, gains are 12.9%, 10.6%, and 9.7% on the three benchmarks, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Constant-memory frame packing for long-video understanding; efficient token/frame selection.
papers.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FramePack-U enables VLMs to understand arbitrarily long videos with constant memory by packing prompt-relevant, diverse frames into a fixed-size visual representation.

papers.abstract: Adaptive image tokenizers compress an image into a variable number of tokens matched to its complexity, and recent work makes this allocation controllable: conditioned on a target reconstruction error, the tokenizer itself decides how many tokens an image needs. However, the fidelity measure guiding this allocation shapes which aspects of the image are preserved under compression. The pixel-wise error used in prior work is blind to the spatial structure that carries an image's meaning, and under heavy compression such tokenizers are prone to abruptly discarding tokens that encode essential content. We introduce GIST (Guided Image Semantic Tokenizer), an adaptive tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested semantic fidelity. Its token allocation is jointly controlled by pixel-level and semantic target errors, with semantic error measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. This joint control enables semantic protection: with the semantic target fixed at zero, the reconstruction target can be relaxed to discard pixel detail while preserving what the image depicts. In a controlled comparison on ImageNet-100, GIST outperforms its pixel-controlled counterpart KARL at every token count, with up to $30\%$ lower LPIPS and $37\%$ lower DreamSim. On average, lowering its semantic target reduces LPIPS $2\times$ faster per token than lowering the reconstruction target, and up to $5\times$ in the low-token regime. Semantic fidelity is thus an effective control signal for adaptive tokenization: it lets a tokenizer see, and so preserve, what an image depicts.
authors: Danilo de Goede, Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani, Yuki M. Asano, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Pixel-wise error can discard semantically important content when token budgets are tight.
GIST uses a frozen DINOv3 feature space to measure semantic error alongside reconstruction error.
Fixing the semantic target while relaxing pixel fidelity enables detail removal without losing what the image depicts.
On ImageNet-100, GIST improves over KARL at every token count, with up to 30% lower LPIPS and 37% lower DreamSim.
Semantic targets reduce perceptual error faster per token, especially in low-token settings.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive image tokenization with semantic-fidelity-controlled token allocation; directly relevant to token pruning and efficiency.
papers.title: Semantically Steerable Image Tokenization
papers.tldr: GIST adaptively allocates image tokens using both pixel and semantic fidelity, preserving image content better under compression than pixel-only control.

papers.abstract: Quantization plays a crucial role in efficiently deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. Post-training quantization does not require access to the original dataset or retraining the full model. Current methods that achieve high performance close to baseline results typically require INT8 fixed-point integers. However, achieving higher model compression with lower bit-widths often leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose VLCQ, a post-training quantization method that relaxes the fixed-point encoding constraint, enabling more flexible exploration of quantization techniques through variable-length encoding. This approach achieves competitive or improved performance while reducing bit-widths, without requiring access to training data or model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and object detection demonstrate that VLCQ improves model compression and accuracy compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization approaches. For per-channel quantization, VLCQ surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (PWLQ) on most evaluated models, achieving up to 6x compression compared with FP32 and up to 1.7x compared with PWLQ. When prioritizing compression with limited accuracy loss, VLCQ achieves up to 12.25x compression compared with FP32 with less than 4% performance degradation. For per-tensor quantization, VLCQ is competitive with Data-Free Quantization (DFQ), while providing greater flexibility to achieve lower bit rates across different tasks and models.
authors: Reem Abdel-Salam, Ahmed H. Abdel-Gawad, Amr G. Wassal
bullets: Avoids access to training data and model fine-tuning.
Relaxes fixed-point encoding constraints through variable-length coding.
Evaluated on image classification, segmentation, and object detection.
Per-channel quantization reaches up to 6× FP32 compression and up to 1.7× PWLQ compression, with accuracy sometimes exceeding FP32.
Can reach up to 12.25× FP32 compression with less than 4% performance degradation; per-tensor results are competitive with DFQ.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces variable length coding for post-training quantization, a technique that manipulates tokens/weights to improve efficiency, fitting the token pruning and eviction subtopic.
papers.title: VLCQ: Post-training quantization for deep neural networks using variable length coding
papers.tldr: VLCQ enables data-free, post-training quantization with variable-length encoding to achieve stronger compression at low bit-widths while preserving or improving model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Foundation models like V-JEPA are increasingly deployed across a heterogeneous edge-cloud continuum spanning smart glasses, phones, robots, and servers. Yet, they are typically trained as rigid, fixed-capacity networks bound to one device, supporting neither reconfigurable compute budgets nor collaborative execution. Existing approaches address only one axis at a time: slimmable and NAS-based methods provide width elasticity but assume single-device inference, whereas split-computing methods enable cross-device collaboration only for fixed partitions and static capacities. We introduce Elastic V-JEPA (EV-JEPA), a single model trained once and deployable everywhere along the continuum. Its width is reconfigurable, and it is natively partitionable across heterogeneous devices. At its core is Transition-Aware Triplet Training (T3). At each step we pick a narrow and a wide width, and train three paths: each width alone, plus a hybrid path that runs the early layers narrow and the rest wide. The hybrid switch point is where one device hands off to another, so the same weights learn both single-device and cross-device execution. Across various benchmarks, EV-JEPA falls within 1 accuracy point of independently trained baselines while improving over previous elastic training approaches by up to 11 accuracy points. Narrow-to-wide cross-device hybrid execution recovers to within 1.1 points of the highest-capacity standalone model and supports many-to-one, any-to-any, and variable-split configurations. Finally, we show that the elastic principle extends beyond the backbone to an elastic token compression mechanism that exposes controllable trade-offs among on-device computation, latency, and accuracy.
authors: Anxhelo Diko, Jieyu Lin, Stefano Ambrogio, Ziyun Li, Mahmoud Assran, Th\'eo Moutakanni, Barbara De Salvo, Chiao Liu
bullets: Supports reconfigurable model widths for different device compute budgets.
Enables native cross-device execution with flexible split points and many-to-one or any-to-any configurations.
Uses Transition-Aware Triplet Training to jointly train narrow, wide, and hybrid narrow-to-wide execution paths.
Matches independently trained baselines within 1 accuracy point and improves prior elastic methods by up to 11 points.
Extends elasticity to token compression, trading on-device computation and latency against accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic V-JEPA enables reconfigurable width and cross-device inference with elastic token compression, reducing compute.
papers.title: EV-JEPA: Elastic V-JEPA for Any Device and Cross-Device Inference
papers.tldr: EV-JEPA is a single V-JEPA model that flexibly adapts its width and splits computation across heterogeneous devices with near-baseline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) are often built using pretrained acoustic encoders as an audio interface to an LLM decoder. However, LLMs scale poorly with input sequence length, while acoustic encoders tend to produce substantially longer sequences than typical textual inputs. This motivates learning to compress encoder outputs while preserving task-oriented information. To this end, we introduce ASSET, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that learns to adaptively compress encoder outputs by first partitioning them into variable-duration segments and then pooling each segment into a continuous audio token. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to train a segmenter with task performance feedback and a token-rate penalty. In automatic speech recognition (ASR) experiments, ASSET achieves performance comparable to a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with approximately 25% fewer audio tokens on English LibriSpeech, while improving on a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL. Exploratory experiments on non-ASR tasks further illustrate how learned segmentation changes when the framework is adapted to tasks beyond transcription.
authors: Cihan Xiao, Yuan Tseng, Matthew Wiesner, Desh Raj, Leibny Paola Garcia Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur, David Harwath
bullets: Addresses the sequence-length mismatch between long acoustic-encoder outputs and speech LLM inputs.
Learns variable-duration segments and pools each into a continuous audio token.
Trains the segmenter with GRPO using task-performance feedback and a token-rate penalty.
Matches a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with about 25% fewer tokens on English LibriSpeech.
Outperforms a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL; non-ASR behavior is explored but not fully characterized.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based adaptive compression of speech encoder outputs into fewer audio tokens for speech LLMs; relevant to token efficiency and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: ASSET: Adaptive Speech Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ASSET uses reinforcement learning to adaptively segment and compress speech encoder outputs into fewer task-relevant audio tokens while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
authors: Yiyang Fu, Zihao Huang, Dongchen Han, Shukai Gong, Zhen Dong, Qiyang Min, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Addresses variable per-turn compute needs without using separate models or rebuilding history states when switching.
Uses lightweight full-token modules, ratio-specific boundary routers, and cross-ratio training in a shared backbone.
Fixed-ratio modes outperform compute-matched MoE baselines in all six reported comparisons and remain competitive with specialists.
Mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy–compute trade-off on CodeChat and CoSQL, with lower FLOPs than the Large MoE.
Under matched turn-wise budgets, it reduces FLOPs versus routing among independent models, demonstrating flexible shared-model inference.
papers.selection_reason: Single shared MoE model supporting multiple compute budgets via token-to-concept compression, fitting efficient AI and LLM architecture topics.
papers.title: One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns
papers.tldr: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE enables one shared model to flexibly use 2×, 4×, or 8× token-to-concept compression across conversation turns, improving accuracy–compute trade-offs while avoiding model-switching overhead.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. We introduce DoSA (Dots Sparse Attention), a lossless method for making this computation conditional while preserving exact token selection. Its central observation is that Top-K selection requires sufficient evidence to reject a candidate, not necessarily its full score. A seed set supplies a lower bound on the winning threshold. Nonnegative head projections and joint residual bounds upper-bound positive contributions, while activation-informed aggregation bounds the magnitude subtracted by negative heads. The certificate directs full scoring toward candidates that remain eligible; exact-score filtering further reduces writeback and selection work. We establish the certificate and its exact-selection conditions, and analyze how geometry and selection margins govern its effectiveness. Our GPU implementation accelerates the complete Indexer by up to 2.74 times over SGLang and 1.69 times over LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads. End-to-end evaluation on GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves up to 1.94 times and 1.50 times time-to-first-token speedups over the two baselines, respectively.
bullets: Sparse attention can remain expensive because every candidate may still be scored by each indexer head.
A seed set establishes a lower bound on the Top-K threshold, while bounds identify candidates that cannot be eliminated without full scoring.
The method uses nonnegative projections, residual bounds, and activation-informed bounds for negative contributions, followed by exact-score filtering.
GPU experiments report up to 2.74× faster indexing than SGLang and 1.69× faster than LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads.
End-to-end time-to-first-token improves by up to 1.94× on GLM-5.2 and 1.50× on DeepSeek-V3.2 versus the baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Lossless conditional sparse attention with exact Top-K key selection; directly targets efficient attention and token selection for LLM inference.
papers.title: DoSA: Dots Sparse Attention
papers.tldr: DoSA accelerates sparse-attention index selection by conditionally avoiding unnecessary key scoring while preserving exact Top-K results.

papers.abstract: Compact acoustic models face a challenging quality-capacity trade-off. We investigate two factors in this regime: encoder context and Mel-spectrogram supervision. A receptive-field-scaling study shows that expanding self-attention beyond 15 phonemes provides no consistent gains in pitch, energy, or duration prediction. Guided by this finding, we introduce a fixed-receptive-field convolutional encoder that reduces the respective prediction errors by 36.0%, 17.3%, and 3.4%. We further show that directly transferring image-domain gradient-variance supervision restores fine-scale variation but degrades predicted quality, motivating a Mel-specific formulation with axis-specific gradients, overlapping local statistics, and log-domain variance matching. GrainSpeech contains only 264.8K parameters and achieves 17.9x real-time Mel generation on a microcontroller (MCU), while attaining UTMOS scores comparable to substantially larger models with less than 1.5% of their parameters. Source code and demos are available at https://github.com/lab-emi/GrainSpeech.
bullets: Expanding encoder attention beyond 15 phonemes yields no consistent gains in pitch, energy, or duration prediction.
A fixed-receptive-field convolutional encoder reduces prediction errors by 36.0% for pitch, 17.3% for energy, and 3.4% for duration.
Image-domain gradient-variance supervision restores detail but harms quality; GrainSpeech instead uses axis-specific gradients, overlapping local statistics, and log-domain variance matching.
The 264.8K-parameter model generates Mels at 17.9× real time on an MCU and reaches UTMOS scores comparable to much larger models.
Scope: the approach targets compact, resource-constrained acoustic modeling, with results focused on Mel generation and predicted speech quality.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a compact speech synthesis model that reduces context length (receptive field) to improve efficiency, relevant to token-level efficiency methods.
papers.title: GrainSpeech: Less Context, More Detail for Compact Speech Synthesis
papers.tldr: GrainSpeech shows that compact speech synthesizers can retain fine acoustic detail with limited context, using a fixed-field encoder and Mel-specific gradient-variance supervision.

papers.abstract: Dynamic vocabularies built on-the-fly via Lempel-Ziv-Welch (LZW) compression let a language model represent the same text in fewer tokens, but prior work shows that this efficiency comes at a cost to reasoning and perplexity. We show that this quality gap is not a fundamental price of compression but can be substantially closed through targeted improvements to the compression layer and LZW codec, without modifying the underlying pretrained language model. Our analysis reveals four key issues: (1) LZW's compression algorithm creates an implicit conflict between the input embedding and the output embedding, a tension that a single shared embedding cannot resolve; (2) naively applying RoPE to LZW-compressed sequences ignores that merged tokens can span multiple tokens; (3) merging certain tokens (notably digits) disproportionately hurts downstream accuracy; and (4) dynamic vocabularies introduce an inherent segmentation ambiguity that confounds standard evaluation. We address these through decoupled input/output dynamic embedding layer, size-aware RoPE positioning, and a modified LZW codec supporting selective merges and multi-view segmentations. Across four models, our recipe improves perplexity on every corpus we evaluated as well as mathematical reasoning accuracy, closing roughly half the quality gap between zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar compression ratio on general text. This represents a significant step toward lossless adaptive-vocabulary compression for language models.
authors: Saibo Geng, Andrea Gentilini, Xinxian Ma, Nathan Ranchin, Yunzhen Yao, Robert West
bullets: Identifies four issues: shared input/output embeddings, RoPE misalignment for merged tokens, harmful digit merging, and segmentation ambiguity.
Uses decoupled input/output dynamic embeddings, size-aware RoPE, selective token merges, and multi-view segmentations.
Improves perplexity across all evaluated corpora and improves mathematical reasoning accuracy across four models.
Closes roughly half the quality gap between compressed zip2zip and the uncompressed baseline at a similar general-text compression ratio.
Targets adaptive-vocabulary compression while preserving the underlying model.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time token compression via dynamic LZW vocabularies and token merging directly targets token-level efficiency.
papers.title: zip2zip++: Towards Inference-Time Token Compression with Minimal Quality Loss
papers.tldr: zip2zip++ reduces the quality loss of inference-time LZW token compression through targeted embedding, positional, codec, and evaluation improvements—without changing the pretrained language model.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. However, treating audio tokens as generic, isotropic features smooths over spectral transitions, destroying fine-grained phonetic transitions essential for decoding speech. In contrast, speech signals exhibit highly structured temporal patterns where information density peaks at acoustic transitions. We propose AudioTETRIS, a training-free, two-stage framework that uses the audio encoder's representation geometry as an acoustic prior for token importance before applying attention-based compression. Instead of discarding encoder structure after the encoding stage, AudioTETRIS propagates this prior directly into the LLM decoder to compute a per-token fused score. This score drives progressive top-$k$ token selection across decoder layers without requiring additional training or auxiliary models. Evaluated on Qwen2-Audio-7B, Phi-4-Multimodal, and Audio Flamingo 3, AudioTETRIS retains near-uncompressed performance on several speech tasks using only 25% of audio tokens, matches or surpasses full-token accuracy at moderate compression rates, and consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Targets the high inference cost caused by hundreds of audio tokens and quadratic self-attention.
Uses encoder representation geometry to identify transition-rich, information-dense tokens.
Fuses acoustic-prior and decoder attention signals into per-token importance scores.
Progressively selects top-k tokens across decoder layers without training or auxiliary models.
Evaluated on three audio LLMs, it retains near-uncompressed speech-task performance and outperforms training-free baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free token elimination for audio LLMs using acoustic transition priors; fits token pruning and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: AudioTETRIS: Token Elimination via Transitional Importance Signals for Efficient Audio LLMs
papers.tldr: AudioTETRIS efficiently compresses audio tokens by preserving acoustically important transitions, maintaining near-full performance with only 25% of tokens.

papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models use the same network depth for every input, although forecasting windows differ in structure and difficulty. We test whether whole Transformer blocks can be removed at inference time in two pretrained models: Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5. Our bypasses avoid the original block computation and preserve the dense model exactly when all blocks are enabled. Masks are selected only on calibration windows and evaluated on 1,088 held-out windows from ETTh1, Traffic, Weather, and Exchange. At moderate sparsity, Chronos-Bolt with 7/11 candidate blocks and TimesFM with 16/20 blocks show little change in mean relative forecasting quality across datasets while reducing median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% and 13.4%. More aggressive TimesFM skipping accelerates inference further but substantially harms Traffic and Weather. Across both models, different equal-budget masks win on different windows, and a retrospective oracle significantly improves over the best static mask on every dataset. However, dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not support reliable unseen-domain routing. These results establish cross-architecture structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, but not a deployable dynamic inference method.
bullets: Evaluates structured whole-block skipping in Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5 using calibration-selected masks and 1,088 held-out windows across four datasets.
Moderate sparsity reduces median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% for Chronos-Bolt and 13.4% for TimesFM with little change in mean relative forecasting quality.
More aggressive skipping can accelerate TimesFM further but substantially degrades performance on Traffic and Weather.
Different masks are best for different windows; a retrospective oracle outperforms the best static mask on every dataset.
Dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not enable reliable unseen-domain routing.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates structured block skipping in time-series foundation models to reduce inference latency. A technical contribution to Efficient AI methods.
papers.title: How Much Computation Does Every Forecast Need? Structured Block Skipping in Two Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Pretrained time-series foundation models can skip some Transformer blocks to reduce latency with little average quality loss, but reliable input-adaptive routing remains unsolved.

papers.abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.
authors: Yongxin Zheng, Hao Wu, Fang Li, Hu Fu, Peiran Yin, Xudong Wang, Haozhe Hu, Xinghao Chen, Yunpu Ma, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Addresses high inference cost from repeated cross-view observations and processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer.
GeoSemZip builds compact 3D voxel-token representations using semantic saliency and spatial coverage, while retaining discarded information in contextual anchors.
GroupRoute uses late entry, early exit, and recoverable group-wise skipping to adapt visual computation to token relevance.
Using a 67K-sample compression-aware post-training set, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of dense-model performance on two 7B 3D VLMs.
It accelerates LLM prefill by 6.8× and 6.1×, demonstrating applicability to models with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding.
papers.selection_reason: Compresses 3D visual tokens and skips LLM layers for efficient 3D VLMs, directly relevant to token pruning and multimodal efficiency.
papers.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
papers.tldr: GeoGR makes multi-view 3D vision-language models substantially faster by compressing redundant scene tokens and selectively routing visual tokens through LLM layers while preserving most performance.

papers.abstract: Fewer latent tokens promise cheaper diffusion. Yet aggressive latent compression creates a reconstruction-generation dilemma: adding channels improves reconstruction but makes generation harder. We introduce APEX, short for Asynchronous Prefix denoising for EXtreme compression, which pairs a hierarchical latent space with asynchronous denoising over channel groups. Our autoencoder orders channel prefixes from structure to detail, while one shared denoiser generates them at staggered local times without adding tokens. On ImageNet-512, APEX outperforms existing methods at every evaluated channel count under 64x and 128x compression. At matched training and guided sampling compute, it also outperforms a 256-token model at every evaluated budget, with larger gains at lower compute. Code is available at https://daviddinkevich.github.io/APEX.
authors: David Dinkevich, Nisan Chiprut, Yoav HaCohen, Dani Lischinski
bullets: Addresses the reconstruction–generation trade-off in aggressively compressed latent spaces.
Uses an autoencoder with channel prefixes ordered from global structure to fine detail.
A shared denoiser generates channel groups at staggered local times without adding tokens.
On ImageNet-512, it outperforms prior methods across evaluated channel counts at 64× and 128× compression.
It also surpasses a 256-token model at matched compute, with larger gains at lower budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a compression method for diffusion models using asynchronous denoising, improving efficiency in video generation and addressing token management.
papers.title: APEX: Asynchronous Prefix Denoising for Extreme Compression
papers.tldr: APEX enables extreme latent compression by asynchronously denoising hierarchical channel groups, improving image generation quality without increasing token count.

papers.abstract: Mid-prefill pruning can reduce the sequence processed by deeper transformer layers, but attention concentration alone does not certify that discarded context is dispensable. We formulate EntroPrefill as a Renyi-guided proposal mechanism coupled to explicit constraints on discarded attention mass. Sink-isolated, regularized head pooling respects grouped-query attention while exposing a quantitative trade-off between specialization and worst-head coverage. We derive a mixture-to-head deletion envelope, a computable upper bound on feasible token removal, and a finite-sample observer guarantee that remains valid when the pruning layer is selected adaptively. We then establish a conditional transformer perturbation bound with explicit sufficient Lipschitz constants and a first-token decision-margin corollary. A counterexample shows why shallow observations alone cannot imply an unconditional future-output guarantee. The systems analysis distinguishes query-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payload, and gives an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning. This manuscript is theoretical in scope: it defines the procedure, its assumptions, and its formal limits, but does not report measured acceleration or task-accuracy preservation. Experiments are reserved for subsequent validation of the assumptions, approximation tightness, and end-to-end resource trade-offs.
bullets: Addresses the lack of formal guarantees that low-attention context tokens are safely dispensable.
Uses Rényi-guided proposals, sink-isolated regularized head pooling, and constraints on discarded attention mass.
Derives deletion bounds, adaptive finite-sample observer guarantees, and conditional transformer perturbation and decision-margin bounds.
Separates attention-head unions, physical page allocation, and KV-transfer payloads, yielding an arithmetic break-even condition for pruning.
Theoretical only: no measured speedup or task-accuracy results are reported, and guarantees depend on stated assumptions.
papers.selection_reason: Context pruning with guarantees for RAG; directly fits token pruning and KV cache efficiency.
papers.title: EntroPrefill: Renyi-Guided Context Pruning with Conditional Stability Guarantees for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: EntroPrefill provides a theoretically bounded method for pruning RAG context during prefill while clarifying when output stability and systems-level savings can—and cannot—be guaranteed.

papers.abstract: The memory-bound nature of the decoding stage of large language model (LLM) inference incurs significant latency. Layer-wise training-free network pruning approaches guided by the Hessian have been a prominent solution to this problem, as pruning reduces the number of nonzero parameters read from memory during decoding. Nevertheless, typical methods in this line compute the Hessian using pre-collected natural sequences, whereas the model is fed self-generated tokens during decoding, creating a distribution shift between the two sequences. The Hessian calculated on the natural sequence is different from that calculated on the generated sequence. We observe that this discrepancy causes the activation distribution during generation to deviate from that used for pruning, further hurting the pruned model performance. Moreover, most existing LLM pruning methods that bring actual speedup primarily target the sparse matrix-matrix (SpMM) multiplication, providing limited support for the sparse matrix-vector (SpMV) operations, which dominate decoding. To solve these problems, we introduce SparseDecoding, a principled decoding-aware pruning framework tailored for accurate and efficient LLM decoding. Specifically, at the algorithmic axis, SparseDecoding constructs calibration matrices from layer-wise activations collected during the dense-model autoregressive generation, excluding prefill, thereby aligning the pruning objective with the decoding activations. At the system axis, we develop an optimized N:M sparse matrix-vector kernel with bitmask indexing and fixed-step traversal. Substantial empirical results on representative LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-14B / 32B) demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms standard fixed-text calibration on the long-form generation benchmarks while achieving up to 1.48x end-to-end wall-clock decoding speedup on A100 GPUs.
authors: Qitong Wang, Xinwei Niu, Mingluo Su, Shanwei Zhao, Shiai Zhu, Huan Wang
bullets: Addresses distribution shift between natural-text calibration and autoregressive decoding, which can degrade pruned-model quality.
Collects layer-wise activations during dense-model generation, excluding the prefill stage, to make pruning decoding-aware.
Introduces an optimized N:M sparse matrix-vector kernel using bitmask indexing and fixed-step traversal.
Outperforms standard fixed-text calibration on long-form generation benchmarks across several representative LLMs.
Achieves up to 1.48× end-to-end decoding speedup on A100 GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces decoding-aware pruning for LLM inference to improve efficiency and accuracy.
papers.title: SparseDecoding: Decoding-Aware Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM Inference
papers.tldr: SparseDecoding improves LLM decoding accuracy and efficiency by calibrating pruning on generated-token activations and accelerating sparse matrix-vector operations.

papers.abstract: Most image generation models rely on uniform tokenization, allocating the exact same computational budget to equally-sized image patches. This static paradigm cannot adapt to different resource constraints at inference time, and yields suboptimal quality-cost tradeoff by devoting the same effort to both plain backgrounds and intricate details. We propose BudgetPix, an adaptive tokenization framework that dynamically allocates compute based on visual complexity and spatial layout, enabling flexible computational budgeting at inference time. BudgetPix comprises three key components: (1) an adaptive encoder that maps a fixed-size image to a variable-length token sequence using an entropy-guided quadtree alongside a multi-scale patch embedder; (2) a scale-aware decoder reconstructs fixed-resolution images from multi-scale token sets; and (3) a flexible training and sampling schedule that enables pixel-space denoisers to operate across variable token counts. BudgetPix seamlessly integrates with existing pixel-space diffusion architectures, enabling a single checkpoint to be operated at a wide range of compute budgets. Evaluated on text-to-image generation, BudgetPix matches the fidelity of MiniT2I-L at $512^2$ and PixelDiT at $1024^2$ using just 25% of the original compute budget. In class-conditional generation using a MeanFlow backbone, BudgetPix requires merely 60% of the full compute budget to produce images with near-zero quality degradation, observing a marginal 0.8-point increase in FID. Comprehensive assessments by human and VLM judges confirm that BudgetPix establishes a significantly improved quality-efficiency tradeoff over prior budget-adaptive baselines. More details are available at our project page: https://karaozgur.com/BudgetPix
authors: Ozgur Kara, Yujia Chen, Daniel Watson, David Forsyth, James Matthew Rehg, Wen-Sheng Chu, Du Tran
bullets: Uniform patch tokenization wastes compute on simple regions and cannot adapt to inference-time resource constraints.
An entropy-guided quadtree and multi-scale patch embedder produce variable-length token sequences based on visual complexity.
A scale-aware decoder and flexible training/sampling schedule support variable token counts in existing pixel-space diffusion models.
It matches reported baselines at 512² and 1024² using 25% of their compute budget, and achieves near-unchanged class-conditional quality at 60% compute, with a 0.8-point FID increase.
Human and VLM evaluations report better quality–efficiency tradeoffs than prior budget-adaptive methods.
papers.selection_reason: Compute-adaptive tokenization for pixel-space diffusion, dynamically selecting tokens by complexity, fitting token-level efficiency methods.
papers.title: BudgetPix: Compute-Adaptive Tokenization for Pixel-Space Image Diffusion
papers.tldr: BudgetPix adaptively allocates pixel-space diffusion compute according to image complexity, allowing one model to operate across flexible inference budgets with improved quality–efficiency tradeoffs.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made remarkable progress in bridging vision and language, facilitating various perception tasks essential for human-machine interaction, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, existing MLLM-based perception methods predominantly rely on text-based coordinate representation, which suffers from excessive token overhead, or fixed-range quantization, which suffers from range and precision constraints, especially for 3D domains with unbounded spatial range and high localization accuracy requirements. To address these challenges, we propose a dynamic vector decoding method named DVD, which unifies the representation of 2D and 3D perception tasks. Specifically, we first transform diverse perceptual representation (i.e., 2D bounding boxes, 2D masks, and 3D bounding boxes) into 1D vector sequences, which are then mapped to compact discrete tokens in the high-dimensional space. Then, a lightweight de-tokenizer enables seamless integration with MLLMs by decoding output tokens back to original 2D and 3D perceptual representations. Extensive experiments on 2D and 3D perception benchmarks including RefCOCO series, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, nuScenes demonstrate that DVD achieves superior performance in 2D and 3D tasks and reduces significantly the token overhead and inference latency. DVD provides an efficient and general framework for integrating perception capabilities into MLLMs, overcoming the inherent limitations of existing methods.
authors: Jinghua Hou, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of text-based coordinates and the range/precision limits of fixed quantization, particularly for unbounded 3D scenes.
Converts 2D boxes, 2D masks, and 3D boxes into 1D vector sequences mapped to compact discrete tokens.
Uses a lightweight de-tokenizer to reconstruct the original 2D or 3D representations from MLLM outputs.
Evaluated on RefCOCO, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, and nuScenes, with reported strong performance across 2D and 3D perception tasks.
The abstract reports reduced token overhead and inference latency, while the method unifies representation across perception tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficiency in MLLMs for perception tasks using dynamic vector decoding to reduce token overhead, relevant to both Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: DVD: Dynamic Vector Decoding for Efficient MLLM-based Perception
papers.tldr: DVD efficiently represents 2D and 3D perceptual outputs as compact dynamic vector tokens, reducing token overhead and inference latency in MLLM-based perception.

papers.abstract: Processing long visual token sequences from high-resolution images makes multi-step reasoning computationally expensive for multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Existing one-shot pruning and aggregation methods compress visual tokens into a fixed context before decoding. However, visual evidence needs can shift as reasoning unfolds, making it difficult for a fixed compressed context to retain all the details needed across stages. To address this challenge, we propose ViMoD, a lightweight framework that maintains a compact visual context while preserving access to original fine-grained evidence as reasoning needs evolve. Deformable Aggregation of Region-wise Tokens (DART) learns content-adaptive groups and aggregation capacities, constructing compact Coarse representations linked to recoverable original Fine tokens. Temporal Routing for Adaptive Contextual Evidence (TRACE) integrates decoding history to anticipate upcoming evidence needs and select, retain, or replace active Fine-token groups. Selected Fine tokens augment the persistent Coarse context in the frozen backbone, enabling stage-specific evidence access without continuously attending to all visual tokens. On Qwen3-VL-4B, ViMoD outperforms all evaluated baselines on all eight reasoning benchmarks at a 20% target visual token budget, improving the mean normalized score by 39.0% over the strongest evaluated one-shot baseline. These gains are achieved with only 0.0546% additional trainable parameters relative to the frozen backbone.
authors: Yicheng Xue, Han Wu, Jufeng Yang, Minjing Dong, Xinghao Chen, Hanting Chen, Jianyuan Guo
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed one-shot visual-token compression for multi-step reasoning.
DART builds compact coarse representations linked to recoverable original fine-grained tokens.
TRACE uses decoding history to select, retain, or replace fine-token groups during reasoning.
At a 20% visual-token budget, ViMoD outperforms evaluated baselines across eight reasoning benchmarks.
On Qwen3-VL-4B, it improves the mean normalized score by 39.0% over the strongest one-shot baseline with 0.0546% additional trainable parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient visual token selection and memory for multimodal LLM reasoning, fitting token pruning/eviction and MLLM topics.
papers.title: Look Back, Think Ahead: Visual Memory on Demand for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: ViMoD enables efficient multimodal reasoning by dynamically retrieving fine-grained visual evidence from a compact visual memory as reasoning needs change.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises student-generated trajectories with token-level teacher signals. Its sampled-token variant avoids the cost of full-vocabulary probabilities. Yet we find that training on fewer tokens can outperform full-token OPD, challenging the intuition that more supervision improves learning. This motivates selecting tokens by learning value. Existing disagreement-based criteria ignore probability scale: tokens assigned negligible probability by both models, termed low-low tokens, can receive large log-ratio rewards and hinder learning. We propose DIAL-OPD, a token-selection method that bridges log-probability and probability spaces by weighting reward magnitude with the logarithmic mean of teacher and student probabilities. A parameter beta controls this weighting, and the highest-scoring tokens are retained. Across 4 teacher-student pairs and 7 mathematical reasoning benchmarks, we compare DIAL-OPD with 9 baselines. Retaining only 40% of tokens, it outperforms Vanilla OPD and its full-token variants, with mean accuracy gains reaching 5.25 percentage points over Vanilla OPD, and doubles AIME25 Pass@16 from 13.33% to 26.67%. It also achieves up to an 18% relative improvement in mean accuracy over the strongest token-selection baseline at matched retention ratios. With a 4B teacher, DIAL-OPD surpasses the strongest full-token baseline using an 8B teacher at both student scales, showing that effective supervision allocation can outweigh teacher scaling. Further analysis shows that moderate beta balances suppressing low-low tokens against preserving useful disagreements. Token-level evidence reveals that DIAL-OPD filters high-reward tokens with limited reasoning value while preserving supervision critical to reasoning correctness.
authors: Anhao Zhao, Haoran Xin, Junlong Tong, Yingqi Fan, Xuan Lu, Ping Nie, Wenjie Li, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Motivation: Large log-ratio rewards from low-probability tokens assigned by both teacher and student can harm learning, so more token supervision is not always better.
Method: Scores tokens using reward magnitude weighted by the logarithmic mean of teacher and student probabilities; a parameter β controls the balance, and top-scoring tokens are retained.
Evaluation: Tested across 4 teacher–student pairs and 7 mathematical reasoning benchmarks against 9 baselines.
Results: At 40% token retention, DIAL-OPD outperforms Vanilla OPD, with mean accuracy gains up to 5.25 percentage points and AIME25 Pass@16 increasing from 13.33% to 26.67%.
Scope: Moderate β values best balance suppressing low-low tokens while preserving disagreements useful for reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Token-level selection for distillation improves efficiency and performance; fits efficient AI token selection.
papers.title: DIAL-OPD: Learning More from Fewer Tokens in On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: DIAL-OPD improves on-policy distillation by selecting tokens according to both reward magnitude and teacher–student probability scale, achieving stronger reasoning performance with only 40% of tokens.

papers.abstract: To adapt billion-parameter Vision Transformers for long-video understanding, recent methods freeze the backbone and train lightweight convolutional modules. While effective for parameter-efficient training, existing adapters do not reduce inference-time computation, leaving scalability with respect to video length largely unaddressed. Token selection can reduce attention cost by pruning redundant tokens, but it breaks the spatial grid structure required by convolutional adapters. This forces an expensive dense reconstruction, nullifying much of the potential speedup. We address this by introducing native sparse 2D convolutions, a primitive that allows these adapters, for the first time, to operate directly and efficiently on dynamically pruned token sets. We integrate this primitive into SV-TAD, an adapter framework for temporal action detection, reducing VideoMAEv2-L computation by up to 64% and achieving 2.2x faster inference, while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy on THUMOS-14 and ActivityNet-1.3. When scaled to InternVideoNext-L, our approach surpasses the previous state of the art at roughly half its computational cost. Moreover, the sparse formulation naturally supports auxiliary task tokens, which improves fine-grained assembly detection on ATTACH.
authors: Ricardo Pizarro, Roberto Valle, Jos\'e M. Buenaposada, Luis M. Bergasa, Luis Baumela
bullets: Addresses the inference-cost bottleneck of frozen ViT adapters for long-video understanding.
Introduces native sparse 2D convolutions that operate directly on dynamically pruned tokens, avoiding dense spatial reconstruction.
Reduces VideoMAEv2-L computation by up to 64% and delivers 2.2× faster inference.
Maintains state-of-the-art temporal action detection accuracy on THUMOS-14 and ActivityNet-1.3.
Scales to InternVideoNext-L with stronger performance than prior work at roughly half the computational cost; also supports auxiliary task tokens for fine-grained assembly detection.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SV-TAD, an adapter framework for temporal action detection that uses native sparse 2D convolutions to handle pruned tokens. This directly addresses token pruning/eviction for efficiency in video understanding.
papers.title: SV-TAD: Native Sparse Convs for Efficient Temporal Action Detection
papers.tldr: SV-TAD uses native sparse convolutions to make token-pruned video adapters computationally efficient without sacrificing detection accuracy.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based LLMs (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) LLMs by enabling bidirectional parallel refinement, alleviating the sequential decoding bottleneck of AR generation. However, their parallel iterative refinement mismatches AR accelerators optimized for sequential decoding and their discrete token generation differs from DiT accelerators designed for continuous denoising. Recent dLLM accelerators have explored workload-specific optimizations to reduce vocabulary processing overhead and redundant computation across denoising iterations. However, these approaches retain all tokens in parallel execution, despite varying token refinement utility and execution requirements. This paper presents DynaTE, a hardware--software co-design architecture that dynamically adapts accelerator execution to evolving token states during dLLM decoding. DynaTE first enables adaptive token execution by skipping low-utility token computation, while a dimension-reconfigurable PE array maintains high utilization under varying active-token patterns. Second, DynaTE exploits dynamic token dependencies through FLDD to refine a small number of locally dependent tokens within the current iteration, reducing the overall number of denoising iterations, while a Merge--Split--Merge dataflow hides the resulting serial overhead. Third, a streaming vocabulary engine interleaves multiple token streams from the LM head to accommodate irregular output variations caused by selective token computation and uneven vocabulary-selection demands. Evaluated on two representative dLLMs, DynaTE achieves 2.05--2.78$\times$ speedup and 2.99--3.93$\times$ higher energy efficiency over state-of-the-art dLLM accelerators, while delivering 2.55$\times$ speedup and 6.07$\times$ higher energy efficiency over Jetson AGX Orin.
authors: Minghan Jiang, Jiayi Wang, Shuaiting Li, Haibin Shen, Kejie Huang
bullets: Targets the mismatch between dLLM’s parallel iterative refinement and accelerators built for autoregressive or continuous-denoising workloads.
Skips low-utility token computation and uses a dimension-reconfigurable processing-element array to sustain utilization across changing active-token patterns.
Uses FLDD to refine locally dependent tokens within an iteration, reducing denoising iterations; Merge–Split–Merge hides added serial overhead.
Adds a streaming vocabulary engine to handle irregular outputs from selective token execution.
On two representative dLLMs, achieves 2.05–2.78× speedup and 2.99–3.93× energy-efficiency improvement over prior dLLM accelerators.
papers.selection_reason: Hardware-software co-design for dynamic token execution in diffusion LLMs, reducing computation and energy through selective token skipping.
papers.title: DynaTE: Accelerating Diffusion LLMs via Dynamic Token Execution
papers.tldr: DynaTE accelerates diffusion LLM decoding by dynamically computing only useful tokens and exploiting their dependencies through a hardware–software co-designed architecture.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities but suffer from substantial computational overhead, as vision tokens dominate the input sequence. This motivates vision token compression as a key direction to alleviate the burden. However, with the emergence of hybrid architectures incorporating linear attention (\eg, Qwen3.5), prior methods designed for softmax attention struggle to generalize. Our analysis reveals that both attention- and similarity-based approaches suffer notable performance degradation, underscoring the urgent need for compression methods tailored to this regime. To this end, we propose \textbf{V-CoLA}, an efficient training-free token compression framework specifically designed for linear attention. V-CoLA introduces a novel \textit{uniqueness-aware importance criterion} for identifying critical vision tokens, coupled with an \textit{adaptive token merging strategy} that performs compression. All components are optimized at the implementation level to remain compatible with the chunk-wise parallelism of linear attention, ensuring strong practical value. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of V-CoLA: it achieves 99.5\% of the original performance with only 50.0\% of vision tokens, and over 88.0\% with as few as 12.5\%, while delivering a 1.86$\times$ to 6.15$\times$ prefill speedup.
authors: Hao Jiang, Yiru Mao, Tianpeng Bu, Hao Zhou, Hongtao Duan, Wang Jing, Bowen Xu, Xin Chen, Lulu Hu, Bin Yang, Yongliang Tao, Minying Zhang
bullets: Targets the computational burden caused by vision tokens in VLMs, especially hybrid models using linear attention.
Uses a uniqueness-aware importance criterion to identify critical vision tokens.
Applies adaptive token merging with implementation optimized for linear-attention chunk-wise parallelism.
Retains 99.5% of original performance with 50.0% of vision tokens and over 88.0% with 12.5%.
Achieves reported prefill speedups of 1.86×–6.15× across multiple benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free vision token compression for linear-attention VLMs; direct fit to token pruning/eviction.
papers.title: V-CoLA: Vision Token Compression with Linear Attention
